docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 8 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Kāvya Kalpalatā: Literature and Poetics. It is a first map of the literatures of the Indian subcontinent and of the Indian theory of literature (alaṅkāraśāstra), written for students of Indian studies and comparative literature, for teachers preparing a course, and for general readers who want a reliable account in one volume. It assumes no knowledge of the languages concerned.

The book follows the literatures roughly in historical order: Vedic, epic and Sanskrit court poetry, drama and prose (Chapters 2–4); the Pali, Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa literatures of the same centuries (Chapter 5); the theory of literature that grew up around them (Chapter 6); classical Tamil, fable and maxim, and bhakti and Sufi poetry (Chapters 7–9); the regional literatures (Chapters 10–11); Persian and Urdu (Chapter 12); and the modern period (Chapter 13). Each chapter can be read on its own, and cross-references lead to the place where a poet or work receives its main treatment. The introduction (Chapter 1) explains the ideas of kāvya, the poet and the reader, and sets out the languages and periods.

Verses are quoted in transliteration with a close translation, and only where the wording and the reference could be checked. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such. Each chapter ends with suggestions for further reading, and a glossary and a chronology close the book. No survey of this size can be complete: readers will want to go on to the editions and translations cited, and quotations used for scholarly purposes should be checked against a critical edition.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Kāvya and the Literatures of India
docs.text: kāvyaṃ yaśase ’rthakṛte vyavahāravide śivetarakṣataye | sadyaḥ paranirvṛtaye kāntāsammitatayopadeśayuje || Poetry is for fame, for profit, for knowledge of the ways of the world, for warding off misfortune, for immediate and supreme delight, and for instruction offered in the manner of a beloved. — Mammaṭa, Kāvyaprakāśa 1.2

docs.title: 1.1 A Multilingual Literary Inheritance
docs.text:
The literatures of the Indian subcontinent form one of the longest-documented literary histories in the world. Their earliest layer, the hymns of the Ṛgveda, is usually dated to c. 1500–1200 BCE; their latest layer is being written today in more than twenty major languages. Between these lie the Sanskrit epics and court poetry, the Tamil anthologies of love and war, the Pali and Prakrit literatures of Buddhist and Jain communities, the devotional songs of the bhakti and Sufi poets, the Persian and Urdu literature of the Indo-Islamic courts, and the novels, short stories and free verse of the modern period.

The title of this volume borrows the image of the kalpalatā, the wish-granting creeper of Indian myth, for this tradition. The image should not mislead: Indian literature was never a single organism. It was produced by many communities, in many languages, for different audiences and purposes, and it contains as much argument, satire and dissent as it does praise and devotion. What gives it a recognisable shape is not uniformity but a set of shared resources — the epic narratives, a common stock of images and conventions, and above all a long tradition of reflection on what poetry is and how it works.

Sheldon Pollock has described the first millennium CE as the age of a “Sanskrit cosmopolis”, in which Sanskrit served as the language of political and literary expression from Afghanistan to Java, followed in the second millennium by a “vernacular millennium” in which regional languages were consciously shaped into literary languages, often on Sanskrit models (Pollock 2006). The essays in Pollock (2003) trace this process language by language. The model has been debated — Tamil, for example, had an independent classical literature centuries before the vernacular turn — but it usefully reminds us that literary languages are made, not simply inherited.

Indian literary culture was also, for most of its history, multilingual in the life of individual writers. A poet in a medieval court might compose in Sanskrit for one audience, in Prakrit or Apabhraṃśa for another and in the regional language for a third; Vidyāpati wrote in Sanskrit, Avahaṭṭha and Maithili, Hemacandra in Sanskrit and Prakrit, Amīr Khusrau in Persian and Hindavi, Ghālib in Persian and Urdu, and Tagore in Bengali and English. Languages were matched to genres and occasions — Sanskrit for learned theory and court epic, Prakrit for love lyric, the regional languages for devotion and narrative, Persian for history and administration under the sultanates and the Mughals. Reading Indian literature language by language, as modern histories usually do, can obscure this interplay.

docs.title: 1.2 Defining Kāvya
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word kāvya, “the work of a poet (kavi)”, refers to literature composed with deliberate artistry. It is narrower than “literature” (it excludes, for instance, technical treatises and most scripture) but broader than “poetry”, since it includes artistic prose (gadya), mixed prose and verse (campū) and drama (dṛśya kāvya or rūpaka). The theorists of poetics (ālaṅkārikas) offered a series of definitions, each emphasising a different element.

Bhāmaha, Kāvyālaṅkāra 1.16

śabdārthau sahitau kāvyaṃ gadyaṃ padyaṃ ca tad dvidhā Poetry is word and meaning together; it is of two kinds, prose and verse.

Daṇḍin, Kāvyādarśa 1.10

śarīraṃ tāvad iṣṭārthavyavacchinnā padāvalī Its body is a string of words marked off by a desired meaning.

Mammaṭa, Kāvyaprakāśa 1.4

tad adoṣau śabdārthau saguṇāv analaṅkṛtī punaḥ kvāpi Poetry is word and meaning free from faults, possessed of excellences, and sometimes even without (obvious) ornaments.

Viśvanātha, Sāhityadarpaṇa 1.3

vākyaṃ rasātmakaṃ kāvyam Poetry is a sentence whose soul is rasa.

The last major theorist, Jagannātha (seventeenth century), defined poetry as “language that expresses a delightful meaning” (ramaṇīyārthapratipādakaḥ śabdaḥ kāvyam; on him see Section 6.8). Read in sequence, these definitions trace the history of the discipline itself: from the early concern with the union of sound and sense and the avoidance of faults, to the later conviction that the essence of poetry lies in its emotional and suggestive power. The debate is discussed in Chapter 6; good surveys are De (1960) and Gerow (1977).

docs.title: 1.3 The Purposes of Kāvya
docs.text:
Mammaṭa’s verse quoted at the head of this chapter lists six purposes (prayojana) of poetry. His own commentary illustrates each: fame, as Kālidāsa won it; wealth, as Dhāvaka is said to have received from King Śrī Harṣa; knowledge of proper conduct towards kings and others; protection from misfortune, as Mayūra is said to have been cured by his hymn to the Sun; the immediate delight of the reader, which Mammaṭa calls the chief purpose of all; and instruction “in the manner of a beloved” (kāntāsammita). The last phrase rests on a well-known triad: scripture commands like a master (prabhusammita), history and legend advise like a friend (suhṛtsammita), and poetry persuades as a beloved does, by delighting.

The idea that aesthetic delight is a kind of “tasting” close to the bliss of liberation was developed by Abhinavagupta, and later formulated by Viśvanātha, who called the experience of rasa “a twin of the tasting of brahman” (brahmāsvādasahodara, Sāhityadarpaṇa 3.2). It should be remembered that this is a claim of theorists writing within particular philosophical schools, not a description of how every reader in India experienced poetry.

docs.title: 1.4 The Poet: Talent, Learning and Practice
docs.text:
Indian theory asked what makes a poet. Daṇḍin answered with a famous triad:

Daṇḍin, Kāvyādarśa 1.103

naisargikī ca pratibhā śrutaṃ ca bahunirmalam | amandaś cābhiyogo ’syāḥ kāraṇaṃ kāvyasampadaḥ || Inborn imagination, extensive and accurate learning, and unremitting application are the cause of excellence in poetry.

Mammaṭa (Kāvyaprakāśa 1.3) restated the triad as śakti (innate capacity), nipuṇatā (skill gained by studying the world, the sciences and earlier poetry) and abhyāsa (practice under the guidance of those who understand poetry), insisting that the three together, not separately, are the cause of poetry. Bhāmaha had already said that poetry arises “only rarely, in someone gifted with imagination” (Kāvyālaṅkāra 1.5).

The fullest account of the poet’s formation is the Kāvyamīmāṃsā of Rājaśekhara (early tenth century), a handbook for the working poet (Dalal and Anantakrishna Shastry 1916). Rājaśekhara distinguishes two kinds of pratibhā: the “creative” (kārayitrī) imagination of the poet and the “appreciative” (bhāvayitrī) imagination of the critic or connoisseur. He discusses the subjects a poet must study, the daily routine of a poet, the legitimate and illegitimate borrowing of other poets’ ideas, and the geography a poet should know. His remark that his wife Avantisundarī held views on poetics worth citing is a rare glimpse of a woman’s participation in this learned culture.

docs.title: 1.5 The Sahṛdaya: The Responsive Reader
docs.text:
From the ninth century onwards Indian theory gave great weight to the reader or spectator, the sahṛdaya (“one whose heart is in tune”). In his Locana commentary on the Dhvanyāloka, Abhinavagupta describes sahṛdayas as those whose minds have become like a clear mirror through constant familiarity with poetry, so that they are able to identify with what is described (Ingalls et al. 1990). On this view rasa is realised only in the experience of such a reader; the text supplies the conditions, the reader completes the work.

Scholarly Note: Generalisation

The concept of sādhāraṇīkaraṇa (“making common” or “generalisation”), associated with Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka and developed by Abhinavagupta, explains how an emotion depicted in a work becomes an aesthetic experience. When we watch Rāma grieve for Sītā we do not feel Rāma’s private grief, nor do we feel a grief of our own; the emotion is freed from its ties to particular persons, times and places and is “tasted” as rasa. Pollock’s A Rasa Reader translates the key texts of this debate (Pollock 2016).

docs.title: 1.6 Oral Performance and the Manuscript
docs.text:
Much Indian literature was composed for performance and transmitted orally. The Vedic hymns were preserved for many centuries by elaborate recitation techniques (the pāṭhas) before they were written down, and the epics, the Tamil songs and the devotional poetry of later centuries all lived primarily in recitation and song. Classical Sanskrit poetry, too, was meant to be heard: metre, sound-pattern and the recitation of verses in courtly gatherings were central to its appreciation.

Writing nevertheless played a large role from early on. The inscriptions of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest securely dated Indian writing, and from the early centuries CE onwards literary works circulated in manuscripts — on palm leaf in the south and east, on birch bark in Kashmir and the north-west, and later on paper. The great inscriptions of the classical period, such as Hariṣeṇa’s Allahabad praise-poem for Samudragupta (fourth century) or the Aihole inscription of Ravikīrti (634 CE), are themselves accomplished pieces of kāvya. The elaborate prose of Subandhu and Bāṇa presupposes readers who could pore over a written text (Figures 1.1 and 1.2).

Figure 1.1. Bundles of palm-leaf manuscripts held between wooden boards and tied with cords, in a museum display (Batticaloa Museum, Sri Lanka). Palm-leaf books were made in this way across South Asia: the leaves were strung on cords through holes and protected by wooden boards. Photo: Anton Croos, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 1.2. A painted wooden cover for a palm-leaf manuscript, Kathmandu Valley, c. twelfth century (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Boards of this kind protected the leaves of palm-leaf books. This one is illustrated with scenes from Kālidāsa’s Śakuntalā: two seated couples among trees, with a pair of deer, in the forest setting of the play’s hermitage (on the play see Section 3.6.3). Painted manuscript cover, Nepal, c. 12th century, Metropolitan Museum of Art; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 1.6.1 Literature on Stone: Inscriptions and Praśasti
docs.text: Some of the earliest dated Sanskrit kāvya survives not in manuscripts but on stone and copper. Royal inscriptions recording victories, donations and the building of temples were often composed by court poets as praśasti (“praise”), with genealogies of the dynasty in ornate verse. The Junāgaḍh rock inscription of the Śaka ruler Rudradāman (c. 150 CE), in elaborate Sanskrit prose, is the earliest long inscription in classical Sanskrit and already uses the long compounds and figures of later prose kāvya. Hariṣeṇa’s praise of Samudragupta on the Allahabad pillar mixes prose and verse; Ravikīrti’s Aihole inscription (634 CE) praises the Cāḷukya king Pulakeśin II and names Kālidāsa and Bhāravi; and thousands of later inscriptions in Sanskrit and the regional languages, especially in South India, contain verse of real literary quality. Because they are dated and unchanged by copying, inscriptions are among the most reliable evidence for the history of literary style and for the early development of regional literary languages such as Kannada, Telugu and Tamil.

docs.title: 1.7 The Classification of Kāvya
docs.text:
The theorists divided literature first into what is heard or read (śravya) and what is seen performed (dṛśya). Heard literature is subdivided by form into verse (from the long court epic to the single stanza), prose and mixed forms; seen literature into the ten major types of drama (rūpaka) described in the Nāṭyaśāstra and a varying number of minor types (uparūpaka) added by later writers. Figure 1.3 gives a simplified scheme; the genres themselves are treated in Chapters 2–4.

Figure 1.3. A simplified classification of kāvya in Sanskrit theory. The muktaka is the single self-contained stanza, collected in centuries (śataka) and anthologies. Classifications differed between authors; the scheme is illustrative only.

Such dates are necessarily rough: inscriptions often precede literary texts by centuries, and what counts as the “first” work of a language is frequently disputed. docs.title: 1.9 A Chronological Outline
docs.text:
Any periodisation of so long and varied a history is a convenience. Table 1.2 gives the outline used in this volume.

Table 1.2. A chronological outline of Indian literary history Period Approximate dates Major developments Vedic c. 1500–500 BCE Ṛgveda and later Vedic texts; Brāhmaṇas; early Upaniṣads Epic and early classical c. 400 BCE–400 CE Composition and growth of the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa; Pali canon; Aśvaghoṣa; Tamil Caṅkam poems; Hāla’s anthology; the Nāṭyaśāstra Classical c. 400–1100 CE Kālidāsa, Bhāravi, Māgha, Bāṇa, Bhavabhūti; Tamil bhakti hymns; theory from Bhāmaha to Abhinavagupta; Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa narrative; first Kannada and Telugu classics Late classical and early regional c. 1100–1500 CE Jayadeva; Kalhaṇa; Śrīharṣa; Vīraśaiva vacanas; Marathi and Kashmiri saint-poets; Amīr Khusrau; Kabīr Early modern c. 1500–1800 CE Tulsīdās, Sūrdās, Mīrā; Eḻuttacchaṉ; Telugu prabandha; Haridāsas; Punjabi and Sindhi Sufi poetry; Urdu ghazal; Jagannātha Modern c. 1800–present Prose fiction and print culture; Bankim, Tagore, Premchand, Bharati, Kumaran Asan; Urdu modernism; Dalit and women’s writing; writing in English

The order of the chapters follows this outline only loosely. The Sanskrit genres come first because they supplied the models and the theory against which much later writing defined itself; the Pali and Prakrit literatures, which are as old as classical Sanskrit or older, follow at once, before the theory that drew many of its examples from them.

Two cautions apply. First, the traditional dates found in many popular accounts — for example, placing the epics in the fourth millennium BCE or Kālidāsa in the first century BCE — are not supported by historical evidence, and the ranges above follow mainstream scholarship. Second, the epics were not composed at a single moment: the Mahābhārata grew over several centuries, and the critical edition prepared at Pune (about 75,000 verses) is considerably shorter than the traditional figure of 100,000 verses.

docs.title: 1.10 Patronage and Its Alternatives
docs.text:
Royal patronage shaped much of Indian literature. Kings rewarded poets, held literary assemblies and in several cases were poets themselves. Table 1.3 lists some of the best-documented literary courts.

Table 1.3. Some major literary courts Court Period Region Poets and scholars associated Pāṇḍya, Cōḻa and Cēra chiefs c. 1st–3rd c. CE Tamil country Caṅkam bards (as recorded in the poems) Gupta 4th–6th c. CE North India Kālidāsa (probably); Hariṣeṇa Harṣa of Kanauj 7th c. CE North India Bāṇa, Mayūra; Harṣa himself as dramatist Rāṣṭrakūṭa 8th–10th c. CE Deccan Nṛpatuṅga (Kavirājamārga); Ponna; Puṣpadanta Vemulavāḍa and Kalyāṇa Cāḷukyas 10th–12th c. CE Karnataka Pampa; Ranna; Bilhaṇa Kashmir 9th–12th c. CE Kashmir Ānandavardhana (under Avantivarman); Kṣemendra; Kalhaṇa Paramāra Bhoja 11th c. CE Malwa Bhoja’s own works on poetics Vijayanagara 14th–16th c. CE South India Kṛṣṇadevarāya and the Telugu court poets Mughal and Deccan sultanates 16th–18th c. CE North India, Deccan Persian poets; Dakhni and Urdu poets; Rahīm

Alongside the courts there was always literature produced elsewhere: in monasteries and temples, in merchant and artisan communities, and in the songs of wandering devotees. Many of the most loved Indian poets — Kabīr the weaver, Ravidās the leather-worker, Tukārām the petty trader, Cokhāmeḷā the Mahar — composed outside or against courtly culture. Their poetry was carried by communities of singers rather than by patrons, and it often criticised the caste hierarchy that courtly literature took for granted (see Chapter 9).

docs.title: 1.11 The Social Life of Poetry
docs.text:
Classical Sanskrit poetry lived in gatherings. The Kāmasūtra describes the cultivated man-about-town (nāgaraka) attending literary salons (goṣṭhī) where poems were recited and discussed, and lists among the arts expected of an accomplished person the completion of a verse from a given line, the composition of riddles and the recitation of poetry. Rājaśekhara’s Kāvyamīmāṃsā describes royal assemblies in which poets were examined and honoured, and recommends that a king hold literary gatherings and reward the best poets. A favourite exercise was samasyāpūraṇa, “completing the problem”: the poet was given a final line, often deliberately paradoxical, and had to compose a stanza that made it meaningful. Many verses in the anthologies probably originated in such contests.

Legends grew around these gatherings. The Bhojaprabandha of Ballāla (sixteenth century) imagines the court of the eleventh-century king Bhoja of Dhārā as a place where Kālidāsa, Bhavabhūti, Daṇḍin and other poets of different centuries met and competed; the stories are delightful but entirely unhistorical. Tamil tradition similarly imagined the Caṅkam academies, and Telugu tradition the “eight elephants” of Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s court. Such legends tell us less about history than about how later readers imagined the ideal literary culture: a court where learning and wit were prized and poets were rewarded.

Beyond the courts, poetry was performed by professional reciters and storytellers. The epics were recited by bards (sūta, kathaka) and later by temple storytellers in the regional languages; the Tamil pāṇar and viṟaliyar (male and female bards) sang the praises of chiefs; and in the second millennium the kathā and kīrtan performances of religious storytellers, combining recitation, song and commentary, brought the epics, the Purāṇas and the poetry of the saints to audiences of every social level.

docs.title: 1.12 Literature and Performance
docs.text: Indian literature was rarely a purely textual phenomenon. The Nāṭyaśāstra treats poetry, music, dance and stagecraft as aspects of one art of theatre (nāṭya); devotional poetry was, and is, sung; and regional theatre forms such as Kathakaḷi, Yakṣagāna, Bhavāī and Nauṭaṅkī bring literary narrative to life in performance. The theatre traditions themselves are treated in Volume 9 of this series, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya; here they appear where they bear on literary history.

docs.title: 1.13 Indian Literature beyond India
docs.text: Indian literature never stayed within the subcontinent. Buddhist monks carried Sanskrit and Pali texts to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Tibet, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia, where they were translated and became the foundation of new literatures; much Indian Buddhist literature, including the complete Buddhacarita, survives only in such translations. In Southeast Asia, Sanskrit inscriptions of high literary quality were composed from about the fifth century onwards (in Borneo and Java, and soon afterwards in Cambodia), and the epics were reshaped into local classics: the Old Javanese kakawin, the Khmer Reamker, the Thai Ramakien and the shadow-puppet repertoire of Java and Bali. Westward, the Pañcatantra travelled through Persian and Arabic into Europe (Chapter 8). In each case the texts were not simply copied but adapted to new languages, religions and audiences, so that the study of Indian literature leads naturally into the literary history of much of Asia.

docs.title: 1.14 Comparative Perspectives
docs.text: Comparisons between Indian and European literary theory have been popular since the nineteenth century. Some contrasts are real: Indian theory took drama rather than epic as its model of literature, centred its account on the audience’s experience (rasa) rather than on imitation (mimesis), and developed an unusually detailed analysis of implicature and suggestion (dhvani). Other contrasts are overdrawn. It is often said that Sanskrit drama “had no tragedy”; it is truer to say that theorists prescribed an auspicious ending for the major dramatic form and forbade the showing of death on stage, while poets such as Bhāsa (Chapter 3) and Bhavabhūti explored suffering with great seriousness. Comparison is most useful when it attends to such specifics rather than to large claims about national “essences”.

docs.title: 1.16 How to Use This Volume
docs.text: The chapters that follow can be read in sequence or separately. Chapters 2 to 4 treat Vedic and epic poetry and the Sanskrit court literature of verse, drama and prose; Chapter 5 turns to the Pali, Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa literatures of the same centuries; and Chapter 6 sets out the theory of literature built upon both. Chapters 7 to 9 treat classical Tamil, wisdom literature and devotional poetry; Chapters 10 and 11 survey the regional literatures; Chapter 12 treats Persian literature in India and the Urdu literature that grew from it; and Chapter 13 follows the themes that cross all the languages in the modern period. A poet or work discussed in several chapters receives its main treatment in one of them, and cross-references lead there from the others. Each chapter ends with suggestions for further reading drawn from the select bibliography. A glossary of technical terms and a chronology of the principal works and authors are provided at the end of the book. Where quotations are given, the original is printed in transliteration with a literal translation, so that readers without the languages can see something of the form as well as the sense; where a work could not be quoted reliably, it is described rather than quoted.

docs.title: 1.17 A Note on Transliteration and Sources
docs.text: Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST); Tamil words follow the conventions of the Tamil Lexicon; for modern languages common anglicised spellings are used for personal names where these are standard (Tagore, Premchand). Verses are quoted only where the wording and reference have been checked; where a text is described rather than quoted, readers are referred to standard translations. Warder’s multi-volume Indian Kāvya Literature remains the most detailed history of the classical literature (Warder 1972–2011); useful one-volume histories are Keith (1928) and Lienhard (1984), and Winternitz (1927) covers religious as well as secular literature.

docs.title: 1.18 How We Know These Texts
docs.text: Readers of a survey such as this one should be aware how much of what we know about early Indian literature depends on fragile chains of transmission. Very few literary manuscripts older than about the twelfth century survive, because palm leaf and birch bark decay quickly in the Indian climate; texts survived because they were copied again and again, usually every few generations. Each copying introduced variants, and popular works accumulated additions. The result is that most classical works exist in several recensions — regional versions that differ in wording, in the order of verses, and sometimes in whole episodes. Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala, for instance, survives in Bengali, Devanāgarī, Kashmiri and South Indian recensions of differing length; Hāla’s Prakrit anthology and Bhartṛhari’s śatakas survive in recensions that share only part of their contents.

docs.title: 1.18.1 Commentaries
docs.text: The Indian tradition met this problem with the commentary. Most classical poems were read with a commentary that glossed difficult words, resolved compounds, identified figures of speech and explained allusions. The commentaries of Mallinātha (fourteenth–fifteenth century) on the five great mahākāvyas and the Meghadūta became so authoritative that later readers knew these poems largely through his readings. Commentators also preserved alternative readings and sometimes discussed the authenticity of verses. For the history of interpretation they are invaluable; for the original form of a text they are witnesses to be weighed, not final authorities.

docs.title: 1.18.2 Critical Editions
docs.text:
From the nineteenth century onwards, scholars in India and Europe began to prepare critical editions, comparing manuscripts in order to reconstruct the earliest recoverable form of a text and to record its variants. The greatest such project was the critical edition of the Mahābhārata prepared at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune between 1919 and 1966, followed by the Baroda critical edition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. Both showed how much these texts had grown in transmission: passages familiar from popular versions were often found only in some manuscripts and were relegated to appendices. In Tamil, the editorial work of C. W. Tāmōtaram Piḷḷai and U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries rescued the classical anthologies and epics from manuscripts that were on the point of disappearing (Chapter 7).

Critical editions do not settle every question. For works composed and transmitted orally, such as devotional song, there may never have been a single original, and the variety of recensions is part of the work’s life. Kabīr, Sūrdās and Mīrā are known through collections compiled long after their deaths, which differ widely and which include many poems composed by later singers in their names (Chapter 9). The quotations in this volume follow standard editions; readers using them for scholarly purposes should consult the critical apparatus of those editions.

docs.title: 1.18.3 Anthologies and Lost Works
docs.text: Much of Indian literature is lost. Guṇāḍhya’s Bṛhatkathā, all but fragments of two of the five Tamil “great epics”, most of the plays named by early theorists, and the works of many poets known only through quotations have not survived. The great anthologies (Chapter 8) and the illustrative verses quoted by theorists preserve thousands of stanzas from works otherwise lost, and some poets — among them several women poets of Sanskrit — are known only from such quotations. Any history of the literature is therefore a history of what happened to survive, and the picture may be distorted in ways we cannot fully measure.

docs.title: 1.19 Writing the History of Indian Literature
docs.text:
The idea of a history of “Indian literature” is itself modern. Pre-modern India had rich traditions of literary criticism, anthologies, commentaries and stories about poets — the Jain prabandha collections, the hagiographies of the saints, the legends of the Caṅkam academies — but not narrative histories of literature in the European sense. The first such histories were written by European scholars in the nineteenth century: Albrecht Weber’s lectures on the history of Indian literature (1852; English translation 1878) and, above all, Moriz Winternitz’s Geschichte der indischen Litteratur (1904–1920), whose English translation is still useful (Winternitz 1927). These works concentrated on Sanskrit and on religious texts, and treated the literatures of the regional languages, if at all, as a late appendix.

From the late nineteenth century Indian scholars wrote histories of their own languages, often as part of a movement of linguistic and regional self-assertion. Ramchandra Shukla’s history of Hindi literature (1929), whose periodisation is still in use (Chapter 11), is one example among many. Such histories shaped the canons taught in schools and universities; they also tended to project modern linguistic boundaries back into the past, giving a single language and community a continuous history that the multilingual reality of earlier centuries does not always support.

After independence the Sahitya Akademi set out to present Indian literature as a whole, through its awards in many languages, its translation programme and its six-volume Encyclopaedia of Indian Literature (Datta 1987). Whether there is an “Indian literature” in the singular, rather than many literatures that happen to share a state, has been much debated. Aijaz Ahmad argued that the category is hard to sustain, since few readers have access to more than a handful of its languages and much of its apparent unity is produced through English translation and national institutions (Ahmad 1992). Others, such as Sisir Kumar Das, whose comparative history of modern Indian literatures treats the major languages together (Das 1991), have stressed the shared forms, themes and histories that justify a unified account. More recently Sheldon Pollock and his collaborators have proposed to study “literary cultures” — the practices of writing, reading and performance in particular places and times — rather than national literatures (Pollock 2003). This volume follows that approach as far as a survey can: it treats the literatures of India as a family of interrelated traditions, each with its own history.

docs.title: 1.20 Who Wrote, Who Read
docs.text:
It is easy to speak of “Indian literature” as if it belonged equally to everyone in the subcontinent. Historically it did not. Sanskrit literary education was, for most of its history, restricted in principle to men of the upper varṇas, and the overwhelming majority of known Sanskrit poets and theorists were brahmin or royal men. The theorists’ ideal reader, the sahṛdaya, presupposed years of training in grammar and poetics. Women appear in Sanskrit literature far more often as subjects than as authors, and the Prakrit spoken by women on the Sanskrit stage marks their exclusion from the learned language (Chapter 3).

Other literary communities had different boundaries. Buddhist and Jain monasteries trained monks and nuns of varied social origins and wrote for lay audiences; the Therīgāthā preserves the voices of nuns, and Jain narrative addressed merchants and householders (Chapter 5). Classical Tamil poetry names poets from many walks of life, including some thirty women (Chapter 7). The devotional traditions of the second millennium drew poets from artisan, peasant and untouchable castes and from among women, and were sung to mixed audiences in temples, pilgrimages and village gatherings (Chapter 9). Courtesans and professional women performers were trained in poetry and music and composed songs, though their work was seldom recorded under their own names. In the modern period, print and schooling vastly widened the circle of readers and writers, and Dalit and women’s writing have challenged the assumptions of the older canons (Chapter 13).

Keeping these differences in view does not diminish the achievements of classical literature. It helps us to read it more accurately — to notice whose experience a text records and whose it leaves out — and to value the many traditions that existed beside the courtly one.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Warder (1972–2011): the most detailed history of classical kāvya, with full discussion of authors and dates.

  • Keith (1928), Dasgupta and De (1947) and Lienhard (1984): older and newer one-volume histories of classical literature.

  • Winternitz (1927): a survey covering Vedic, epic, Buddhist, Jain and scientific literature as well as kāvya.

  • Pollock (2003) and Pollock (2006): literary history across languages; the “Sanskrit cosmopolis” and the vernacular millennium.

  • Gerow (1977) and De (1960): introductions to Sanskrit poetics.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Sanskrit Poetry from the Veda to the Mahākāvya
docs.text: sargabandho mahākāvyam ucyate tasya lakṣaṇam | āśīr namaskriyā vastunirdeśo vāpi tanmukham || A composition in cantos is called a mahākāvya; its definition is (as follows). It opens with a blessing, a salutation, or an indication of the subject. — Daṇḍin, Kāvyādarśa 1.14

docs.title: 2.1 Before Kāvya: Vedic and Epic Poetry
docs.text: The Sanskrit theorists did not count the Veda as kāvya. For them it was revelation (śruti), which commands like a master rather than delighting like a beloved (Section 1.3), and for the Mīmāṃsā philosophers it had no human author at all. The epics stood nearer: the Rāmāyaṇa was the “first poem”, the Mahābhārata a work of history and instruction. Yet both bodies of text are poetry by any modern measure, and much of the later literature grew out of them. Their religious content, transmission and history are the subject of Volumes 1 and 2 (Veda Prakāśa and Upaniṣad Dīpikā) and Volume 7 (Itihāsa–Purāṇa) of this series; this section considers them only as poetry.

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Ṛgveda as Poetry
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) is a collection of 1,028 hymns (sūkta) in ten books (maṇḍala), composed by families of poets over several centuries and preserved by oral recitation of extraordinary exactness. Its poets called themselves kavi and ṛṣi, “seers”, and they spoke of their work as a craft: a hymn is fashioned as a carpenter fashions a chariot, polished and offered to the gods in competition with the hymns of rival poets. Stephanie Jamison and Joel Brereton, whose translation is now standard, stress how self-conscious this art is, with its riddles, its play on the sounds and forms of words, its ring compositions that return at the end to the words of the beginning, and its habit of placing a hidden or paradoxical statement at the centre of a hymn (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Its metres, counted by syllables, are the ancestors of the classical ones: the three-line gāyatrī of eight syllables to the line, and the four-line triṣṭubh and jagatī of eleven and twelve, from which the indravajrā and its relatives later developed.

Most hymns praise and invoke gods such as Agni, Indra and Soma in a dense language of epithet and allusion. Some are poetry of a kind that later readers could recognise at once. The hymns to Dawn (Uṣas) describe the goddess as a young woman uncovering her breast, waking all creatures and ageing the lives of men as she returns each day. A group of dialogue hymns are small dramas: Purūravas pleads with the nymph Urvaśī, who has left him, to return (10.95), a story that Kālidāsa would dramatise (Section 3.6); Yamī urges her twin brother Yama to lie with her and is refused (10.10); the bitch Saramā, messenger of the gods, confronts the Paṇis who have hidden away the cows and scorns their offer to make her their sister (10.108); and the neglected wife Lopāmudrā reproaches the ascetic Agastya (1.179). The gambler’s lament (10.34) is the monologue of a man ruined by the dice, who sees his wife abandoned and his mother grieving and still cannot keep away from the gaming hall. The riddle hymn (1.164) asks questions about the year, speech and the cosmos, and includes its famous reflection on the one reality that the poets call by many names (1.164.46); the hymn of creation (10.129) ends by doubting whether even the highest overseer knows how the world began. There are humorous and secular pieces too, such as the hymn comparing the croaking of frogs at the start of the rains to brahmins chanting at a ritual (7.103), and the hymn to the lady of the forest, Araṇyānī (10.146).

The later Vedic texts carried this art into new forms. The Atharvaveda contains charms for love, healing and the defeat of rivals as well as the long hymn to the Earth (12.1); the Brāhmaṇas tell, in plain and vigorous prose, the stories that explain the rites, among them a prose version of the tale of Purūravas and Urvaśī (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1); and the early Upaniṣads frame their teaching in dialogues and narratives — the boy Naciketas questioning Death, the sage Yājñavalkya debating at the court of Janaka and instructing his wife Maitreyī — that are among the finest prose of ancient India. The epic śloka itself grew out of the Vedic anuṣṭubh.

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Epics as Poetry
docs.text:
The two Sanskrit epics are oral-derived poetry on a vast scale. The Mahābhārata has about 75,000 verses in the Pune critical edition (Section 1.9), in eighteen books; the Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki nearly 19,000 in the Baroda edition, in seven books, against a traditional figure of 24,000. Both were composed and expanded over several centuries, broadly between about 400 BCE and 400 CE, and most scholars regard the first and last books of the Rāmāyaṇa as later additions to a five-book core. Both are composed almost entirely in the śloka, with longer metres for some speeches and set pieces, and both use a large stock of repeated formulas — epithets, phrases for beginning and ending speeches, descriptions of battle — of the kind that oral poets everywhere employ. John Brockington’s The Sanskrit Epics is the standard account of their language, metre and growth (Brockington 1998).

The poetic character of the two works differs. The Mahābhārata is a story inside a story: the bard Ugraśravas tells the sages of the Naimiṣa forest how Vaiśampāyana told King Janamejaya the tale that Vyāsa composed, and within this frame characters tell further tales, so that whole poems — the stories of Nala and Damayantī, of Sāvitrī who wins back her husband from Death, of Śakuntalā, and the dialogue of the Bhagavadgītā — are embedded in the narrative. Its greatest poetry is often in speech: Draupadī’s questions in the assembly hall, the arguments of Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira, and the laments of Gāndhārī and the women of the Kurus over the dead on the battlefield in the eleventh book. The Rāmāyaṇa is more unified, and in its descriptive passages it already shows the programme of the later court epic: the city of Ayodhyā, the forest of Daṇḍaka, the rainy season that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa wait out at Kiṣkindhā while Rāma grieves for Sītā, and Hanumān’s night journey through Laṅkā and the women’s quarters of Rāvaṇa’s palace in the fifth book. Robert Goldman and his collaborators’ translation of the critical edition brings out these qualities (Goldman 1984).

docs.title: 2.1.3 The First Poem
docs.text:
The Sanskrit tradition regarded Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa as the “first poem” (ādikāvya) and its author as the “first poet” (ādikavi). The second chapter of the Rāmāyaṇa tells how Vālmīki, walking by the river Tamasā, saw a hunter kill one of a pair of mating krauñca birds, and in his grief and anger uttered a curse that came out, to his own surprise, in a perfectly measured verse:

Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.14 (critical edition)

mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṃ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ | yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam || Hunter, may you never find rest for endless years, since you killed one of this pair of krauñcas, lost in love.

Vālmīki calls the new metre śloka because it was born of grief (śoka), and Brahmā then commands him to tell the story of Rāma in it. The legend makes poetry the transformation of grief into ordered speech, and Ānandavardhana drew on it to argue that the dominant rasa of the Rāmāyaṇa is pathos (karuṇa), while that of the Mahābhārata, with its vision of the futility of war, is the tranquil (śānta). The epics became the inexhaustible source of plots for later poets and dramatists in every Indian language.

docs.title: 2.2 The Genre of Mahākāvya
docs.text:
The mahākāvya (“great poem”), often called the Sanskrit court epic, is a long narrative poem in cantos (sarga) on an elevated theme, composed in a range of metres and rich in description and figurative language. It was the most prestigious genre of classical Sanskrit poetry and served as the proving ground of poetic ambition for more than a millennium.

Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa (c. 700 CE) gives the classic definition (1.14–19). The poem should open with a blessing, a salutation or a statement of the subject; its story should be drawn from the epics or another true account; its hero should be clever and noble; it should be adorned with descriptions; it should not be too condensed, should be full of rasa and emotion, and should have cantos of moderate length composed in pleasing metres, each canto ending in a different metre. The list of descriptions Daṇḍin expects is given in Table 2.1; in practice no poem contained them all, and Daṇḍin himself allows that a poem lacking some of them is not faulty if the whole is pleasing.

Table 2.1. The descriptions listed by Daṇḍin (Kāvyādarśa 1.16–17) city (nagara) ocean (arṇava) mountain (śaila) seasons (ṛtu) moonrise and sunrise sports in gardens sports in water drinking festivals of love love in separation (vipralambha) marriages birth of a prince counsel (mantra) embassy (dūta) the march (prayāṇa) battle (āji) the triumph of the hero

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Five Great Poems
docs.text:
Later tradition singled out five works as the pañca mahākāvya, the “five great poems”, which were studied in Sanskrit schools with the commentaries of Mallinātha (fourteenth–fifteenth century) and others. They are listed in Table 2.2. Two other early poems, Aśvaghoṣa’s Buddhacarita and Bhaṭṭi’s Rāvaṇavadha, are discussed alongside them.

Table 2.2. The five canonical Sanskrit mahākāvyas Title Author Date Cantos Subject Raghuvaṃśa Kālidāsa c. 5th c. CE 19 The kings of Rāma’s solar dynasty Kumārasambhava Kālidāsa c. 5th c. CE 17 (1–8 by Kālidāsa) Pārvatī’s austerities, her marriage to Śiva, the birth of Kumāra Kirātārjunīya Bhāravi 6th c. CE 18 Arjuna’s combat with Śiva disguised as a hunter Śiśupālavadha Māgha late 7th–8th c. CE 20 Kṛṣṇa’s slaying of Śiśupāla Naiṣadhīyacarita Śrīharṣa 12th c. CE 22 The love and marriage of Nala and Damayantī

docs.title: 2.3 Aśvaghoṣa: The Earliest Surviving Kāvya Poet
docs.text: Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE) is the earliest Sanskrit poet whose mahākāvyas survive. Buddhist tradition associates him with the court of the Kuṣāṇa king Kaniṣka; the colophons of his works describe him as a monk from Sāketa (Ayodhyā) and the son of a woman named Suvarṇākṣī. His poems already show the full apparatus of the genre — cantos in varied metres, descriptions of cities and pleasure gardens, and refined figures of speech — which implies that the form had been developing for some time before him.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Buddhacarita
docs.text: The Buddhacarita (“Acts of the Buddha”) told the life of the Buddha in twenty-eight cantos, from his birth to the distribution of his relics. The Sanskrit text survives only for the first thirteen cantos and part of the fourteenth, taking the story as far as the Awakening; the complete poem is preserved in a Tibetan translation and in a Chinese translation of the early fifth century. The surviving Sanskrit includes celebrated scenes: the young prince’s encounters with old age, sickness and death, the night in the women’s quarters when the sleeping women appear to him as corpses, and his departure from Kapilavastu. E. H. Johnston’s edition and translation remain fundamental; Patrick Olivelle’s translation makes the surviving Sanskrit accessible (Johnston 1936; Olivelle 2008).

docs.title: 2.3.2 Saundarananda
docs.text: The Saundarananda (“Handsome Nanda”) survives complete in eighteen cantos. It tells how the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda, devoted to his wife Sundarī, is led against his will into the monastic life and finally to liberation. The poem’s frank treatment of erotic attachment serves a teaching purpose, and Aśvaghoṣa says so in his closing verses: the poem was written, he explains, to bring peace rather than pleasure, its poetic sweetness being like honey mixed with a bitter medicine to make it palatable.

docs.title: 2.4 Kālidāsa
docs.text: Kālidāsa has been regarded within the Indian tradition as the finest of Sanskrit poets, and modern readers have generally agreed. His surviving works comprise two mahākāvyas (Raghuvaṃśa and Kumārasambhava), the lyric Meghadūta, and three plays (Chapter 3); the Ṛtusaṃhāra, a poem on the six seasons, is traditionally attributed to him, but many scholars doubt the attribution.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Date
docs.text: Nothing certain is known of Kālidāsa’s life. The legend that he was one of the “nine jewels” at the court of a King Vikramāditya of Ujjain who founded the era of 57 BCE has no historical basis. Most scholars place him in the Gupta period, roughly the late fourth to mid fifth century CE, and often connect him with Candragupta II (r. c. 375–415) or Kumāragupta I. Only the latest possible date is fixed: the Aihole inscription of 634 CE, whose poet Ravikīrti claims a fame equal to that of Kālidāsa and Bhāravi, shows that he was famous by then. The earliest possible date is much vaguer. The Mālavikāgnimitra is set at the court of the Śuṅga king Agnimitra, so he cannot be earlier than the second century BCE, and most of the arguments for an exact date within these limits depend on the style and language of his works.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Raghuvaṃśa
docs.text:
The Raghuvaṃśa (“The Lineage of Raghu”) narrates the history of the solar dynasty from Dilīpa to the dissolute Agnivarṇa in nineteen cantos. Its opening verse is one of the best known in Sanskrit.

Raghuvaṃśa 1.1

vāgarthāv iva saṃpṛktau vāgarthapratipattaye | jagataḥ pitarau vande pārvatīparameśvarau || For the right understanding of word and meaning, I salute the parents of the world, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, who are joined like word and meaning.

The verse joins a benediction to a statement of poetics: the divine couple are as inseparable as word and sense, the two components of poetry in Bhāmaha’s definition.

The poem’s structure is broadly as follows. Cantos 1–4 tell of Dilīpa’s service of the cow Nandinī to obtain a son, the birth and youth of Raghu, and Raghu’s conquest of the quarters (digvijaya, canto 4). Canto 5 tells of Raghu’s generosity to the student Kautsa and the birth of Aja; canto 6 describes the bride-choice (svayaṃvara) of the princess Indumatī, and canto 7 her marriage to Aja; canto 8 contains Aja’s lament on Indumatī’s sudden death, one of the most admired passages of Sanskrit poetry. Canto 9 describes Daśaratha’s fateful hunt; cantos 10–15 tell the story of Rāma in condensed form; and cantos 16–19 follow his descendants to the dynasty’s decline.

Kālidāsa’s similes became proverbial. In the svayaṃvara scene Indumatī passes along the row of suitors, rejecting each in turn:

Raghuvaṃśa 6.67

sañcāriṇī dīpaśikheva rātrau yaṃ yaṃ vyatīyāya patiṃvarā sā | narendramārgāṭṭa iva prapede vivarṇabhāvaṃ sa sa bhūmipālaḥ || Like a moving lamp-flame at night, whichever king the bride passed by fell into darkness, like a mansion on the royal highway.

The image — each face lit up as she approaches and dimmed as she passes, like buildings along a street as a lamp is carried past — earned the poet the epithet “Dīpaśikhā Kālidāsa”. It illustrates the anonymous verse that sums up the classical estimate of the great poets:

Anonymous subhāṣita

upamā kālidāsasya bhāraver arthagauravam | daṇḍinaḥ padalālityaṃ māghe santi trayo guṇāḥ || Simile is Kālidāsa’s, weight of meaning Bhāravi’s, grace of diction Daṇḍin’s; in Māgha all three qualities are found.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Kumārasambhava
docs.text:
The Kumārasambhava (“The Birth of Kumāra”) tells how the gods, oppressed by the demon Tāraka, need a son of Śiva to lead them, and how Pārvatī, daughter of the Himālaya, wins the ascetic god as her husband. Only the first eight cantos are by Kālidāsa; cantos 9–17, which narrate the birth of Kumāra and the defeat of Tāraka, are a later continuation. The poem opens with a description of the Himālaya.

Kumārasambhava 1.1

asty uttarasyāṃ diśi devatātmā himālayo nāma nagādhirājaḥ | pūrvāparau toyanidhī vigāhya sthitaḥ pṛthivyā iva mānadaṇḍaḥ || In the northern quarter is the king of mountains named Himālaya, whose soul is divine; plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring-rod of the earth.

Its great episodes are the coming of spring and the burning of Kāma, the god of love, by the fire of Śiva’s third eye (canto 3); the lament of Kāma’s wife Rati (canto 4); Pārvatī’s austerities and her encounter with Śiva disguised as a young ascetic who tests her by disparaging the god (canto 5); the wedding (canto 7); and the couple’s love-making (canto 8). The last canto, describing the love of the supreme deities, was criticised by later theorists as a breach of propriety (aucitya); Ānandavardhana discusses the case in the Dhvanyāloka. Hank Heifetz’s translation conveys the poem’s richness (Heifetz 1985).

The poem’s central idea — that the god of asceticism can be won not by the arrows of desire but by Pārvatī’s own austerity, which transforms desire into a deeper union — has attracted many readings. It is also one of the earliest Sanskrit poems to make a woman’s resolve the engine of the plot.

docs.title: 2.4.4 Meghadūta
docs.text:
The Meghadūta (“The Cloud Messenger”) is a short poem (about 110–120 verses, depending on the recension) entirely in the slow mandākrāntā metre of seventeen syllables to the line. A yakṣa, a demigod in the service of Kubera, has been exiled for a year to Rāmagiri in central India for neglect of duty. At the onset of the monsoon he asks a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife in the Himālayan city of Alakā.

Meghadūta 1

kaścit kāntāvirahaguruṇā svādhikārapramattaḥ śāpenāstaṃgamitamahimā varṣabhogyeṇa bhartuḥ | yakṣaś cakre janakatanayāsnānapuṇyodakeṣu snigdhacchāyātaruṣu vasatiṃ rāmagiryāśrameṣu || A certain yakṣa, negligent of his duty, his greatness brought low by his master’s curse — heavy with separation from his beloved, to be endured for a year — made his dwelling in the hermitages of Rāmagiri, whose waters were made holy by the bathing of Janaka’s daughter and whose trees gave dense shade.

The first part (Pūrvamegha) describes the cloud’s route northward over rivers, mountains and cities — Vidiśā, Ujjayinī and others — in a sequence of vivid vignettes; the second (Uttaramegha) describes Alakā, the yakṣa’s house and grieving wife, and the message itself. Strictly, the Meghadūta is not a mahākāvya but a short poem (khaṇḍakāvya); it founded a whole genre of messenger poems (sandeśakāvya or dūtakāvya), from Dhoyī’s Pavanadūta in Bengal to Vedānta Deśika’s Haṃsasandeśa in the south and vernacular imitations in many languages.

docs.title: 2.5 Bhāravi
docs.text:
Bhāravi (sixth century CE) is known only from his Kirātārjunīya and from the Aihole inscription mentioned above. The poem, in eighteen cantos, takes an episode from the Mahābhārata. During the Pāṇḍavas’ exile in the forest, Draupadī and Bhīma urge Yudhiṣṭhira to break the agreement and make war (cantos 1–2); the sage Vyāsa advises that Arjuna should first win divine weapons by austerity (canto 3). The middle cantos follow Arjuna’s journey to the Himālaya, with descriptions of autumn and the mountains and an attempt by celestial nymphs to distract him; in the final cantos Śiva appears in the guise of a mountain hunter (kirāta), quarrels with Arjuna over a boar both have shot, fights him, and, pleased with his valour, grants him the pāśupata weapon.

Bhāravi’s quality is arthagaurava, “weight of meaning”. The political debate of the first two cantos is famous for its maxims. Yudhiṣṭhira, answering Bhīma’s call for immediate war, says:

Kirātārjunīya 2.30

sahasā vidadhīta na kriyām avivekaḥ param āpadāṃ padam | vṛṇate hi vimṛśyakāriṇaṃ guṇalubdhāḥ svayam eva saṃpadaḥ || One should not act rashly; lack of discrimination is the chief seat of misfortunes. Good fortune, eager for merit, chooses of her own accord the man who acts after reflection.

Canto 15, describing the battle, is a showcase of “picture poetry” (citrakāvya): verses that read the same backwards and forwards, verses built on only one or two consonants (including one using only the consonant n), and verses that can be written out in geometric patterns. Indira Peterson’s study shows how such virtuosity serves the poem’s design and argument rather than being mere display (Peterson 2003).

docs.title: 2.6 Māgha
docs.text:
Māgha (late seventh or early eighth century) states in a closing passage that his grandfather Suprabhadeva was minister to a king Varmalāta, known from an inscription of 625 CE; this places the poet a generation or two later. His Śiśupālavadha (“The Slaying of Śiśupāla”), in twenty cantos, retells the episode of the Mahābhārata in which Kṛṣṇa kills the insolent king Śiśupāla at Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration. The narrative is slight; the poem’s interest lies in its set pieces, among them the Raivataka mountain described in elaborate verbal patterns (canto 4), the descriptions of the seasons, water-sports and drinking, the dawn (canto 11), and the battle of canto 19, which, like Bhāravi’s canto 15, is full of citrakāvya.

Māgha deliberately set out to surpass Bhāravi, and the tradition credited him with success in a well-known saying: “Bhāravi’s light shines only until Māgha rises” (tāvad bhā bhāraver bhāti yāvan māghasya nodayaḥ).

docs.title: 2.7.1 Naiṣadhīyacarita
docs.text: Śrīharṣa (twelfth century), a poet at the court of the Gāhaḍavāla kings of Kanauj, was also the author of the Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya, a celebrated work of Advaita Vedānta dialectic directed against the Nyāya logicians. His Naiṣadhīyacarita retells in twenty-two cantos the story of Nala and Damayantī, but ends with their marriage and wedding night, before the famous misfortunes begin. The poem is dense with learning, double meanings and allusions to grammar, logic and philosophy — most famously in canto 13, where the goddess Sarasvatī introduces Nala and four gods disguised as Nala in verses each of which can be read as describing any of the five. Its reputation is captured in the saying naiṣadhaṃ vidvadauṣadham, “the Naiṣadha is a tonic for scholars”.

docs.title: 2.7.2 Bhaṭṭi and the “Poem of Learning”
docs.text: Bhaṭṭi (seventh century), who wrote at Valabhī in Gujarat, composed the Rāvaṇavadha, usually called the Bhaṭṭikāvya, in twenty-two cantos. It tells the story of Rāma while systematically illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar and, in its middle section, the figures of speech. It is the most famous example of the śāstrakāvya, the poem that teaches a discipline.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Other Court Epics
docs.text: Many other mahākāvyas were written in the following centuries, including Kumāradāsa’s Jānakīharaṇa, associated with Sri Lanka; Ratnākara’s enormous Haravijaya (ninth century, Kashmir); and numerous Jain mahākāvyas. A distinctive later development was the “poem of simultaneous narration” (dvisandhāna), in which every verse tells two stories at once through sustained double meaning, as in Kavirāja’s Rāghavapāṇḍavīya, which narrates the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata together. Yigal Bronner’s study traces this movement across Sanskrit, Telugu and other languages (Bronner 2010).

docs.title: 2.8 Lyric and Short Poems
docs.text:
Beside the court epic stood a rich literature of short poems (khaṇḍakāvya), collections of single stanzas (muktaka), and centuries (śataka). The single stanza, complete in itself, was in many ways the basic unit of Sanskrit poetry; anthologies such as Vidyākara’s Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa (Chapter 8) preserve thousands of them, beautifully translated by Daniel Ingalls (Ingalls 1965). Table 2.3 lists some notable short poems and collections.

Table 2.3. Some notable short poems and collections Work Author Date Form and subject Meghadūta Kālidāsa c. 5th c. Messenger poem in mandākrāntā Ṛtusaṃhāra attributed to Kālidāsa uncertain The six seasons and their effect on lovers Śatakatraya Bhartṛhari c. 5th–7th c. Three centuries on worldly wisdom, love and renunciation (Chapter 8) Amaruśataka Amaru c. 7th–8th c. A century of love stanzas, much cited by theorists Caurapañcāśikā Bilhaṇa 11th c. Fifty stanzas of remembered love, each beginning “even now” (adyāpi) Āryāsaptaśatī Govardhana 12th c. Seven hundred love stanzas in the āryā metre, modelled on Hāla’s Prakrit anthology Gītagovinda Jayadeva 12th c. Songs and verses on the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa

docs.title: 2.8.1 Jayadeva’s Gītagovinda
docs.text:
The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva, a poet associated with the court of Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal in the late twelfth century, is a unique fusion of court poetry and song. Its twelve cantos alternate narrative and descriptive verses in classical metres with twenty-four songs (prabandhas, popularly called aṣṭapadīs, “eight-steppers”, from their usual eight stanzas), each assigned a rāga and tāla. It tells of Kṛṣṇa’s dalliance with the cowherd women, Rādhā’s jealousy and longing, and the lovers’ reconciliation. The third song begins with a description of spring in Vṛndāvana:

Gītagovinda 1, song 3

lalitalavaṅgalatāpariśīlanakomalamalayasamīre | madhukaranikarakarambitakokilakūjitakuñjakuṭīre || When the soft sandal-mountain breeze caresses the graceful clove-creepers, and the forest bowers resound with cuckoos’ calls mingled with the humming of swarms of bees …

The poem was absorbed into temple worship at Purī, became a central text for the dance traditions of Odisha and Manipur and for later Vaiṣṇava devotion, and inspired a large body of painting, especially in the Rajput and Pahari courts. Barbara Stoler Miller’s edition and translation is standard (Miller 1977).

docs.title: 2.9 Historical Kāvya and Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī
docs.text:
Sanskrit poets frequently wrote about historical rulers. Bāṇa’s prose Harṣacarita (Chapter 4) is the first major example; it was followed by verse biographies such as Padmagupta’s Navasāhasāṅkacarita (c. 1000) on the Paramāra king Sindhurāja, and Bilhaṇa’s Vikramāṅka­deva­carita (late eleventh century) on the Cāḷukya king Vikramāditya VI. These works are panegyrics: they celebrate a patron and his lineage within the conventions of the mahākāvya, mixing historical events with mythological framing.

Bilhaṇa’s career illustrates the life of a court poet. Born in Kashmir in the eleventh century, he left home to seek patronage, wandered through Mathurā, Kanauj, Prayāga, Banaras, Gujarat and the Deccan, and finally became chief poet to Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇa, whose life he celebrated in eighteen cantos. The last canto of the Vikramāṅkadevacarita is an autobiography of the poet himself, describing his native Kashmir with nostalgic affection, and his travels — a rare personal document in Sanskrit literature.

The Rājataraṅgiṇī (“River of Kings”) of Kalhaṇa is of a different kind. Completed in 1149–50 CE, it is a verse history of the kings of Kashmir from legendary times to the poet’s own day, in eight books (taraṅga, “waves”) and nearly 8,000 verses. Kalhaṇa was the son of Campaka, a minister of King Harṣa of Kashmir (r. 1089–1101), and he wrote without a royal patron. In his introduction he describes his method: he examined eleven earlier chronicles, the Nīlamata Purāṇa, and inscriptions recording the foundation of temples and grants of land. He also states the ideal of impartiality:

Rājataraṅgiṇī 1.7

ślāghyaḥ sa eva guṇavān rāgadveṣabahiṣkṛtā | bhūtārthakathane yasya stheyasyeva sarasvatī || Only that gifted poet is worthy of praise whose word, like that of a judge, stays free of love and hatred in recounting the past.

The early books are largely legendary and their chronology is unreliable; Kalhaṇa assigns impossible reigns of three hundred years and misplaces Aśoka and the Kuṣāṇas. From the seventh-century Kārkoṭa dynasty onwards, however, his account becomes increasingly detailed and, for the eleventh and twelfth centuries, is based on the experience of his own family and contemporaries. Books 7 and 8 give a vivid and often bitter account of court intrigue, rebellions of the landholding ḍāmaras, the confiscation of temple wealth by Harṣa, famine and civil war. Kalhaṇa names the tranquil sentiment (śānta rasa) as the dominant mood of his work: the spectacle of the rise and fall of kings is meant to lead the reader to reflect on the impermanence of power.

The Rājataraṅgiṇī is the closest pre-modern Sanskrit work to history in the modern sense, and it was continued by later Kashmiri authors — Jonarāja and his pupil Śrīvara in the fifteenth century, and Prājyabhaṭṭa and Śuka in the sixteenth — into the period of the Kashmir sultanate and Mughal conquest. M. A. Stein’s annotated translation (1900) remains a monument of scholarship and a foundation for the historical geography of Kashmir (Stein 1900).

docs.title: 2.9.1 Other Historical Poems
docs.text:
Kalhaṇa’s work was exceptional, but the poem about a historical patron or event was a regular genre, and its range is wider than the label “panegyric” suggests. Sandhyākaranandin’s Rāmacarita (early twelfth century), written in Bengal under the Pālas, tells two stories at once in every verse through sustained double meaning (compare Section 2.7): that of Rāma, and that of the Pāla king Rāmapāla, who recovered the northern Bengal region of Varendrī after a rebellion led by the Kaivarta chief Divya. Read with the commentary that survives for its first part, it is a principal source for that rebellion. Jayānaka’s Pṛthvīrājavijaya (late twelfth century), by a Kashmiri poet at the Cāhamāna court of Ajmer, celebrates Pṛthvīrāja III; it survives, incomplete, in a single birch-bark manuscript found in Kashmir, with a commentary by Jonarāja. In Gujarat the Jain poets of the Caulukya and Vāghelā courts wrote poems on their patrons, such as Someśvara’s Kīrtikaumudī on the minister Vastupāla (thirteenth century), and developed a distinctive genre of historical anecdote, the prabandha, of which Merutuṅga’s Prabandhacintāmaṇi (1305) is the best known. Later works carried the genre into the courts of the second millennium: Nayacandra Sūri’s Hammīramahākāvya (fifteenth century) on the Cāhamāna king who died defending Ranthambhor against ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (on the siege see Volume 20, Yuddha and Dhanurveda); Gaṅgādevī’s Madhurāvijaya (Section 2.11); Sanskrit poems for sultans, such as Udayarāja’s Rājavinoda on Maḥmūd Begaṛhā of Gujarat; and Kavīndra Paramānanda’s Śivabhārata (seventeenth century) on the Maratha king Śivājī.

European scholars of the nineteenth century often concluded that India had no historical writing. The judgement rested on a narrow idea of history and on neglect of the inscriptions (Section 1.6.1), chronicles, genealogies and Persian histories (Chapter 12) that recorded the past in other forms. Velcheru Narayana Rao, David Shulman and Sanjay Subrahmanyam have argued that writers in South India from the sixteenth century wrote history in forms their readers recognised as factual, signalled by tone and texture rather than by a separate genre (Rao et al. 2001). The historical kāvya belongs to this larger picture: its poets idealised and mythologised their patrons, but they also recorded campaigns, foundations and genealogies in forms their audiences knew how to read.

docs.title: 2.10.1 The Cloud’s Journey
docs.text:
The first half of the Meghadūta is a journey across India seen from the air. The yakṣa tells the cloud to rise from Rāmagiri and rest on the mountain Āmrakūṭa, then to see the river Revā (Narmadā) spread out at the foot of the Vindhyas like ornamental lines on an elephant’s body. It is to pass over the country of Daśārṇa and its capital Vidiśā on the river Vetravatī, to make a detour to visit Ujjayinī — “do not miss the mansions of Ujjayinī”, he urges — and to attend the evening worship of Śiva Mahākāla, offering its thunder as drum-music. Further north it crosses the Carmaṇvatī, the field of Kurukṣetra, where it is reminded of the war of the Mahābhārata, and the Gaṅgā at Kanakhala, before rising through the Himālaya by the Krauñca pass to Kailāsa and Alakā.

Each place is described through a small scene: peasant women gazing up at the cloud with eyes that know nothing of the coquetry of city women; rivers personified as women longing for their absent lovers; the cloud itself as a lover who drinks from rivers and lingers on mountains. The journey is at once a geography, a series of erotic vignettes, and a slow building up of the longing that the second half will release. The poem’s success lies in this interplay of landscape and feeling — a technique that the Sanskrit theorists would later describe in terms of vibhāvas, the circumstances that excite emotion.

docs.title: 2.10.2 The Lament of Aja
docs.text:
In the eighth canto of the Raghuvaṃśa, King Aja and Queen Indumatī are enjoying a garden when a garland falling from the lute of the sage Nārada, passing overhead, strikes the queen, who dies at once. Aja’s long lament over her body — addressed to the dead woman herself, recalling her habits and asking why so soft a thing as a garland could kill, while the poisoned arrows of Death had spared him — moves from disbelief to bitterness to grief. A disciple of the family priest Vasiṣṭha consoles him with a teaching on the impermanence of life: Indumatī was a celestial nymph under a curse, now released. Aja accepts the consolation intellectually but not emotionally; he lives on only until his son Daśaratha is old enough to rule, and then gives up his body at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarayū.

The episode shows several features of Kālidāsa’s art: the use of a small, almost absurd cause to produce catastrophe; the refusal to let philosophy simply cancel grief; and the way an episode within a dynastic chronicle becomes an independent lyric of loss. Later theorists cited it as a supreme example of the pathetic sentiment (karuṇa rasa).

docs.title: 2.11 Women Poets of Sanskrit
docs.text:
Sanskrit literature was overwhelmingly written by men, but it was not entirely so. Rājaśekhara, in the early tenth century, remarked that women too can be poets, since talent belongs to the soul and does not depend on sex; he cited the views of his own wife Avantisundarī on poetics. The anthologies (Chapter 8) preserve verses ascribed to more than thirty women, often known only by name. The most famous is Vijjakā (or Vijjā), who is credited with a verse answering the opening of Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa, where the goddess of speech, Sarasvatī, is called “all white”:

Verse ascribed to Vijjakā in the anthologies

nīlotpaladalaśyāmāṃ vijjakāṃ mām ajānatā | vṛthaiva daṇḍinā proktaṃ sarvaśuklā sarasvatī || Not knowing me, Vijjakā, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, Daṇḍin said in vain that Sarasvatī is all white.

Another, Śīlābhaṭṭārikā, is credited with a stanza that Mammaṭa quotes at the very beginning of his Kāvyaprakāśa as an example of poetry that has no evident figure of speech and is carried by its emotion:

Ascribed to Śīlābhaṭṭārikā; quoted in Kāvyaprakāśa 1

yaḥ kaumāraharaḥ sa eva hi varas tā eva caitrakṣapās te conmīlitamālatīsurabhayaḥ prauḍhāḥ kadambānilāḥ | sā caivāsmi tathāpi tatra suratavyāpāralīlāvidhau revārodhasi vetasītarutale cetaḥ samutkaṇṭhate || He who took my maidenhood is my husband still; these are the same nights of spring, the same strong breezes from the kadamba trees, fragrant with opening jasmine; and I am the same woman. Yet my heart longs for the play of love under the reeds on the bank of the Revā.

Married life has not dimmed the speaker’s longing for the secret love of her girlhood — a sentiment that the poem never states but conveys through its catalogue of things unchanged. In later centuries the Vijayanagara princess Gaṅgādevī wrote the Madhurāvijaya (fourteenth century), a mahākāvya on her husband Kampaṇa’s conquest of Madurai; Tirumalāmbā wrote a campū at the court of Acyutarāya (Chapter 4); and Rāmabhadrāmbā wrote a poem on her patron Raghunātha Nāyaka of Tanjavur (on the Nāyaka courts see Section 10.3). Their works are a small fraction of the whole, but they show that the exclusion of women from Sanskrit learning was never complete, especially at royal courts.

docs.title: 2.12 Amaru and the Art of the Single Stanza
docs.text: The Amaruśataka, a “century” of love stanzas ascribed to an otherwise unknown Amaru (perhaps seventh or eighth century), was regarded by the theorists as the model of the self-contained stanza (muktaka). Ānandavardhana remarked that Amaru’s stanzas, overflowing with the erotic sentiment, were well known to be as full as entire compositions, and a later saying claims that one verse of Amaru is worth a hundred long poems. Its verses present moments in the relations of lovers — the quarrel, the reconciliation, the first night, the husband’s departure on a journey — often through the eyes of the heroine or her friend, and frequently through a single gesture or detail. The work exists in several recensions with different contents, and many of its verses were quoted by theorists as examples of suggestion. The collection was attributed in later legend to the philosopher Śaṅkara, who was supposed to have learned the art of love in another man’s body in order to win a debate — an indication of how highly the work was esteemed. Ingalls’s translations from Vidyākara’s anthology include many of its finest stanzas (Ingalls 1965).

docs.title: 2.13 The Conventions of Kāvya
docs.text:
Classical Sanskrit poetry rested on a shared stock of conventions, which Rājaśekhara called the “poets’ agreements” (kavisamaya): things that poets describe in a certain way not because they are so in nature but because the tradition has fixed them. The cakora bird drinks moonlight; the cakravāka birds, a pair of ruddy geese, are condemned to spend each night apart on opposite banks of a river and call to each other in sorrow; the aśoka tree blossoms at the touch of a beautiful woman’s foot, and the bakula when she sprinkles it with wine from her mouth; day-lotuses close at night and night-lotuses open at moonrise; fame and laughter are white, infamy and sin black. Mountains have wings that Indra clipped; the ocean is the father of the moon and of the goddess Lakṣmī; Kāma’s bow is made of sugarcane and strung with bees, and his arrows are flowers.

Such conventions allowed poets to compress a great deal of meaning into a single image, since every reader knew what a cakravāka or an aśoka implied. They also defined the “world” of kāvya — a stylised realm of courts, gardens, seasons and lovers, idealised and ordered. The best poets used the conventions with freshness and wit, playing them against one another or giving them unexpected turns; lesser poets reproduced them mechanically, which is why later readers sometimes found classical poetry artificial. Understanding the conventions is the first step to reading the poetry as its original audience did.

The seasons provided a particularly rich field. Each season had its characteristic flowers, birds, winds and pastimes, and its associated moods: spring (vasanta), with the mango blossom, the cuckoo and the southern breeze from the Malaya mountains, was the season of love; the rains (varṣā), with clouds, peacocks and lightning, the season of longing for absent lovers; autumn (śarad), with clear skies, white clouds and lotus ponds, the season for kings to set out on campaign. Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta is built on the conventions of the rains, and the season descriptions of the mahākāvyas draw on this common store.

docs.title: 2.14 The Hymn (Stotra) as Poetry
docs.text:
One of the largest bodies of Sanskrit verse is also one of the least studied as literature: the hymn of praise (stotra, stuti). Hymns were composed by poets of every religious community, and many of them use the full resources of kāvya — the long classical metres, figures of speech, double meanings and the conventions of love poetry — in the service of devotion. Because they were recited daily rather than studied in courts, they were among the most widely known Sanskrit poems.

Buddhist hymnody is among the earliest. The hymns of Mātṛceṭa, above all the Śatapañcāśatka (“Hundred and Fifty Verses”), praise the Buddha in simple but polished stanzas; the Chinese pilgrim Yijing, who visited India in the late seventh century, reported that monks everywhere learned them by heart. Jain poets answered with hymns to the tīrthaṅkaras, of which Mānatuṅga’s Bhaktāmarastotra, revered by both Śvetāmbaras and Digambaras, is still recited in Jain homes and temples. At the court of Harṣa, Mayūra’s Sūryaśataka and Bāṇa’s Caṇḍīśataka, each a century of verses in the long sragdharā metre, showed that a hymn could be as ornate as any court poem; the legend that Mayūra was cured of leprosy by his hymn to the Sun is the one Mammaṭa recalls (Chapter 1).

Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava hymns form the bulk of the genre. The Śivamahimnaḥ Stotra attributed to Puṣpadanta became one of the best-known hymns to Śiva; in Kashmir the philosopher Utpaladeva (tenth century) wrote the Śivastotrāvalī, which joins non-dual theology to personal longing, and Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa (fourteenth century) composed the long Stutikusumāñjali. In the south, the Mukundamālā attributed to the king Kulaśekhara and Yāmuna’s Stotraratna brought the devotional intensity of the Tamil Āḻvārs (Chapter 9) into Sanskrit, and Vedānta Deśika wrote dozens of hymns of great technical brilliance. Many hymns circulate under the name of Śaṅkara, among them the Saundaryalaharī on the Goddess; most scholars doubt that he wrote them, but their popularity is unaffected. Later examples include the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta of Līlāśuka and Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri’s Nārāyaṇīyam (Chapter 10).

Hymns were also where Sanskrit poetics met religious feeling most directly. The theorists debated whether devotion to a deity (devaviṣayā rati) could be a full rasa or only a subordinate emotional state (bhāva); the hymn-writers in practice treated it as the highest, and Rūpa Gosvāmin later gave that practice a theory (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.15 Sanskrit Poetry in the Second Millennium
docs.text:
It was once common to speak of a “decline” of Sanskrit literature after the twelfth century. Recent scholarship, including Pollock’s work on the vernacular millennium, has qualified this picture: Sanskrit lost its monopoly of literary prestige, but a great deal of fine Sanskrit poetry continued to be written, often by poets who also wrote in a regional language (Pollock 2006). The essays collected by Yigal Bronner, David Shulman and Gary Tubb trace the innovations of this later poetry and of the earlier kāvya from which it departed (Bronner et al. 2014).

Jain authors were especially prolific. Hemacandra’s Dvyāśraya illustrates the rules of grammar while narrating the history of the Caulukya dynasty of Gujarat, and a long series of Jain mahākāvyas retold the lives of the tīrthaṅkaras and of Jain kings and merchants. In the south, Vedānta Deśika (thirteenth–fourteenth century), the great Śrīvaiṣṇava theologian, wrote the mahākāvya Yādavābhyudaya and the messenger poem Haṃsasandeśa. Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita (seventeenth century) of Madurai wrote satirical poems such as the Kalividambana (“Mockery of the Kali Age”), lampooning doctors, astrologers and pedants; and the theorist Jagannātha (Section 6.8) wrote at the court of Shāh Jahān the lyric stanzas of the Bhāminīvilāsa. Hymns continued to be composed throughout the period (Section 2.14). Sanskrit literary composition has continued into modern times; the Sanskrit scholar and poet Satya Vrat Shastri received the Jnanpith Award in 2006.

docs.title: 2.16 Metres of the Mahākāvya
docs.text:
Classical Sanskrit verse uses two main types of metre: syllabic metres in which each line has a fixed pattern of heavy and light syllables, and the śloka (anuṣṭubh), the four-line stanza of eight-syllable quarters used for narrative from the epics onwards. A canto of a mahākāvya is normally in a single metre, with a change of metre in its closing verse or verses. Table 2.4 lists some common metres.

Table 2.4. Some common metres of classical Sanskrit poetry Metre Syllables per quarter Remarks Anuṣṭubh / śloka 8 The narrative metre of the epics; used for many cantos of the mahākāvya Indravajrā, Upendravajrā, Upajāti 11 Upajāti mixes the first two; very common in Kālidāsa Vaṃśastha 12 Frequent in mahākāvya cantos Vasantatilakā 14 A favourite metre for single stanzas and drama Mālinī 15 Often used for closing verses Mandākrāntā 17 Slow and stately; the metre of the Meghadūta Śikhariṇī 17 Used for reflective and emotional verses Śārdūlavikrīḍita 19 The commonest long metre for single stanzas Sragdharā 21 The longest of the common metres Āryā (measured by morae) A moraic metre inherited from Prakrit poetry

docs.title: 2.17 From Sanskrit to the Regional Languages
docs.text:
The poets who made the first classics of Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and Hindi knew the mahākāvya well, and many of them built their works on epic themes using its conventions, adapted to new metres and idioms (Table 2.5); these works are discussed in Chapters 7, 10 and 11. Its conventions also travelled across the Bay of Bengal: the Old Javanese kakawin, such as the Rāmāyaṇa Kakawin (ninth century) and Mpu Kaṇwa’s Arjunawiwāha (eleventh century), adopt Sanskrit metres and the descriptive programme of the mahākāvya. Figure 2.1 places the major Sanskrit poets of the genre in time.

Table 2.5. Some regional works shaped by the mahākāvya model Language Work Author and date Remarks Kannada Vikramārjunavijaya Pampa, 941 CE Mahābhārata in campū form, identifying Arjuna with the poet’s patron Tamil Irāmāvatāram Kampaṉ, c. 12th c. A free and powerful Tamil recreation of the Rāma story Telugu Manucaritramu Allasāni Peddana, 16th c. The classic Telugu prabandha Malayalam Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu Eḻuttacchaṉ, 16th c. Devotional Rāma story in the “parrot song” form Avadhi Rāmcaritmānas Tulsīdās, 1574–c. 1577 Devotional Rāma epic in dohā–caupāī verse Figure 2.1. Approximate dates of the major mahākāvya poets, on a time axis drawn to scale (years CE). Each bar spans the range of dates given in the text; all these dates are uncertain.
