docs.title: Chapter 3: Sanskrit Drama: Dṛśya Kāvya
docs.text: na taj jñānaṃ na tac chilpaṃ na sā vidyā na sā kalā | nāsau yogo na tat karma nāṭye ’smin yan na dṛśyate || There is no knowledge, no craft, no learning, no art, no technique and no action that is not seen in this drama. — Nāṭyaśāstra 1.116 (Ghosh’s numbering)

docs.title: 3.1 Drama in Indian Aesthetics
docs.text:
For the Sanskrit theorists drama (nāṭya, rūpaka) was the paradigm of literature. The theory of rasa was first formulated for the theatre, and later writers on poetry continued to illustrate it from plays. Drama was “poetry to be seen” (dṛśya kāvya): it combined verse and prose with music, dance, gesture, costume and the physical presence of actors.

The foundational text is the Nāṭyaśāstra attributed to the sage Bharata, a large compendium on all aspects of theatre. It is a composite work, compiled over several centuries; most scholars place its main body between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, with later additions. Manomohan Ghosh’s translation remains the standard English version (Ghosh 1950).

The first chapter tells how the gods asked Brahmā for an entertainment that could be seen and heard by all, since the Vedas could not be recited in the hearing of Śūdras. Brahmā therefore created a fifth Veda, open to all classes (sārvavarṇika), drawing on the four existing Vedas:

Nāṭyaśāstra 1.17

jagrāha pāṭhyam ṛgvedāt sāmabhyo gītam eva ca | yajurvedād abhinayān rasān ātharvaṇād api || He took recitation from the Ṛgveda, song from the Sāmaveda, acting from the Yajurveda and the sentiments (rasa) from the Atharvaveda.

The story is revealing in two ways. It claims Vedic authority for the theatre, and it acknowledges the exclusion of Śūdras from Vedic learning, presenting drama as a form of instruction and pleasure available to everyone.

docs.title: 3.2 The Nāṭyaśāstra: Contents
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra has thirty-six or thirty-seven chapters, depending on the recension, and their numbering differs between editions. Table 3.1 summarises its contents in broad groups following Ghosh’s arrangement. Its treatment of music, dance and stagecraft is discussed in Volume 9 of this series, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya; this chapter is concerned with drama as literature.

Table 3.1. The contents of the Nāṭyaśāstra (approximate chapter groups) Chapters Subject 1–5 Origin of drama; the playhouse and its consecration; the tāṇḍava dance with its 108 karaṇas (units of movement); the preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga) 6–7 Rasa and bhāva (sentiments and emotional states) 8–14 Bodily acting (āṅgika abhinaya): head, eyes, hands and body; the 32 cārīs (movements of the feet and legs); gaits; zones of the stage and regional styles 15–19 Verbal acting (vācika abhinaya): phonetics and grammar, prosody, poetic figures, qualities and faults, the languages and dialects of the stage, modes of address 20–22 The ten types of play; the structure of plot; the dramatic styles (vṛtti) 23 Costume and make-up (āhārya abhinaya) 24–27 General acting; the representation of love; “success” in performance 28–33 Music: tones, scales, instruments and drumming 34–36 Types of characters; distribution of roles; the descent of drama to earth

docs.title: 3.2.1 The Playhouse
docs.text: The second chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra describes the theatre building (nāṭyamaṇḍapa). It recognises three shapes — rectangular (vikṛṣṭa), square (caturaśra) and triangular (tryaśra) — and three sizes, the largest 108 cubits (hasta) long, the medium 64 and the smallest 32. It recommends the medium rectangular hall, 64 cubits by 32, as best, because in a larger house the actors’ voices and facial expressions would be lost. The hall is divided between the auditorium and the stage, which has a front area for acting and a rear area behind a curtain for the actors’ preparation, from which entrances are made through two doors. The text gives detailed instructions on the choice of site, the laying of foundations, the pillars, and the rites of consecration that protect the performance from obstacles. Its insistence on audibility and visibility reflects the importance of speech and facial expression in Indian acting. Whether actual theatres followed these prescriptions is unknown; the only surviving early structures sometimes identified as theatres, such as the cave at Sītābeṅgā in Chhattisgarh, are uncertain, and the temple theatres (kūttampalam) of Kerala date from the second millennium.

docs.title: 3.2.2 The Four Modes of Acting
docs.text: The text distinguishes four modes of acting: āṅgika (bodily), vācika (verbal), āhārya (costume, make-up and properties) and sāttvika (the involuntary signs of emotion such as tears, trembling, perspiration and change of colour, which the actor must be able to produce).

docs.title: 3.3 Types of Drama
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra, and after it Dhanañjaya’s Daśarūpaka (late tenth century), the most widely used later handbook of dramaturgy, recognise ten types of play (rūpaka; Table 3.2).

Table 3.2. The ten types of rūpaka Type Acts Characteristics Nāṭaka 5–10 Story from legend or history; a renowned, noble hero, usually royal or divine; dominant rasa heroic or erotic Prakaraṇa 5–10 Invented plot; hero a brahmin, minister or merchant; the heroine may be a courtesan Bhāṇa 1 Monologue by a man-about-town (viṭa) who converses with imaginary interlocutors Prahasana 1 Farce, often satirising ascetics, brahmins or officials Ḍima 4 Spectacular play with gods, demons and supernatural events; furious sentiment Vyāyoga 1 Martial episode from the epics; few female characters Samavakāra 3 Conflict of gods and demons Vīthī 1 Short piece with one or two characters Aṅka (Utsṛṣṭikāṅka) 1 Pathos; laments, often of women, after a battle Īhāmṛga 4 A hero’s pursuit of a divine woman who is hard to win

Later writers added a varying list of “minor” types (uparūpaka), several of which involve music and dance (Table 3.3). The most important for literature are the nāṭikā, a four-act court comedy such as Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī, and the saṭṭaka, a similar play written wholly in Prakrit, such as Rājaśekhara’s Karpūramañjarī.

Table 3.3. Some uparūpaka forms Form Characteristics Nāṭikā Four acts; court intrigue around a king, his queen and a young heroine (Ratnāvalī, Priyadarśikā) Saṭṭaka Like the nāṭikā, but entirely in Prakrit (Karpūramañjarī) Toṭaka Several acts, with divine and human characters; Kālidāsa’s Vikramorvaśīya is sometimes so classified Rāsaka, Hallīśaka Forms dominated by dance and song, the latter a circular dance of women around a single man

docs.title: 3.4.1 The Structure of the Plot
docs.text:
Sanskrit dramaturgy analysed plot in three parallel sets of five terms:

  • five stages of action (avasthā) in the hero’s pursuit of his goal: beginning (ārambha), effort (yatna), prospect of success (prāptyāśā), certainty of success (niyatāpti) and attainment (phalāgama);

  • five elements of the plot (arthaprakṛti): the seed (bīja) from which the action grows, the drop (bindu) that keeps it continuous when interrupted, the extended episode (patākā), the brief episode (prakarī) and the outcome (kārya);

  • five junctures (sandhi) that join stages and elements into the structure of the play: opening (mukha), progression (pratimukha), development (garbha), crisis or pause (vimarśa) and conclusion (nirvahaṇa).

docs.title: 3.4.2 Hero and Heroine
docs.text:
The theorists classified heroes by temperament. Each type was meant to be self-possessed (dhīra); the four types are set out in Table 3.4.

Table 3.4. The four types of hero (nāyaka) Type Qualities Standard examples Dhīrodātta Noble, controlled, magnanimous Rāma; Yudhiṣṭhira; often Duṣyanta Dhīralalita Carefree, devoted to the arts and pleasure King Udayana (Vatsarāja) in Harṣa’s nāṭikās Dhīrapraśānta Calm and virtuous; usually a brahmin or merchant Cārudatta in the Mṛcchakaṭika; Mādhava in the Mālatīmādhava Dhīroddhata Proud, fierce and boastful Bhīma; Paraśurāma; Rāvaṇa

Heroines (nāyikā) were classified with equal elaboration — as one’s own wife, another’s wife or a courtesan; by age and experience; and by situation, in the eightfold scheme (aṣṭanāyikā) that became central to later poetry, painting and dance (the heroine waiting in the trysting place, the heroine separated by a quarrel, the heroine whose lover is abroad, and so on).

docs.title: 3.4.3 Conventions of Performance
docs.text: A performance began with preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga) and a benediction (nāndī), followed by a prologue (prastāvanā) in which the stage manager (sūtradhāra) and usually an actress introduce the play and its author. The theorists forbade showing on stage, among other things, death, battle, the overthrow of a kingdom, eating, bathing, sleeping and love-making; such events are reported, often in interludes (viṣkambhaka, praveśaka) between the acts. The nāṭaka was to end auspiciously, with the hero’s success. Two further conventions, the brahmin jester and the assignment of languages to characters by status and gender, are discussed below.

docs.title: 3.4.4 The Vidūṣaka
docs.text: The brahmin jester is the most distinctive stock character of Sanskrit drama. Ugly, greedy for sweets, cowardly and fond of misusing learned words, he speaks Prakrit although a brahmin, and serves as the king’s friend and confidant, carrying messages, devising schemes and puncturing the hero’s romantic rhetoric with comic literalism. In Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala Māḍhavya complains of the hardships of the hunt and is sent away before the king’s secret can be revealed; in Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī the jester’s blunders nearly ruin the lovers. Scholars have traced the figure to ritual clowns and popular entertainers, and he lives on in the regional theatres, above all in the Cākyār actor’s long satirical monologues in Kūṭiyāṭṭam, where the vidūṣaka comments in Malayalam on contemporary society. His comedy depends on the incongruity between his brahmin status and his behaviour, and thus on the social hierarchy itself.

docs.title: 3.5 Bhāsa and the Trivandrum Plays
docs.text:
Bhāsa was known for centuries only by reputation: Kālidāsa names him in the prologue of the Mālavikāgnimitra as one of the famous dramatists of the past, and later authors quote him. In 1909–10 the scholar T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī found in Kerala manuscripts of thirteen anonymous plays which he attributed to Bhāsa and published from 1912 in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series. The attribution remains debated: the plays share features of style and structure, and one of them corresponds to a play that later writers ascribe to Bhāsa, but the texts as we have them may be acting versions transmitted and adapted by the Cākyār actors of Kerala. Bhāsa’s date is uncertain; he preceded Kālidāsa. The principal plays are listed in Table 3.5.

Table 3.5. Some of the Trivandrum plays attributed to Bhāsa Play Source of story Notes Svapnavāsavadatta Udayana cycle Queen Vāsavadattā, believed dead, lives in disguise while her husband takes a second wife for political reasons; the dream scene of Act 5 Pratijñā­yaugandha­rāyaṇa Udayana cycle The minister Yaugandharāyaṇa’s plan to rescue the captive king Ūrubhaṅga Mahābhārata The dying Duryodhana on stage, reconciled and dignified Karṇabhāra Mahābhārata Karṇa gives away his protective armour to Indra disguised as a brahmin Madhyamavyāyoga Mahābhārata Bhīma meets his son Ghaṭotkaca, who does not recognise him Dūtavākya, Pañcarātra Mahābhārata Kṛṣṇa’s embassy; an episode of the Virāṭa book Pratimānāṭaka, Abhiṣekanāṭaka Rāmāyaṇa Episodes of the Rāma story Cārudatta Invented A four-act fragment closely related to the Mṛcchakaṭika

The Ūrubhaṅga (“The Breaking of the Thighs”) is especially important for the history of the theatre. It shows Duryodhana mortally wounded by Bhīma’s unfair blow and dying on stage, surrounded by his blind parents, his wives and his small son. The play, in a single act (its genre is disputed; it is often classed as an utsṛṣṭikāṅka, the one-act play of lament), grants the epic’s villain a nobility and pathos that the epic itself only partly allows, and it shows that the conventions of the theorists were not always observed in practice.

docs.title: 3.5.1 The Vision of Vāsavadattā
docs.text: The Svapnavāsavadatta, the most admired of the Trivandrum plays, shows the subtlety these works can achieve. King Udayana of Vatsa has lost his kingdom; his minister Yaugandharāyaṇa believes that it can be recovered only through an alliance with the king of Magadha by marriage to the princess Padmāvatī. Since Udayana is devoted to his queen Vāsavadattā and will not remarry, the minister spreads the news that the queen has died in a fire, and leaves her, disguised as his sister, in Padmāvatī’s care. Vāsavadattā must thus watch her husband court and marry another woman for the sake of his kingdom. In the fifth act the king, asleep in a pavilion, speaks Vāsavadattā’s name in a dream; she, entering by chance, adjusts the hand that has slipped from his bed and slips away, and on waking he cannot be sure whether he dreamed her presence or not. The play ends with recognition, the recovery of the kingdom and the reconciliation of the two queens. Its quiet, restrained treatment of loss and loyalty has made it a favourite of modern readers.

docs.title: 3.6 Kālidāsa’s Plays
docs.text: Kālidāsa wrote three plays. Barbara Stoler Miller and her collaborators translated all three in Theater of Memory, whose introduction is an excellent guide to Kālidāsa’s dramaturgy (Miller 1984).

docs.title: 3.6.1 Mālavikāgnimitra
docs.text:
Mālavikāgnimitra (“Mālavikā and Agnimitra”), probably the earliest, is a five-act palace comedy set at the court of the Śuṅga king Agnimitra (second century BCE), who falls in love with the dancer Mālavikā, a princess in disguise serving his queen. In the prologue the stage manager defends the staging of a new play by a living author against the prestige of Bhāsa and other older dramatists:

Mālavikāgnimitra 1.2

purāṇam ity eva na sādhu sarvaṃ na cāpi kāvyaṃ navam ity avadyam | santaḥ parīkṣyānyatarad bhajante mūḍhaḥ parapratyayaneyabuddhiḥ || Not everything is good just because it is old, nor is a poem to be blamed because it is new. The discerning test both and choose; the fool’s judgement is led by the opinion of others.

docs.title: 3.6.2 Vikramorvaśīya
docs.text: Vikramorvaśīya (“Urvaśī Won by Valour”) dramatises in five acts the ancient story, already found in the Ṛgveda and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, of King Purūravas and the celestial nymph Urvaśī. Its fourth act, in which the king, believing Urvaśī lost, wanders through a forest addressing clouds, peacocks, a river and an elephant, is a celebrated study of love-madness (unmāda). In one recension the act includes songs in Apabhraṃśa, among the earliest literary uses of that language.

docs.title: 3.6.3 Abhijñānaśākuntala
docs.text:
The Abhijñānaśākuntala (“Śakuntalā Recognised by a Token”) is Kālidāsa’s masterpiece and the most famous of all Sanskrit plays. In seven acts it tells of King Duṣyanta’s love for Śakuntalā, foster-daughter of the sage Kaṇva, their secret marriage, the curse that makes the king forget her, and their eventual reunion.

The play opens with Duṣyanta out hunting. He follows a deer into Kaṇva’s hermitage and sees Śakuntalā watering the trees with her two friends. In the second act the lovesick king confides in the vidūṣaka and finds a pretext to stay near the hermitage, and in the third the lovers meet and, it is implied, marry by mutual consent (gāndharva vivāha). An interlude at the start of the fourth act reveals that the irascible sage Durvāsas, neglected by the absent-minded Śakuntalā, has cursed her to be forgotten by her lover until he sees a token of recognition. The rest of that act is her departure from the hermitage for the king’s court, one of the most moving scenes in Sanskrit drama. At court, in the fifth act, the king does not know her. The ring he gave her has been lost on the way, and she is rejected and carried away by a heavenly light. In the sixth act a fisherman finds the ring in a fish, and the king’s memory returns with a remorse that consumes him. In the last act, returning from a battle fought on behalf of the gods, Duṣyanta finds Śakuntalā and their son Bharata in the celestial hermitage of Mārīca.

At the beginning of Act 5, before Śakuntalā arrives, the king hears a song sung by one of his queens and feels an unaccountable longing. He reflects:

Abhijñānaśākuntala 5.2

ramyāṇi vīkṣya madhurāṃś ca niśamya śabdān paryutsuko bhavati yat sukhito ’pi jantuḥ | tac cetasā smarati nūnam abodhapūrvaṃ bhāvasthirāṇi jananāntarasauhṛdāni || When even a happy man grows restless on seeing beautiful things and hearing sweet sounds, surely he is remembering, without knowing it, the loves of former lives, fixed firmly in his heart.

The verse states the play’s central theme of memory and forgetting. Kālidāsa’s source, the story of Śakuntalā in the first book of the Mahābhārata, contains no curse and no ring: there Duṣyanta knowingly denies Śakuntalā when she comes to court with their son, and acknowledges her only when a heavenly voice confirms her claim. By introducing the curse Kālidāsa relieves the king of responsibility; modern readers have been divided over whether this ennobles the story or evades the moral issue that the epic version raises so sharply.

docs.title: 3.6.4 Śakuntalā’s Departure
docs.text:
The fourth act was singled out by the tradition as the heart of the play. Kaṇva, returning from a pilgrimage, learns of Śakuntalā’s marriage and her pregnancy and arranges for her to go to her husband. The act is a sequence of leave-takings: the hermit women adorn her with ornaments given by the trees of the forest; she bids farewell to her friends, to the creeper she called her sister, and to a fawn she raised, which tugs at her garment. Kaṇva, an ascetic who has renounced all attachment, finds himself overcome:

Abhijñānaśākuntala 4.6

yāsyaty adya śakuntaleti hṛdayaṃ saṃspṛṣṭam utkaṇṭhayā kaṇṭhaḥ stambhitabāṣpavṛttikaluṣaś cintājaḍaṃ darśanam | vaiklavyaṃ mama tāvad īdṛśam idaṃ snehād araṇyaukasaḥ pīḍyante gṛhiṇaḥ kathaṃ nu tanayāviśleṣaduḥkhair navaiḥ || “Śakuntalā goes today”: at the thought my heart is touched with sorrow, my throat choked with held-back tears, my sight dulled with care. If such is the distress, through affection, of a forest-dweller like me, how must householders suffer at the fresh pain of parting from a daughter?

The scene draws on the universal experience of a daughter leaving her parents’ home at marriage, and it is still the best-loved passage of the play in India. It also prepares, by contrast, for the cold reception that awaits Śakuntalā at court.

docs.title: 3.7 Śūdraka: The Little Clay Cart
docs.text:
The Mṛcchakaṭika (“The Little Clay Cart”), attributed to a king Śūdraka of whom nothing reliable is known, is usually dated between the third and fifth centuries CE. It is a prakaraṇa in ten acts, expanding the plot of the Cārudatta fragment of the Trivandrum plays. The impoverished but generous brahmin merchant Cārudatta loves, and is loved by, the courtesan Vasantasenā. The king’s boorish brother-in-law Śakāra, whose advances she rejects, tries to strangle her and accuses Cārudatta of her murder; Cārudatta is condemned and led to execution, but is saved when Vasantasenā, who has survived, appears, and when a popular rising led by the cowherd Āryaka overthrows the tyrant Pālaka.

The play is remarkable for its range of urban characters — gamblers, a thief who cites a treatise on burglary, a masseur turned Buddhist monk, executioners, courtiers and judges — and for its humour and suspense. Its title comes from a scene in which Cārudatta’s small son cries because his clay toy cart is not a gold one like his playmate’s, and Vasantasenā fills it with her jewels.

docs.title: 3.8.1 Mudrārākṣasa
docs.text: Viśākhadatta’s Mudrārākṣasa (“Rākṣasa and the Signet Ring”), in seven acts, is a political drama without a love plot. Its date is uncertain; proposals range from the fifth to the ninth century. Cāṇakya, having helped Candragupta Maurya to overthrow the Nandas, works to win over Rākṣasa, the able and loyal minister of the old dynasty, by an elaborate web of spies, forged letters and a stolen signet ring. The contest between two intelligent and principled opponents, and Cāṇakya’s final success in making Rākṣasa Candragupta’s minister, give the play a character unique in Sanskrit drama. Fragments of another play by Viśākhadatta, the Devīcandragupta, survive in quotations.

docs.title: 3.8.2 Harṣa
docs.text: King Harṣavardhana of Kanauj (r. 606–647) is credited with three plays: two nāṭikās, Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā, polished comedies of court intrigue centred on King Udayana; and the Nāgānanda (“Joy of the Serpents”), the best-known Sanskrit play on a Buddhist theme.

docs.title: 3.8.3 The Court Comedy: Ratnāvalī
docs.text:
Harṣa’s Ratnāvalī became the model nāṭikā for the theorists, who quote it constantly. A princess of Sri Lanka, Ratnāvalī, destined by prophecy to marry a world-ruler, is shipwrecked on her way to King Udayana and enters the household of his queen Vāsavadattā as a maidservant under the name Sāgarikā. She falls in love with the king, paints his portrait, and is discovered; the jealous queen has her confined; a magician’s illusion of a fire allows the king to rescue her; and when her identity is revealed the queen consents to the marriage. The play’s spring festival, its painting and portrait scenes, and the comic schemes of the vidūṣaka set the pattern for a whole genre of court comedy, in which a king’s pursuit of a new love is played out against the authority of his chief queen.

The Nāgānanda is more unusual. Its first three acts are a conventional love comedy in which the prince Jīmūtavāhana, who has renounced his kingdom to serve his parents in the forest, wins the princess Malayavatī. In the last two acts the tone changes entirely: Jīmūtavāhana learns that the serpents must send one of their number each day to be eaten by Garuḍa, and he takes the place of the young serpent Śaṅkhacūḍa, whose mother is lamenting. Garuḍa, devouring him, is astonished by his calm, repents and vows to kill no more, and the goddess Gaurī restores the prince to life. The play opens with a benediction to the Buddha and celebrates the Mahāyāna ideal of self-sacrifice for others, yet it ends with the intervention of a Hindu goddess — a mixture that reflects the religious world of Harṣa’s court, which patronised both Buddhists and brahmins.

docs.title: 3.9 Bhavabhūti
docs.text:
Bhavabhūti (early eighth century), a brahmin from Vidarbha who lived at the court of Yaśovarman of Kanauj, wrote three plays: the Mahāvīracarita on the early life of Rāma; the Mālatīmādhava, a ten-act prakaraṇa of love, adventure and the macabre (including a scene in a cremation ground and a planned human sacrifice by a Kāpālika ascetic); and the Uttararāmacarita. He was conscious of standing apart from his contemporaries. In the prologue of the Mālatīmādhava he answers his critics:

Mālatīmādhava 1.6 (Kale’s edition; 1.8 in some others)

ye nāma kecid iha naḥ prathayanty avajñāṃ jānanti te kim api tān prati naiṣa yatnaḥ | utpatsyate ’sti mama ko ’pi samānadharmā kālo hy ayaṃ niravadhir vipulā ca pṛthvī || Those who show contempt for me — they know something, no doubt; this effort is not for them. There will arise, or there exists, someone of like nature to mine; for time is boundless and the earth is wide.

docs.title: 3.9.1 Uttararāmacarita
docs.text:
The Uttararāmacarita (“The Later Story of Rāma”) takes up the most painful part of the Rāma story: Rāma’s abandonment of the pregnant Sītā because of the gossip of his subjects. Bhavabhūti alters the ending: where the Rāmāyaṇa ends with Sītā’s return to the earth, the play ends with reconciliation. Its seven acts are outlined in Table 3.6.

Table 3.6. The seven acts of the Uttararāmacarita Act Content 1 Rāma and the pregnant Sītā view paintings of their earlier life; the spy reports the people’s slander; Rāma resolves to abandon Sītā 2 Twelve years later Rāma comes to the Daṇḍaka forest to kill the Śūdra ascetic Śambūka 3 The “shadow” scene: Sītā, made invisible, watches the grieving Rāma at Pañcavaṭī 4 Janaka and Kausalyā meet at Vālmīki’s hermitage and see the boy Lava 5 Lava fights Candraketu, guardian of Rāma’s sacrificial horse 6 Rāma meets Lava and Kuśa and is moved without knowing why 7 A play staged by Vālmīki depicts Sītā’s fate; Sītā is restored and the family reunited

The second act retains the episode of Śambūka, the Śūdra killed by Rāma for practising asceticism forbidden to his class — an episode taken from the last book of the Rāmāyaṇa which troubled many later readers. Bhavabhūti retains it, but uneasily: his Rāma strikes while reproaching his own hand as the hand that banished Sītā, and Śambūka at once appears in a divine form to thank him. In the third act the river Tamasā speaks a verse that became a touchstone in the theory of rasa:

Uttararāmacarita 3.47

eko rasaḥ karuṇa eva nimittabhedād bhinnaḥ pṛthak pṛthag ivāśrayate vivartān | āvartabudbudataraṅgamayān vikārān ambho yathā salilam eva tu tat samagram || There is one rasa, pathos alone; through difference of cause it is altered and seems to take on separate forms, just as water takes the forms of eddies, bubbles and waves, though all of it is only water.

docs.title: 3.10 Later Drama
docs.text: Drama continued to be written throughout the second millennium. Notable works include Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa’s Veṇīsaṃhāra (on the Mahābhārata war), much cited by the theorists; Murāri’s ornate Anargharāghava (ninth century); the plays of Rājaśekhara (early tenth century), including the Prakrit saṭṭaka Karpūramañjarī; and Kṛṣṇamiśra’s Prabodhacandrodaya (late eleventh century), an allegorical play whose characters are abstractions such as Discrimination, Delusion and Knowledge. The Veṇīsaṃhāra (“The Binding of the Braid”), probably of the seventh or eighth century, dramatises the Mahābhārata war from Draupadī’s vow not to bind up her hair, dishevelled when she was dragged into the assembly, until Bhīma has avenged her insult; its fierce scenes made it a favourite source of examples of the heroic and furious rasas. In Kerala, Śaktibhadra’s Āścaryacūḍāmaṇi (“The Wondrous Crest-Jewel”), a play on the Rāma story probably of the ninth century, became a staple of the Kūṭiyāṭṭam repertoire. The bhāṇa monologue, of which four early examples survive in the collection known as the Caturbhāṇī, gives a satirical picture of urban life among courtesans and men-about-town.

docs.title: 3.10.1 Farce: The Mattavilāsa and the Bhagavadajjuka
docs.text: Two early one-act farces (prahasana) show the satirical side of the Sanskrit theatre. The Mattavilāsa (“Drunken Revelry”), by the Pallava king Mahendravarman I of Kāñci (early seventh century), shows a drunken Kāpālika ascetic and his female companion who lose their begging bowl, a skull, and accuse a Buddhist monk of stealing it; a Pāśupata ascetic is called in to judge, and the bowl is finally recovered from a madman who had snatched it from a dog. The play mocks the pretensions of religious sects with impartial glee. The Bhagavadajjuka (“The Saint and the Courtesan”), of uncertain authorship and date, is a comedy in which a yogin, to demonstrate his powers, enters the body of a dead courtesan, while the god of death’s messenger, to correct his mistake, puts the courtesan’s soul into the yogin’s body; the courtesan-yogin and the yogin-courtesan then behave hilariously out of character. Both plays are still performed in the Kūṭiyāṭṭam repertoire.

docs.title: 3.11 Language, Gender and Caste on the Stage
docs.text:
The Nāṭyaśāstra, and the later handbooks that refined its rules, assign languages to characters by social position. Kings, brahmins, ministers and other high-ranking men speak Sanskrit; women, including queens, generally speak Śaurasenī Prakrit, and in the classical plays their verses and songs are usually in Māhārāṣṭrī; servants, the vidūṣaka, and low-status characters speak Prakrit, and characters of the lowest status speak varieties such as Māgadhī. Exceptions were allowed: Buddhist nuns, courtesans and some exceptional women may speak Sanskrit, as the learned Kāmandakī does in the Mālatīmādhava.

This linguistic hierarchy has often been praised as a sign of the theatre’s realism. It is better understood as a convention that encoded social hierarchy. It reflects the fact that Sanskrit learning was restricted, in principle, to men of the upper varṇas, and it places women of every rank linguistically alongside servants. Similarly, the stock types of the theatre — the gluttonous brahmin jester, the courtesan with a heart of gold, the comic low-caste executioner — were shaped by the assumptions of a courtly and largely male audience. The Mṛcchakaṭika and some prahasanas show that dramatists could use these conventions to satirise the powerful, but the plays should not be read as neutral mirrors of society. The issue of who could be a dramatist is related: almost all known authors of Sanskrit drama were men of brahmin or royal background.

docs.title: 3.12 From Sanskrit Drama to Regional Theatre
docs.text:
By the early second millennium new composition of Sanskrit drama had become a largely learned pursuit, but the theatre itself lived on and was transformed in the regional languages. In Kerala, Kūṭiyāṭṭam preserved the staging of Sanskrit plays, while two new dance-dramas grew up beside it: Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam, based on the Sanskrit Kṛṣṇagīti (1654) of the Zamorin Mānavēda, a work modelled on the Gītagovinda, and Kathakaḷi, with its Malayalam āṭṭakkatha texts (Chapter 10). In Assam, Śaṅkaradeva’s one-act aṅkīyā nāṭ plays of the sixteenth century adopted the benediction and a sūtradhāra who sings, dances and narrates throughout; they remain part of the Sattriya tradition of the Vaiṣṇava monasteries (Chapter 9). In Karnataka and Andhra, Yakṣagāna and its relatives used a narrator-singer (bhāgavata) and episodes from the epics and Purāṇas, and in Tamil Nadu the Bhāgavata Mēḷa dance-dramas of Melattur, composed in Telugu, continued a tradition of devotional theatre performed by brahmin men.

These forms are not simple survivals of classical drama. They are new creations, shaped by devotional movements, regional languages and local performance traditions, which borrowed selectively from Sanskrit theory. Their study belongs to the history of theatre and dance, treated in Volume 9 of this series.

docs.title: 3.13 Sanskrit Drama and the World
docs.text:
European knowledge of Sanskrit drama began with Sir William Jones’s English translation of Śakuntalā (1789). Georg Forster’s German version (1791) was read with enthusiasm by Herder and Goethe, who wrote an admiring epigram on the play and borrowed the device of a prologue spoken by a theatre director for his Faust. Horace Hayman Wilson’s Select Specimens of the Theatre of the Hindus (1826–27) made several more plays available in English. A. B. Keith’s The Sanskrit Drama (1924) was long the standard account of the subject in English (Keith 1924).

Attempts to derive Sanskrit drama from Greek theatre, popular in the nineteenth century, have not been substantiated; the two traditions developed largely independently, and Sanskrit drama’s roots are more plausibly sought in Indian epic recitation, ritual and dance.

docs.title: 3.14 A Living Tradition: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
docs.text:
The only performance tradition of Sanskrit drama to survive continuously is Kūṭiyāṭṭam (“combined acting”) of Kerala, traditionally performed in temple theatres (kūttampalam) by men of the Cākyār community with women of the Naṅṅyār community and Nampyār drummers. Its documented history goes back about a thousand years; the Cēra king Kulaśekhara, author of two Sanskrit plays, is traditionally credited with reforming it. Kūṭiyāṭṭam stages single acts of plays (by Bhāsa, Harṣa, Śaktibhadra and others) over many nights (Figure 3.1), with extended elaborations in which an actor may take hours to develop a single verse through gesture. It uses a codified gestural language (mudrā) described in the manual Hastalakṣaṇadīpikā, and is accompanied by the large copper miḻāvu drums. UNESCO proclaimed Kūṭiyāṭṭam a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2001. Its performance practice is described more fully in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya.

Figure 3.1. A Kūṭiyāṭṭam performance: the actor in elaborate costume and make-up beside a lit oil lamp, with a woman seated on the floor at the left and, at the right, an iṭakka player and a miḻāvu drum in its wooden frame. Photo: Ramesh Lalwani, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (from Flickr)

Modern productions of Sanskrit plays, both in Sanskrit and in translation, have been staged by the National School of Drama and by directors such as K. N. Panikkar and Ratan Thiyam, while Kālidāsa’s plays have been adapted for the stage and screen in many Indian languages.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Ghosh (1950): translation of the Nāṭyaśāstra.

  • Miller (1984): Kālidāsa’s three plays, with an essay on his dramaturgy.

  • Keith (1924): a classic history of Sanskrit drama.

  • Pollock (2016): the theory of rasa in its theatrical context.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Sanskrit Prose: Gadya Kāvya, Story Literature and Campū
4.1 Prose as Art
docs.text:
Prose was used in Sanskrit from the Vedic Brāhmaṇas onwards for ritual exegesis, philosophy, grammar and commentary. Artistic prose (gadya kāvya), however, is a classical creation. A well-known saying calls prose “the touchstone of poets” (gadyaṃ kavīnāṃ nikaṣaṃ vadanti): without the support of metre the writer must sustain rhythm, sound and imagery through word-choice and syntax alone. The great works of Sanskrit prose are few, but they are among the most demanding and distinctive works of the literature.

The theorists distinguished two kinds of prose narrative. Bhāmaha describes the ākhyāyikā as a story told by the hero himself, based on real events, divided into chapters called ucchvāsa and containing verses in particular metres; the kathā is told by someone other than the hero, is invented, and lacks these features. Daṇḍin rejected the distinction as artificial, observing that the supposed rules are not followed in practice and that the two are a single genre under two names. In later usage Bāṇa’s Harṣacarita was regarded as the model ākhyāyikā and his Kādambarī as the model kathā.

docs.title: 4.2 Subandhu: Vāsavadattā
docs.text: The earliest surviving prose romance is the Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (sixth century), who is praised by Bāṇa and therefore preceded him. Its slight plot — Prince Kandarpaketu sees a princess in a dream, finds and elopes with her, loses her when she is turned to stone, and recovers her — serves as a frame for descriptions saturated with double meanings. Subandhu boasts in his introduction that his work is a composition with a pun in every syllable (pratyakṣaraśleṣamayaprabandha). The result is a virtuoso display of śleṣa that delighted learned readers and set a standard for ornate prose.

docs.title: 4.3 Bāṇa
docs.text: Bāṇa (Bāṇabhaṭṭa), who lived at the court of Harṣavardhana of Kanauj (r. 606–647), is the greatest master of Sanskrit prose. His two works are very different in subject but share a style of extraordinary richness: long compounds that can extend over many lines, chains of similes and double meanings, sustained alliteration, and a constant play of learned allusion.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Harṣacarita
docs.text:
The Harṣacarita (“The Deeds of Harṣa”), in eight chapters (ucchvāsa, “breaths”), is the earliest major Sanskrit prose biography of a historical ruler and an important source for seventh-century history. It is unfinished in the sense that it stops long before Harṣa’s reign is fully described.

The first two chapters tell of Bāṇa’s mythological ancestry and of his own early life. Orphaned young, he wandered with a band of friends that included poets, musicians, a snake-doctor and ascetics of several sects, until he was summoned to Harṣa’s court, where he was at first received coolly; this is one of the few extended autobiographical narratives in Sanskrit. The third and fourth chapters turn to the ancestry of the Puṣyabhūti kings of Thanesar, the birth of Rājyavardhana, Harṣa and their sister Rājyaśrī, and Rājyaśrī’s marriage to the Maukhari king Grahavarman. Then disaster follows disaster: their father Prabhākaravardhana dies and their mother burns herself; Grahavarman is murdered; Rājyavardhana defeats the king of Mālava but is treacherously killed by the king of Gauḍa; and Harṣa vows to rid the earth of the Gauḍa king. The last two chapters follow Harṣa’s march and the search for Rājyaśrī, who has fled to the Vindhya forest and is rescued, with the help of the Buddhist teacher Divākaramitra, at the moment she is about to enter the funeral fire.

The work’s set descriptions — of a royal camp, of a dying king’s bedside, of a forest settlement of hunters, of Divākaramitra’s hermitage where followers of many sects live together — give an unrivalled picture of the society of the time. Cowell and Thomas’s translation (1897) is still useful (Cowell and Thomas 1897).

As a historical source the Harṣacarita must be used with care: it is a panegyric, written to glorify Harṣa, and it presents events through the conventions of kāvya. Its account can, however, be checked against inscriptions of Harṣa and against the record of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited Harṣa’s court in the 640s and describes his great religious assemblies at Kanauj and Prayāga. The two sources agree on the main outlines of the reign and differ in emphasis — the pilgrim stressing Harṣa’s patronage of Buddhism, the poet his Brahmanical and royal virtues — and together they make Harṣa one of the best-documented rulers of early India.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Kādambarī
docs.text:
The Kādambarī, a kathā based loosely on a tale from the Bṛhatkathā, is a romance spanning several lifetimes, told through narratives nested inside one another. Bāṇa died before completing it; the second part (Uttarabhāga) was written by his son, whose name is given variously as Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa or Pulinda, and who imitates his father’s style closely. Gwendolyn Layne’s translation conveys the whole (Layne 1991). Table 4.1 sets out its nested narratives.

Table 4.1. The nested narratives of the Kādambarī Level Narrator Content 1 Bāṇa A Caṇḍāla maiden brings a learned parrot, Vaiśampāyana, to the court of King Śūdraka of Vidiśā 2 The parrot His birth in the Vindhya forest, his rescue as a fledgling, and his upbringing in the hermitage of the sage Jābāli 3 Jābāli (as reported by the parrot) The story of Prince Candrāpīḍa of Ujjayinī and his friend Vaiśampāyana, the minister’s son 4 Mahāśvetā (within Jābāli’s story) Her love for the young ascetic Puṇḍarīka, who died of longing for her, and her vow to wait for his return 3 (cont.) Jābāli Candrāpīḍa’s love for Mahāśvetā’s friend, the Gandharva princess Kādambarī; the deaths of Vaiśampāyana and Candrāpīḍa Resolution (Uttarabhāga) Śūdraka is revealed as Candrāpīḍa reborn, the parrot as Puṇḍarīka (reborn as Vaiśampāyana), and the Caṇḍāla maiden as the goddess Lakṣmī; the curses end and both pairs of lovers are united

The Kādambarī is a work about longing, memory and the persistence of love across death and rebirth. Its descriptions — of the Vindhya forest, of Ujjayinī, of the lake Acchoda and of Mahāśvetā practising austerities in a cave — became models for later writers, and the title itself became a common noun (see below). Comparisons with modern European novelists, often made, should not obscure how different the work’s premises are: its interest lies less in individual psychology than in the play of emotion and description within a cosmic order of curses and rebirths.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Bāṇa’s Style
docs.text:
Bāṇa’s sentences can extend over several pages: a single main verb may be preceded by dozens of descriptive compounds, each a miniature image, arranged in patterns of sound and sense. A description of a forest, a city or a woman is built up by accumulation, each phrase adding a simile, a double meaning or a learned allusion, until the object described is seen from every side. Poets and critics of later centuries counted Bāṇa among the masters, and a well-known saying claims that “all the world is Bāṇa’s leftovers” (bāṇocchiṣṭaṃ jagat sarvam), meaning that he left nothing for later writers to describe; modern readers have sometimes found the style exhausting. Read slowly and aloud, as it was meant to be, it achieves effects of richness and rhythm unlike anything else in Indian literature. Table 4.2 compares his prose with Subandhu’s.

Table 4.2. Subandhu and Bāṇa compared Feature Subandhu, Vāsavadattā Bāṇa, Kādambarī Length Short Long; completed by the author’s son Narrative Simple, linear plot Several lives and nested narrators Style Dominated by śleṣa Long compounds, simile, description; śleṣa used more selectively Characters Thinly drawn Fuller portrayal of emotion, especially in Mahāśvetā Influence Model of ornate wordplay Model for later romance; word for “novel” in Marathi and Kannada

docs.title: 4.4 Daṇḍin: Daśakumāracarita
docs.text:
The Daśakumāracarita (“The Adventures of the Ten Princes”) is generally ascribed to Daṇḍin, author of the Kāvyādarśa (c. 700), though the identity of the two has been questioned. The core of the work survives with an introduction (Pūrvapīṭhikā) and conclusion (Uttarapīṭhikā) written by other hands to complete it. The defeated King Rājahaṃsa of Magadha takes refuge in the Vindhya forest, where his son Rājavāhana grows up with nine companions. The ten young men are separated and, on meeting again, each tells his adventures. The narrators include Rājavāhana, Apahāravarman, Upahāravarman, Arthapāla, Pramati, Mitragupta, Mantragupta and Viśruta; the episodes of Somadatta and Puṣpodbhava are told in the added introduction.

The stories take place in a world of gamblers, thieves, courtesans, merchants, corrupt ascetics and scheming ministers. The princes win kingdoms and wives by trickery as often as by valour, and the narrative treats this with relish. Daṇḍin’s prose is lighter and more varied than Bāṇa’s; the most famous tour de force is Mantragupta’s narrative, which avoids all labial consonants because, the story explains, his lips are sore from his lover’s kisses. Isabelle Onians’s translation brings out the work’s wit (Onians 2005).

docs.title: 4.5 Story Literature
docs.text: Beside the ornate prose of the court there flourished a vast literature of tales (kathā), simpler in style, often mixing prose with verse maxims, and connected with oral storytelling.

docs.title: 4.5.1 The Bṛhatkathā and Its Descendants
docs.text: The Bṛhatkathā (“Great Story”) of Guṇāḍhya, said to have been composed in the Paiśācī Prakrit, is lost; its date is uncertain, perhaps the early centuries CE. It is known through later adaptations: the Nepalese Bṛhatkathāślokasaṃgraha of Budhasvāmin (date uncertain, perhaps eighth or ninth century), and two eleventh-century Kashmiri versions, Kṣemendra’s Bṛhatkathāmañjarī and Somadeva’s Kathāsaritsāgara. The frame story concerns Naravāhanadatta, son of King Udayana of Vatsa, and his rise to become emperor of the semi-divine vidyādharas.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Somadeva’s Kathāsaritsāgara
docs.text:
The Kathāsaritsāgara (“Ocean of the Rivers of Story”), composed in verse by Somadeva between about 1063 and 1081 for Queen Sūryamatī of Kashmir, is divided into eighteen books (lambaka) and 124 chapters (taraṅga, “waves”), with over 21,000 verses. Around the frame story it gathers hundreds of tales of every kind: romances, adventures, fables, stories of clever thieves and foolish brahmins, and tales of magic and the supernatural. C. H. Tawney’s translation, edited with extensive notes by N. M. Penzer, runs to ten volumes (Tawney 1924).

The best-known cycle within it is the Vetālapañcaviṃśati (“Twenty-Five Tales of the Vetāla”). King Trivikramasena is asked by an ascetic to bring him a corpse hanging from a tree in a cremation ground. The corpse is possessed by a vetāla, a spirit, which tells the king a story as he carries it and ends with a riddle; if the king knows the answer and stays silent his head will burst, but if he speaks the vetāla returns to its tree. The riddles turn on questions of justice, obligation and identity. The cycle also circulated separately and was retold in many languages, in later versions with King Vikramāditya as hero.

docs.title: 4.5.3 An Example: The Transposed Heads
docs.text: One of the best-known riddles of the Vetālapañcaviṃśati shows how these stories turn on questions of identity and law. A young wife, travelling with her husband and her brother, stops at a temple of the goddess. The husband, overcome by devotion, cuts off his own head as an offering; the brother, finding him, does the same. The wife, about to kill herself in despair, is stopped by the goddess, who tells her to put the heads back on the bodies and they will live. In her haste she puts each head on the wrong body. The vetāla asks: which of the two men is now her husband? The king answers that the one with the husband’s head is her husband, since the head is the chief of the limbs and the seat of identity. The tale was retold many times; Thomas Mann’s novella Die vertauschten Köpfe (1940) and Girish Karnad’s Kannada play Hayavadana (1971) are modern versions.

docs.title: 4.5.4 Jain Story Literature
docs.text: Jain monks were among the most prolific writers of narrative, in Prakrit (Chapter 5) and in Sanskrit alike. Haribhadra’s Dhūrtākhyāna (eighth century, in Prakrit) is a satire in which five rogues compete in telling impossible tales, each of which turns out to have a parallel in the Purāṇas — a pointed critique of Brahmanical mythology. Siddharṣi’s Upamitibhavaprapañcā Kathā (906 CE) is a vast allegory in which the soul’s wanderings through the cycle of rebirth are told as the adventures of a beggar in a city whose inhabitants are the passions and virtues. Hemacandra’s Pariśiṣṭaparvan (twelfth century) collects legends of the Jain patriarchs, including stories of Candragupta Maurya and Cāṇakya. Jain narrative literature, often addressed to merchant audiences, is notable for its realism about trade, travel and family life.

docs.title: 4.5.5 Other Story Collections
docs.text:
Other widely read collections include the Siṃhāsanadvātriṃśikā (“Thirty-Two Tales of the Throne”), in which statuettes on Vikramāditya’s throne tell of his virtues, and the Śukasaptati, described below. The Pañcatantra and Hitopadeśa, the most influential of all, are discussed with the wisdom literature in Chapter 8.

Frame Narratives The “frame story”, in which a narrative contains stories told by its characters, which may themselves contain further stories, is characteristic of Indian story literature from the Mahābhārata onwards. Through Persian and Arabic translations of the Pañcatantra the technique reached the Islamic world and Europe. The frame of the Thousand and One Nights is often traced to Indian models, and it has been argued that Indian collections influenced medieval European frame-tale collections; direct lines of influence on works such as Boccaccio’s Decameron remain debated.

docs.title: 4.5.6 The Parrot’s Seventy Tales
docs.text: The Śukasaptati (“Seventy Tales of the Parrot”) shows the frame story used with comic ingenuity. A merchant’s son goes abroad on business, leaving his young wife with a learned parrot. Bored and tempted, the wife sets out each evening to meet a lover; each evening the parrot, rather than forbidding her, asks how she would extricate herself from a situation like that of some heroine of a story — and then tells the story, so absorbingly that dawn comes before she can leave. Many of the tales concern clever women who escape discovery by quick wit, so that the parrot teaches resourcefulness even while preventing infidelity. The collection, which survives in a “simple” and an “ornate” recension, was translated into Persian as the Ṭūṭīnāma (“Parrot Book”; Section 12.5), of which a richly illustrated copy was made for the young Akbar, and from Persian into Turkish and other languages.

docs.title: 4.5.7 Prose in the Regional Languages
docs.text: Artistic and narrative prose appeared early in several regional languages. The Kannada Vaḍḍārādhane (tenth century), nineteen stories of Jain ascetics, is a landmark of early Dravidian prose; the Marathi Līḷācaritra (c. 1278), episodes from the life of the Mahānubhāva founder Cakradhar, preserves a lively colloquial idiom; Tamil developed a sophisticated prose in the commentaries on classical poetry, such as Naccinārkkiṉiyar’s, and in the maṇipravāḷam commentaries of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas on the Āḻvār hymns; and Braj and Rajasthani prose chronicles (khyāt, vārtā) recorded dynastic history and the lives of Vaiṣṇava devotees. These traditions, rather than Sanskrit court prose alone, formed the background against which the modern prose of the nineteenth century developed.

docs.title: 4.6 The Campū: Prose and Verse Combined
docs.text:
The campū is a narrative kāvya in which prose and verse alternate, both being fully ornate. Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa already names it as a mixed composition of prose and verse, but the earliest surviving examples date from the tenth century; from then on it remained popular in Sanskrit until the nineteenth century, and in Kannada and Telugu several early classics take this form (Table 4.3).

The form is not simply prose interrupted by verse. In a well-made campū the two media divide the work between them. The prose, in long periods rich in compounds like Bāṇa’s (Section 4.3), carries extended description — a city, a forest, a season, a royal assembly — and often sustains a double meaning through whole sentences; the verses, in a variety of classical metres, mark the points of emotional intensity, sum up a scene, give a speech its edge, or move the story quickly over ground that the prose would linger on. Readers trained in both kinds of kāvya could enjoy the changes of pace and texture, and the campū was regarded as a test of a poet’s command of both.

Table 4.3. Some notable campū works Work Author Date Subject Nalacampū Trivikramabhaṭṭa early 10th c. The story of Nala and Damayantī Yaśastilaka Somadeva Sūri 959 CE Jain romance of King Yaśodhara, with a manual of Jain lay ethics Vikramārjunavijaya Pampa (Kannada) 941 CE The Mahābhārata (Chapter 10) Rāmāyaṇacampū attributed to Bhoja 11th c. The Rāma story Varadāmbikāpariṇaya Tirumalāmbā 16th c. The marriage of the Vijayanagara king Acyutarāya, by a woman poet of his court Gopālacampū Jīva Gosvāmin late 16th c. The life of Kṛṣṇa, as Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional narrative Nīlakaṇṭhavijaya Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita 1637 The churning of the ocean and Śiva’s drinking of the poison Viśvaguṇādarśa Veṅkaṭādhvarin 17th c. Two celestial travellers debate the merits and faults of the places and people of India

Trivikramabhaṭṭa’s Nalacampū, also called the Damayantīkathā and the earliest surviving Sanskrit campū, was written at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court in the early tenth century; its author is probably the Trivikrama who composed a copper-plate grant of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Indra III dated 915. It retells the story of Nala and Damayantī from the Mahābhārata in prose so saturated with double meaning (śleṣa) that a great many of its sentences can be read in two ways, and it breaks off in the seventh chapter, long before the end of the story. It shows the campū at its most virtuosic, a display of what Sanskrit could be made to do.

Somadeva Sūri’s Yaśastilaka (959), written by a Digambara Jain monk at the court of a Cāḷukya feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas in present-day Telangana, is the most ambitious. Its story concerns King Yaśodhara, who, to avert the omen of a bad dream, sacrifices not a living animal but a cock made of flour, and is nonetheless condemned, with his mother, to a long series of animal births for the intention of killing; the tale thus dramatises the Jain teaching that the intention to harm is itself violence. Around this narrative Somadeva built an encyclopaedia: descriptions of court life, debates between the religious and philosophical schools of his day, discussions of polity and the arts, and, in the last three of its eight books, a full manual of the duties of the Jain layman. K. K. Handiqui’s study of the work remains a basic source for the cultural history of tenth-century India (Handiqui 1949). Somadeva also wrote the Nītivākyāmṛta, a treatise on polity in aphorisms (see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

The Rāmāyaṇacampū (also called Campūrāmāyaṇa), attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā (Chapter 6), covers the first five books of Vālmīki’s epic; the war book was supplied by later poets, of whom Lakṣmaṇasūri’s continuation became the usual one. Its smooth verses and moderate prose made it a favourite text for teaching kāvya, especially in South India, where it was long read in traditional schools as an introduction to ornate Sanskrit. Anantabhaṭṭa’s Bhāratacampū, of uncertain date, did the same for the Mahābhārata.

The later Sanskrit campūs, many of them from South India, show the range of the form. Tirumalāmbā’s Varadāmbikāpariṇaya, on the marriage of her own king, is one of the few surviving works of Sanskrit court literature by a woman (see Section 2.11). Jīva Gosvāmin’s Gopālacampū, written at Vṛndāvana, made the campū a vehicle for the theology of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas (compare Rūpa Gosvāmin’s theory of devotional rasa, Chapter 6). Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita of Madurai, whose satires are mentioned in Chapter 2, dated his Nīlakaṇṭhavijaya in its opening verses to a year of the Kali era corresponding to 1637, and filled the myth of the churning of the ocean with the wit of a court intellectual. Veṅkaṭādhvarin’s Viśvaguṇādarśa (“Mirror of the Virtues of the World”) turns the form to social observation: two celestial beings travel over India, one finding fault with everything he sees — temples, towns, scholars, priests, the customs of each region — and the other answering by pointing out its merits, so that the work becomes a dialogue on the virtues and vices of the society of its day.

The campū had an equally important life in the Dravidian languages. In Kannada it was the dominant form of the classical age, from Pampa’s Ādipurāṇa and Vikramārjunavijaya (941) to the works of Ponna, Ranna and Janna (Chapter 10), and its prestige was such that the Vīraśaiva poets who rejected court literature defined their own forms against it. Telugu adopted the mixture of verse and prose from Nannaya’s Mahābhāratamu onwards, though verse predominates; and in Malayalam the maṇipravāḷam campūs of the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, among them Punam Nampūtiri’s Rāmāyaṇam, were closely tied to the recitation and exposition of the Cākyār performers of the temple theatre (compare Section 3.14). In each language the form offered what it had offered in Sanskrit: room both for the expansive pleasures of descriptive prose and for the concentrated effect of the stanza.

docs.title: 4.7 From Kathā to Novel
docs.text: When the novel arrived in Indian languages in the nineteenth century, writers and critics looked back to Sanskrit prose for precedents. The word kādambarī became the ordinary term for “novel” in Marathi and Kannada, and in Bengali the novel was at first called upanyāsa, a Sanskrit word for a kind of narrative. Early novelists such as Bankimcandra drew on the descriptive and romantic conventions of Sanskrit prose and drama as well as on Walter Scott. Translations and adaptations of the Kādambarī, the Daśakumāracarita, the Vetālapañcaviṃśati and the Pañcatantra were among the first printed books in many languages. Scholars debate how far the Indian novel grew from these indigenous roots and how far it was a colonial import; most now see a combination of the two, in which a European form was naturalised through older Indian narrative traditions.

docs.title: 4.8 Prose and Its Readers
docs.text: Who read Bāṇa and Subandhu? Their works presuppose readers with a thorough training in Sanskrit grammar, lexicography and poetics, able to resolve long compounds and to catch double meanings and allusions — in practice, a small élite of court poets, scholars and connoisseurs. The story collections reached a far wider audience, both in their Sanskrit forms and, above all, through oral retelling and translation into the regional languages, so that their tales became part of the common stock of Indian storytelling. The contrast between the two kinds of prose — the one an exercise of supreme verbal art for a few, the other a vehicle of narrative for many — mirrors a wider contrast in Indian literary culture between the courtly and the popular, which the devotional poets and, later, the modern novelists would each in their own way try to bridge.

docs.title: 4.9 An Outline of Sanskrit Prose
docs.text:
Table 4.4 summarises the main phases of Sanskrit narrative prose discussed in this chapter.

Table 4.4. The development of Sanskrit narrative prose Period Authors and works Characteristics Vedic and early Brāhmaṇas, Upaniṣads, early sūtra commentary Expository prose; embedded narratives 6th–8th c. Subandhu, Bāṇa, Daṇḍin High literary prose; long compounds, śleṣa, description 10th–12th c. Campū authors; Kṣemendra, Somadeva Mixed forms; verse retellings of story literature 12th c. onwards Story collections; later campūs and prose romances Wider audiences; regional adaptations
