  • Onians (2005): Daṇḍin’s Daśakumāracarita.

  • Tawney (1924): Somadeva’s Kathāsaritsāgara, with notes on its tales’ spread.

  • Handiqui (1949): Somadeva Sūri’s Yaśastilaka and tenth-century Deccan culture.

  • Warder (1972–2011): the fullest history of prose kāvya and story literature (later volumes).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Pali, Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa Literature
docs.text: sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti, sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti, sabbaratiṃ dhammarati jināti, taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jināti. The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts; the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes; delight in the Dhamma surpasses all delights; the destruction of craving overcomes all suffering. — Dhammapada 354

docs.title: 5.1 Introduction: The Middle Indo-Aryan Literatures
docs.text:
The literatures of this chapter are as old as classical Sanskrit kāvya, and in part older: the Pali canon was taking shape before Aśvaghoṣa wrote, and Hāla’s Prakrit anthology was known to Bāṇa and quoted by the theorists of the next chapter. Alongside Sanskrit, the Indo-Aryan languages of the subcontinent developed through a “middle” stage, the Prakrits (prākṛta, “natural” or “derived”), before giving rise to the modern languages. Several of these became literary languages in their own right. Pali became the scriptural language of Theravāda Buddhism; Ardhamāgadhī and other Prakrits served the Jains; Māhārāṣṭrī was the language of lyric poetry and of songs in drama; and Apabhraṃśa, the latest stage, was used for narrative poetry, especially by Jain authors, from about the sixth to the fifteenth century (Table 5.1).

Table 5.1. Middle Indo-Aryan literary languages Language Principal literary use Pali The Theravāda Buddhist canon, commentaries and chronicles Ardhamāgadhī The canon of the Śvetāmbara Jains Jain Śaurasenī Digambara Jain doctrinal texts Māhārāṣṭrī Lyric and court poetry (Hāla, Pravarasena); Jain narrative; verse in drama Śaurasenī Prose of women and middle-ranking characters in drama Māgadhī Speech of some low-status characters in drama Paiśācī Guṇāḍhya’s lost Bṛhatkathā (by tradition) Apabhraṃśa Jain narrative poetry; Buddhist and other mystical songs; transitional to the modern languages

docs.title: 5.1.1 Why Not Sanskrit?
docs.text: The choice of a literary language was never neutral. Early Buddhist tradition records that the Buddha refused a request to put his teaching into Vedic metre and allowed monks to learn it in their own dialects; whatever the historical basis of the story, it expresses an ideal of accessibility. Jain tradition held that Mahāvīra preached in Ardhamāgadhī, a language understood by all beings. Over time, however, both communities adopted Sanskrit as well: northern Buddhist schools composed their scriptures and philosophy in Sanskrit from the early centuries CE, and Jain scholars wrote in Sanskrit from the fifth century onwards. The Prakrits themselves became learned, standardised languages, studied through grammars such as Vararuci’s Prākṛtaprakāśa and Hemacandra’s grammar (see Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā); Hāla’s Māhārāṣṭrī poetry is as artful as any Sanskrit kāvya. The history of the Middle Indo-Aryan literatures is thus not a simple story of “popular” languages opposed to an “elite” one, but of several literary languages, each with its own prestige and its own communities, interacting over many centuries. Andrew Ollett has argued that Prakrit was, from the start, a language of literary art deliberately set beside Sanskrit, and that the two together formed a single “language order” within which poets chose the register that suited their work (Ollett 2017).

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Tipiṭaka
docs.text: The Pali canon (Tipiṭaka, “Three Baskets”) consists of the Vinaya Piṭaka (monastic discipline), the Sutta Piṭaka (discourses attributed to the Buddha and his disciples, in five collections or nikāyas) and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka (systematic analysis of doctrine). According to Sri Lankan tradition it was written down in the first century BCE, after centuries of oral transmission. The fifth collection of the Sutta Piṭaka, the Khuddaka Nikāya (“Minor Collection”), contains most of the canon’s poetry. K. R. Norman’s Pāli Literature and Oskar von Hinüber’s Handbook of Pāli Literature are the standard surveys (Norman 1983; Hinüber 1996). This chapter treats the canon as literature; its doctrine and history, and those of the Jain canon below, are the subject of Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā.

docs.title: 5.2.2 The Dhammapada
docs.text:
The Dhammapada (“Verses on Dhamma”), with 423 verses in 26 chapters (vagga), is the best known of all Pali texts. As literature it belongs to the Indian tradition of gnomic verse: most of its stanzas are in the same śloka metre as the Sanskrit epics, and many have close parallels in the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, the Sanskrit Udānavarga and even in Brahmanical and Jain maxims. Its art is one of compression and pairing. The first chapter, “Pairs” (Yamaka), sets verse against verse, the corrupted mind against the pure one; its famous opening stanza on the primacy of the mind is discussed as psychology in Volume 22, Manas and Śikṣā, and as a specimen of Pali grammar in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā. A few stanzas later comes the most quoted of all:

Dhammapada 5

na hi verena verāni sammantīdha kudācanaṃ | averena ca sammanti esa dhammo sanantano || Never here are hatreds stilled by hatred; they are stilled by non-hatred. This is the eternal law.

The stanza turns on a single word repeated and then negated (vera, avera), and it closes with a phrase, dhammo sanantano, that Brahmanical texts used for their own eternal law. Elsewhere a whole doctrine is distilled into a single observation:

Dhammapada 277

sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā ti yadā paññāya passati | atha nibbindati dukkhe esa maggo visuddhiyā || “All conditioned things are impermanent”: when one sees this with wisdom, one turns away from suffering. This is the path to purity.

Table 5.2. Some chapters of the Dhammapada Ch. Vagga Verses Theme 1 Yamaka (Pairs) 20 Paired verses contrasting wholesome and unwholesome minds 2 Appamāda (Vigilance) 12 Heedfulness as the path to the deathless 3 Citta (Mind) 11 Taming the restless mind 5 Bāla (The Fool) 16 The ways of the foolish 6 Paṇḍita (The Wise) 14 The ways of the wise 14 Buddha 18 The Buddhas and their teaching 20 Magga (The Path) 17 The eightfold path 26 Brāhmaṇa 41 The true brahmin is defined by conduct, not birth

Some of its chapters are summarised in Table 5.2. The last chapter is notable for redefining the word brāhmaṇa: the true brahmin is not one born of a brahmin mother, but one who is free from attachment and has destroyed the defilements — an implicit challenge to the hereditary claims of the Brahmanical order.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Theragāthā and Therīgāthā
docs.text:
The Theragāthā (“Verses of the Elder Monks”) and Therīgāthā (“Verses of the Elder Nuns”) are anthologies of poems attributed to early disciples who attained liberation. The Therīgāthā contains 73 poems (about 520 verses) attributed to nuns. Its poems were composed over several centuries and their attributions are traditional, but they form one of the earliest anthologies of poems in women’s voices in any literature. They speak of the hardships of women’s lives — domestic drudgery, marriage, the death of children, ageing — and of the freedom found in renunciation. The mother of Sumaṅgala rejoices at being free of the pestle, the cooking pots and a husband she did not respect; Paṭācārā, who lost her husband, children and parents in a single catastrophe, finds peace; the former courtesan Ambapālī contrasts the beauty of her youth with her aged body in a refrain of impermanence. Charles Hallisey’s translation is the most recent in English (Hallisey 2015).

The Theragāthā, the larger collection (264 poems, about 1,280 verses), is equally rich. Its monks speak of the joy of solitude in the forest during the rains, with peacocks calling and clouds thundering, of the struggle against desire and pride, and of the peace of liberation. Some poems are vivid autobiographies — of a former brahmin, a former king, a former outcaste scavenger, Sunīta, who tells how he was despised by all until the Buddha received him into the order. Together the two collections form one of the earliest bodies of religious lyric in India, and their imagery of nature and of inner struggle anticipates much later Indian poetry.

docs.title: 5.2.4 The Jātaka
docs.text:
The Jātaka (“Birth Stories”) are tales of the previous lives of the Buddha as a bodhisatta, in which he appears as a king, a merchant, a brahmin, an outcaste, an animal or a tree-spirit. Only the verses are canonical; the prose stories in which they are set are preserved in a commentary of about the fifth century CE, which contains 547 stories. Each story follows a set pattern: a “story of the present” that gives the occasion for telling; the “story of the past”; the verses; a word commentary; and a final “connection” in which the Buddha identifies the characters of the past with people of his own time.

Many Jātaka stories are folk tales and fables shared with the Pañcatantra and other collections. They were carved on the railing of the stūpa at Bharhut (second century BCE) and the gateways of the great stūpa at Sāñcī (first century BCE), painted in the caves of Ajaṇṭā, and illustrated at Borobudur in Java. The last ten stories, the “Great Birth Stories” (Mahānipāta), are each associated in Theravāda tradition with one of the ten perfections (pāramī; Table 5.3).

Table 5.3. The ten “Great Birth” stories and their perfections (Theravāda tradition) Jātaka Perfection Story Temiya Renunciation (nekkhamma) A prince feigns dumbness for years to avoid becoming king Mahājanaka Energy (viriya) A shipwrecked prince swims for seven days Sāma Loving-kindness (mettā) A devoted son, caring for his blind parents, is shot by a king Nemi Resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) A righteous king is shown the heavens and hells Mahosadha Wisdom (paññā) A brilliant counsellor outwits rival ministers and a hostile king Bhūridatta Morality (sīla) A serpent prince keeps his vows though captured by a snake-charmer Candakumāra Patience (khanti) A prince is to be sacrificed through a wicked priest’s scheming Nārada Equanimity (upekkhā) A Brahmā god cures a king of a false doctrine Vidhura Truthfulness (sacca) A wise minister, lost at dice, teaches his captor Vessantara Generosity (dāna) A prince gives away his possessions, his children and his wife

The Vessantara Jātaka, the longest, is the most popular story in the Theravāda world, recited and performed at festivals in Sri Lanka and mainland Southeast Asia. Its hero’s gift of his wife and children to a cruel brahmin has troubled readers for two thousand years, and the story has generated a long tradition of debate on the ethics of giving.

docs.title: 5.2.5 An Example: The Hare in the Moon
docs.text: The Sasa Jātaka (no. 316) shows how simple and how powerful these stories can be. The future Buddha is born as a hare who lives in a forest with three friends, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. On a holy day the four resolve to give alms to anyone who asks. The god Sakka (Indra), wishing to test them, comes in the form of a hungry brahmin. The otter offers fish, the jackal meat and curds, and the monkey mangoes; but the hare, who eats only grass, has nothing to give, and so tells the brahmin to light a fire, into which he leaps to offer his own body as food. The fire does not burn him. Sakka reveals himself and, so that the hare’s virtue may be known throughout the age, paints his image on the face of the moon. The story explains the familiar “hare in the moon” of Indian folklore, and it was retold in Sanskrit by Āryaśūra and depicted in Buddhist art across Asia.

docs.title: 5.2.6 The Sutta Nipāta
docs.text: The Sutta Nipāta, another collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya, contains some of the oldest Buddhist poetry. Its fourth and fifth books, the Aṭṭhakavagga and Pārāyanavagga, are considered by many scholars to be among the earliest strata of the canon; they present a radical ideal of the wandering sage free from all views and attachments. The collection also includes the Mettasutta on loving-kindness, still recited daily in Theravāda countries, and verse narratives of the Buddha’s early life that differ from the later biographies.

docs.title: 5.2.7 Other Pali Literature
docs.text: The Milindapañha (“Questions of Milinda”), a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (second century BCE) and the monk Nāgasena, explains Buddhist doctrine through vivid similes; the famous image of the chariot, which is nothing apart from its parts, illustrates the doctrine of no-self. In Sri Lanka, the commentaries of Buddhaghosa (fifth century) and the chronicles Dīpavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa (fourth to sixth century) carried Pali literature into history-writing, and Pali kāvya continued to be composed there and in Myanmar and Thailand into modern times.

docs.title: 5.2.8 The Chronicles of Sri Lanka
docs.text: The Mahāvaṃsa (“Great Chronicle”), composed in Pali verse by the monk Mahānāma in perhaps the fifth or sixth century, tells the history of Buddhism and of the kings of Sri Lanka from the Buddha’s legendary visits to the island to the fourth century CE. Its central hero is King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, who defeats the Tamil king Eḷāra and builds the great stūpas of Anurādhapura. The chronicle was continued by later authors (the Cūḷavaṃsa) down to the end of the Kandyan kingdom in 1815. Like Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (Chapter 2), it is a work of history written within a religious and literary frame; in modern times its account of the war between Duṭṭhagāmaṇī and Eḷāra has been read as a charter for ethnic and religious nationalism, a use its monastic authors could not have foreseen.

docs.title: 5.2.9 Sanskrit Buddhist Literature
docs.text: Buddhists also wrote extensively in Sanskrit. Besides Aśvaghoṣa (Chapter 2), notable authors include Mātṛceṭa, whose hymns to the Buddha were widely recited; Āryaśūra, whose Jātakamālā retold thirty-four birth stories in polished prose and verse; and Śāntideva (eighth century), whose Bodhicaryāvatāra (“Entering the Path of Awakening”) combines philosophy with intense devotional poetry. The avadāna literature, such as the Divyāvadāna, collects edifying stories, including legends of Aśoka. Much of this literature survives only in Tibetan and Chinese translation.

docs.title: 5.3.1 The Canon
docs.text:
The Śvetāmbara Jains preserve a canon of some forty-five texts in Ardhamāgadhī, fixed, according to tradition, at a council at Valabhī in the fifth century CE: eleven Aṅgas (a twelfth is said to have been lost), twelve Upāṅgas, ten Prakīrṇakas, six Chedasūtras, four Mūlasūtras and two independent texts. The Digambaras do not accept this canon as authentic; their authoritative texts, such as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and the works of Kundakunda, are in Jain Śaurasenī. Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra (c. fourth–fifth century), the systematic summary of Jain doctrine accepted by both traditions, is written in Sanskrit.

The canonical texts include passages of literary quality: the Ācārāṅga’s description of Mahāvīra’s austerities, the parables of the Uttarādhyayana, and the stories of the Nāyādhammakahāo.

docs.title: 5.3.2 Jain Narrative
docs.text: Jain authors produced an immense narrative literature, retelling the epic stories in Jain terms and creating new romances to illustrate the workings of karma. Vimalasūri’s Paümacariya (date disputed, perhaps the early centuries CE), the earliest Jain Rāmāyaṇa, rejects as absurd the idea that Rāvaṇa had ten heads or that monkeys built a bridge: the rākṣasas and vānaras are human clans of vidyādharas, Rāvaṇa is a pious but flawed king killed by Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma ends as a Jain monk who attains liberation. Other major works include Saṅghadāsa’s Vasudevahiṇḍī, a Prakrit version of the Bṛhatkathā material; Haribhadra’s Samarāiccakahā (eighth century), a story of enmity pursued through nine births; and Uddyotana’s Kuvalayamālā (779 CE), a romance famous for its use of many languages and its descriptions of the speech of eighteen regional peoples.

docs.title: 5.3.3 Women in Jain Literature
docs.text: Jain literature gives women a prominent but contested place. The Jain order admitted nuns from the beginning, and nuns have generally outnumbered monks, both in the traditional figures for Mahāvīra’s community and today; stories of exemplary women — Candanā, the slave girl who became the head of Mahāvīra’s order of nuns; Rājīmatī, the bride abandoned by the tīrthaṅkara Neminātha on their wedding day, who followed him into renunciation and rebuked his brother’s advances; the sixteen “virtuous women” (satī) of later tradition — are retold in Prakrit, Sanskrit and the regional languages. Yet the two main Jain traditions disagreed fundamentally about women’s spiritual capacity. The Śvetāmbaras held that women can attain liberation and even that the nineteenth tīrthaṅkara, Mallī, was a woman; the Digambaras held that liberation requires nudity, impossible for women, so that a woman must first be reborn as a man. The debate produced a substantial literature from the early centuries CE onwards. Much Jain narrative also contains warnings against women as sources of attachment, so that its picture of women combines reverence for female ascetics with ascetic misogyny.

docs.title: 5.3.4 Jain Literature in the Regional Languages
docs.text: Jain writers played a major part in the early history of several regional literatures. In Tamil, Jain authors are credited with the Nālaṭiyār, the epic Cīvakacintāmaṇi, and grammars and lexicons; in Kannada, the classical campū poets Pampa, Ponna and Ranna were Jains, and the tenth-century Jain laywoman Attimabbe, a patron of literature, is said to have commissioned a thousand copies of Ponna’s Śāntipurāṇa for distribution; in Gujarat and Rajasthan, Jain monks wrote the earliest poems in the emerging regional language, the narrative and didactic rāsas, and Jain manuscript libraries (bhaṇḍār) at Patan, Jaisalmer and elsewhere preserved not only Jain texts but also many works of Brahmanical and secular literature that might otherwise have been lost. The contribution of Jain scholarship and patronage to Indian literature as a whole is out of all proportion to the size of the community.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Hāla’s Sattasaī
docs.text: The Gāhāsattasaī (Sanskrit Gāthāsaptaśatī, “Seven Hundred Verses”), an anthology of short poems in Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit in the gāthā (āryā) metre, is attributed to Hāla, a king of the Sātavāhana dynasty of the Deccan. The anthology grew over time, and its present form probably dates from around the third to fifth century, though it may contain older material; its recensions differ widely in content. Each stanza is a tiny drama, usually spoken by a woman — a young wife, a mother-in-law, a friend, a village girl — in a world of fields, rivers, threshing floors and hunting, in which love, desire, jealousy and wit are expressed obliquely. Sanskrit theorists of suggestion drew many of their examples from it (Section 6.5), and Govardhana’s Sanskrit Āryāsaptaśatī and Bihārī’s Hindi Satsaī follow its model. Peter Khoroche and Herman Tieken have translated it in full (Khoroche and Tieken 2009).

docs.title: 5.4.2 Prakrit Mahākāvyas and Romances
docs.text:
Prakrit was also used for court epics and romances on the Sanskrit model; some of the principal works are listed in Table 5.4.

Table 5.4. Some major works of Prakrit literature Work Author Date Remarks Setubandha (Rāvaṇavaho) Pravarasena II (Vākāṭaka) 5th c. Court epic on the building of Rāma’s bridge and the war Gauḍavaho Vākpatirāja 8th c. Court epic on Yaśovarman of Kanauj, whose title promises the slaying of a king of Gauḍa Līlāvaī Kautūhala c. 8th c. A verse romance Kuvalayamālā Uddyotana 779 CE Jain romance in prose and verse Karpūramañjarī Rājaśekhara c. 900 A play (saṭṭaka) entirely in Prakrit

docs.title: 5.5 Apabhraṃśa Literature
docs.text:
Apabhraṃśa (“fallen away”, a grammarians’ term for language that deviates from Sanskrit norms) is the name given to the last stage of Middle Indo-Aryan, used in literature from about the sixth century. Its literature is largely Jain, but it also includes the mystical songs and couplets (dohā) of Buddhist Tantric siddhas such as Saraha, which are related to the Old Bengali Caryāpada (Chapter 11), and secular poetry (Table 5.5).

Table 5.5. Major Apabhraṃśa works Work Author Date Remarks Paümacariu, Riṭṭhaṇemicariu Svayambhū 9th c. (?) Jain Rāmāyaṇa and Jain Kṛṣṇa–Neminātha story Mahāpurāṇa Puṣpadanta 10th c. Lives of the 63 great men of Jain tradition; written at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa capital Mānyakheṭa Ṇāyakumāracariu, Jasaharacariu Puṣpadanta 10th c. Shorter Jain narratives Bhavisattakaha Dhanapāla c. 10th c. The adventures of a merchant’s son Dohā collections Saraha and other siddhas c. 8th–12th c. Buddhist mystical couplets Saṃdeśarāsaka ʿAbd ur-Raḥmān (Addahamāṇa) 12th–13th c. A messenger poem in the tradition of the Meghadūta, by a Muslim poet

The Apabhraṃśa epic used a new verse form, the kaḍavaka, a group of rhyming couplets closed by a refrain-like stanza; rhyme, almost absent from classical Sanskrit verse, became a characteristic of Apabhraṃśa and of the modern Indo-Aryan languages that followed. The Saṃdeśarāsaka is notable as a work of the twelfth or thirteenth century by a Muslim author writing within the Indian poetic tradition.

docs.title: 5.6 Hemacandra
docs.text: The Jain monk Hemacandra (1088/89–1172/73), who enjoyed the patronage of the Caulukya kings Jayasiṃha Siddharāja and Kumārapāla of Gujarat, was one of the most prolific scholars of medieval India. His grammar, the Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana, treats Sanskrit in its first seven chapters and the Prakrits and Apabhraṃśa in the eighth; its illustrations of Apabhraṃśa include many fine dohās, some of which are among the earliest poetry in a form close to Gujarati and Hindi. He also wrote a work on poetics (Kāvyānuśāsana), lexicons, a treatise on yoga, a “double-purpose” poem (Dvyāśraya) that illustrates his grammar while narrating the history of his patrons’ dynasty, and the vast Sanskrit Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita, the lives of the sixty-three great men of Jain tradition.

docs.title: 5.7 Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa in the Later Literatures
docs.text: These literatures reappear throughout the rest of the book. The theorists of the next chapter took many of their finest examples of suggestion from Hāla’s anthology. The Jātaka shares its stories with the Pañcatantra (Section 8.12). The Apabhraṃśa dohā and the rhyming kaḍavaka passed into the devotional poetry of Kabīr and Tulsīdās (Chapter 9). And the Jain poets of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Karnataka wrote the first works of several regional literatures (Chapters 10 and 11).

  • Ollett (2017): Prakrit as a literary language beside Sanskrit.

  • Hallisey (2015): the poems of the first Buddhist nuns.

  • Khoroche and Tieken (2009): Hāla’s Prakrit anthology.

  • Lienhard (1984): classical poetry in Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Alaṅkāraśāstra: The Indian Theory of Literature
docs.text: kāvyasyātmā dhvanir iti budhair yaḥ samāmnātapūrvas tasyābhāvaṃ jagadur apare bhāktam āhus tam anye | kecid vācāṃ sthitam aviṣaye tattvam ūcus tadīyaṃ tena brūmaḥ sahṛdayamanaḥprītaye tatsvarūpam || The wise have long held that the soul of poetry is suggestion (dhvani). Some have denied that it exists; others have called it a secondary meaning; some have said its nature lies beyond the reach of words. We shall therefore explain its nature, for the delight of the hearts of sensitive readers. — Ānandavardhana, Dhvanyāloka 1.1

docs.title: 6.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Sanskrit possesses one of the longest continuous traditions of literary theory in the world. It is called alaṅkāraśāstra, “the science of ornament”, after its early concern with figures of speech, and also sāhityaśāstra, “the science of literature”. Its texts range from the chapters on poetics in Bharata’s Nāṭyaśāstra to Jagannātha’s Rasagaṅgādhara in the seventeenth century. A recurring question, especially from the ninth century onwards, was: what is the “soul” (ātman) of poetry — the element without which there is no poetry at all? Different writers answered: figuration, style, suggestion, oblique expression, propriety, rasa. Later historians organised these answers into “schools”, although the authors themselves did not always see their work in those terms. The standard histories are De (1960) and Gerow (1977); Pollock (2016) translates the central texts on rasa. The major theorists are listed in Table 6.1.

Table 6.1. Major theorists of Sanskrit poetics Theorist Date Work Principal contribution Bharata (attrib.) c. 200 BCE–200 CE Nāṭyaśāstra Rasa theory for the theatre; first lists of figures, qualities and faults Bhāmaha c. 6th–7th c. Kāvyālaṅkāra Figuration (alaṅkāra) grounded in “oblique” expression Daṇḍin c. 700 Kāvyādarśa Figures; the two “ways” (mārga); the ten qualities (guṇa) Vāmana c. 800 Kāvyālaṅkāra­sūtra­vṛtti Style (rīti) as the soul of poetry Udbhaṭa, Rudraṭa c. 800–900 Kāvyālaṅkāra­sāra­saṅgraha, Kāvyālaṅkāra Refinement of figures; Udbhaṭa lists nine rasas Ānandavardhana mid-9th c. Dhvanyāloka Suggestion (dhvani) as the soul of poetry Rājaśekhara early 10th c. Kāvyamīmāṃsā The poet’s training and craft Kuntaka c. 1000 Vakroktijīvita Oblique expression (vakrokti) Abhinavagupta c. 950–1016 Abhinavabhāratī, Locana Synthesis of rasa and dhvani; śānta rasa Mahimabhaṭṭa 11th c. Vyaktiviveka Critique of dhvani: suggestion as inference Bhoja 11th c. Śṛṅgāraprakāśa The erotic as the one fundamental rasa Kṣemendra 11th c. Aucityavicāracarcā Propriety (aucitya) Mammaṭa c. 1100 Kāvyaprakāśa Standard synthesis, accepting dhvani Ruyyaka 12th c. Alaṅkārasarvasva Systematic treatment of figures Viśvanātha 14th c. Sāhityadarpaṇa Poetry as “a sentence whose soul is rasa” Rūpa Gosvāmin 16th c. Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu Devotion (bhakti) as the supreme rasa Appayya Dīkṣita 16th c. Kuvalayānanda, Citramīmāṃsā Figures Jagannātha 17th c. Rasagaṅgādhara Last major synthesis; independent critique

docs.title: 6.2.1 The Rasa Sūtra
docs.text:
The sixth chapter of the Nāṭyaśāstra defines rasa (literally “juice”, “flavour”, “taste”) in a single prose sentence, the most discussed sentence in Indian aesthetics:

Nāṭyaśāstra 6, prose after verse 31 (Ghosh’s numbering)

vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasaniṣpattiḥ Rasa arises from the combination of the determinants, the consequents and the transitory states.

The determinants (vibhāva) are the causes of an emotion: its object or “support” (ālambana), for example the beloved, and the circumstances that excite it (uddīpana), such as moonlight or spring. The consequents (anubhāva) are its outward signs — glances, gestures, words. The transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva), thirty-three in Bharata’s list, are passing feelings such as anxiety, joy, shame, envy, fatigue and doubt that accompany and colour the dominant emotion. In addition Bharata lists eight involuntary “states of the spirit” (sāttvikabhāva): paralysis, perspiration, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears and fainting.

Each rasa corresponds to a “stable” emotion (sthāyibhāva); Bharata names eight (Figure 6.1). He also gives each a colour and a presiding deity. These correspondences matter chiefly for performance and are tabulated in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya (Chapter 3). For the reader of poetry the more useful question is where each rasa is found. Table 6.2 gives illustrations from works discussed in this volume.

Table 6.2. The rasas illustrated from works discussed in this volume Rasa English Illustrations Śṛṅgāra Erotic Love in separation in the Meghadūta; the Amaruśataka; the Gītagovinda Hāsya Comic The vidūṣaka; the farces Mattavilāsa and Bhagavadajjuka Karuṇa Pathetic Aja’s lament (Raghuvaṃśa 8); the Uttararāmacarita Raudra Furious Bhīma’s vow to avenge Draupadī in the Veṇīsaṃhāra Vīra Heroic Raghu’s conquest of the quarters (Raghuvaṃśa 4); the Kirātārjunīya Bhayānaka Terrible The deer fleeing the king’s chariot (Śākuntala, Act 1) Bībhatsa Odious The cremation-ground scene of the Mālatīmādhava Adbhuta Marvellous The magician’s illusion in the Ratnāvalī; Duṣyanta’s descent from heaven (Śākuntala, Act 7) Śānta Tranquil The Mahābhārata, on Ānandavardhana’s reading; Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī, by its author’s statement Figure 6.1. Bharata’s eight rasas with their stable emotions, and the ninth, śānta, whose status was debated.

docs.title: 6.2.2 The Rasa Debate
docs.text:
What does it mean to say that rasa “arises”? Where is it located — in the character, the actor or the spectator? Four answers, known mainly through Abhinavagupta’s report in his commentary on the Nāṭyaśāstra, the Abhinavabhāratī, shaped the later tradition (Pollock 2016):

  1. Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa (eighth–ninth century) held that rasa is the stable emotion of the original character (Rāma, say), intensified by the determinants and the rest, and attributed to the actor who imitates him. Rasa is “produced” (utpatti).

  2. Śrī Śaṅkuka argued that the spectator infers the emotion from the signs presented by the actor, as one recognises a picture of a horse as a horse; rasa is an imitated emotion apprehended by inference (anumiti).

  3. Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka (ninth–tenth century) objected that neither the character’s emotion nor an inference about it could account for aesthetic pleasure. He proposed that poetic language has, besides denotation, two further powers: one that “generalises” the content, freeing it from personal reference (bhāvakatva), and one that leads the spectator to “enjoy” it (bhojakatva).

  4. Abhinavagupta accepted the generalisation (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) but rejected the special powers, explaining rasa as the suggestion (dhvani) of an emotion that the spectator “tastes” (āsvāda, carvaṇā) through the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) in his own mind. Rasa is manifested (abhivyakti), not produced, and exists only in the experience of the responsive spectator.

Abhinavagupta also discussed the obstacles that prevent aesthetic experience — among them lack of plausibility, absorption in one’s own pleasure or pain, inadequate means of presentation, and doubt — and described the experience itself as a wonder (camatkāra) akin to, but not identical with, the bliss of spiritual realisation.

docs.title: 6.2.3 Śānta and the Number of Rasas
docs.text: Whether there is a ninth rasa, the tranquil (śānta), was one of the great disputes of Indian aesthetics. Udbhaṭa (c. 800) is the earliest theorist known to list nine; some manuscripts of the Nāṭyaśāstra include a passage on śānta that is probably a later addition. Opponents objected that tranquillity, the cessation of emotion, cannot be represented on the stage. Abhinavagupta defended śānta at length, identifying its stable emotion as the knowledge of truth (tattvajñāna) and treating it as the rasa into which all others ultimately resolve (Masson and Patwardhan 1969). Later theorists added others: the affection of parents for children (vātsalya) and, in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition of Rūpa Gosvāmin, devotion (bhakti) as the highest rasa. V. Raghavan’s The Number of Rasas traces these debates (Raghavan 1940).

docs.title: 6.2.4 The Heroine and Her Situations
docs.text:
Much of the practical analysis of love poetry rested on the classification of heroines (nāyikā), first set out in the Nāṭyaśāstra and elaborated by later writers. The best-known scheme describes eight situations in which a heroine may be found (aṣṭanāyikā; Table 6.3).

Table 6.3. The eight situations of the heroine Heroine Situation Vāsakasajjā Dressed and waiting, the chamber prepared, for her lover’s arrival Virahotkaṇṭhitā Distressed because her lover is late Svādhīnabhartṛkā Whose lover is devoted and at her side Kalahāntaritā Separated by a quarrel she herself provoked, and now repentant Khaṇḍitā Angry with a lover who arrives bearing the marks of another woman Vipralabdhā Deceived, having gone to the tryst where her lover does not come Proṣitabhartṛkā Whose husband is away on a journey Abhisārikā Going out to meet her lover, braving darkness, storm or moonlight

These types, and the corresponding classifications of heroes and of messengers and confidantes, gave poets, painters and dancers a shared repertoire of situations. The Hindi rīti poets wrote whole treatises illustrating them, the Pahari painters depicted them, and they remain the basis of expressive dance (abhinaya) in Bharatanāṭyam, Kathak and Odissi. Modern readers have noted that the scheme defines women almost entirely in relation to a male lover, a limitation of the courtly world from which it came.

docs.title: 6.3 Alaṅkāra: Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin
docs.text:
The earliest surviving independent works on poetics, Bhāmaha’s Kāvyālaṅkāra and Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa, are largely devoted to figures of speech (alaṅkāra). Bhāmaha held that what makes language poetic is a certain “crookedness” or obliquity (vakrokti), a departure from ordinary statement, which underlies all figures:

Bhāmaha, Kāvyālaṅkāra 2.85

saiṣā sarvaiva vakroktir anayārtho vibhāvyate | yatno ’syāṃ kavinā kāryaḥ ko ’laṅkāro ’nayā vinā || All this is oblique expression; through it meaning is made to shine. The poet should strive for it: what figure is there without it?

Daṇḍin divided the poetic manner into two “ways” (mārga), the Vaidarbha (of Vidarbha, in the Deccan) and the Gauḍa (of Bengal). He identified ten qualities (guṇa) as the “life” of the Vaidarbha way, which the Gauḍa way often reverses (Table 6.4), and classified a large number of figures with examples.

Table 6.4. Daṇḍin’s ten qualities (Kāvyādarśa 1.41–100) Guṇa Translation Description Śleṣa Compactness Close-knit sound, avoiding loose syllables Prasāda Clarity Meaning easily understood Samatā Evenness Consistency of sound texture Mādhurya Sweetness Presence of rasa; pleasing repetition of sounds Sukumāratā Softness Avoidance of harsh syllables Arthavyakti Explicitness Meaning complete without strain Udāratva Elevation Suggestion of some excellence Ojas Vigour Abundance of compounds Kānti Loveliness Conformity to common experience; avoidance of the far-fetched Samādhi Transference Attribution of the qualities of one thing to another

Vāmana later distinguished ten qualities of sound and ten of sense bearing the same names, while Ānandavardhana and Mammaṭa reduced the qualities to three — sweetness (mādhurya), vigour (ojas) and clarity (prasāda) — understood as properties of rasa rather than of words.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Figures of Speech
docs.text:
The number of recognised figures grew from about forty in Bhāmaha and Daṇḍin to over a hundred in Appayya Dīkṣita’s Kuvalayānanda. Figures were divided into figures of sound (śabdālaṅkāra) and figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra), with some writers recognising mixed figures. Edwin Gerow’s Glossary of Indian Figures of Speech is the standard reference (Gerow 1971). Table 6.5 lists some of the principal figures.

Table 6.5. Some principal figures (alaṅkāra) Figure Approximate equivalent Description Anuprāsa Alliteration Repetition of consonants Yamaka “Twinning” Repetition of a syllable-sequence with different meanings Śleṣa Paronomasia Words bearing two meanings at once Upamā Simile Explicit comparison of subject and standard Rūpaka Metaphor Identification of subject with standard Utprekṣā Poetic fancy Imagining the subject to be something else (“as if”) Atiśayokti Hyperbole Statement exceeding the actual Arthāntaranyāsa Corroboration A particular statement supported by a general truth, or vice versa Vyatireka Contrast The subject shown as superior to the standard Vibhāvanā Peculiar causation An effect described without its usual cause Viśeṣokti Peculiar allegation A cause present but its usual effect absent Svabhāvokti Natural description Vivid description of a thing as it is (its status as a figure was disputed)

docs.title: 6.3.2 Faults
docs.text: The theory of faults (doṣa) was as detailed as that of qualities. Mammaṭa (Kāvyaprakāśa, chapter 7) classifies faults of words (pada), of sentences (vākya), of meaning (artha) and of rasa. Faults of words include harshness of sound (śrutikaṭu), grammatical incorrectness (cyutasaṃskṛti) and the use of words not used by poets (aprayukta); faults of sentence include ambiguity and faulty construction; faults of rasa include naming an emotion directly instead of evoking it, and dwelling on a subsidiary element at the expense of the main one. A fault can, in some contexts, become a merit — harsh sounds, for instance, suit the furious rasa.

docs.title: 6.4 Rīti: Vāmana
docs.text: Vāmana (c. 800), probably a minister of King Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir, wrote his Kāvyālaṅkāra­sūtra­vṛtti in aphorisms with his own commentary. He declared that “style is the soul of poetry” (rītir ātmā kāvyasya, 1.2.6), defining style as “a particular arrangement of words” (viśiṣṭā padaracanā rītiḥ, 1.2.7) whose particularity consists in the qualities. He recognised three styles: the Vaidarbhī, possessing all the qualities and the best; the Gauḍī, marked by vigour and long compounds; and the Pāñcālī, marked by sweetness and softness.

docs.title: 6.5 Dhvani: Ānandavardhana
docs.text: The Dhvanyāloka (“Light on Suggestion”) of Ānandavardhana, a Kashmiri writer at the court of Avantivarman (r. 855–883), transformed Sanskrit poetics. Earlier theory had analysed poetry largely in terms of its expressed content and its ornaments. Ānandavardhana argued that in the best poetry the most important meaning is not expressed at all but suggested.

docs.title: 6.5.1 The Three Powers of Words
docs.text:
Indian philosophers of language recognised two ways in which words convey meaning. Denotation (abhidhā) conveys the conventional meaning. Indication (lakṣaṇā) operates when the denoted meaning is impossible in context: in the stock example gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ, “a cowherd village on the Ganges”, a village cannot literally be on the river, so the expression indicates “on the bank of the Ganges”. Ānandavardhana added a third power, suggestion (vyañjanā), which conveys a further meaning without the literal meaning being blocked. In the indication example, the speaker’s choice of words also suggests the coolness and purity of the village. Similarly, the sentence “The sun has set” may suggest, according to the speaker and situation, that it is time to stop work, to bring in the cattle, or for a lover to come.

Ānandavardhana, Dhvanyāloka 1.13

yatrārthaḥ śabdo vā tam artham upasarjanīkṛtasvārthau | vyaṅktaḥ kāvyaviśeṣaḥ sa dhvanir iti sūribhiḥ kathitaḥ || That kind of poetry in which the meaning, or the word, subordinating its own (literal) sense, suggests that (other) meaning, is called dhvani by the wise.

docs.title: 6.5.2 A Classic Example
docs.text:
Ānandavardhana’s first illustration of suggestion is a Prakrit stanza, also found in Hāla’s anthology (Section 5.4), in which the suggested meaning is the opposite of what is said:

Quoted in Dhvanyāloka 1.4, vṛtti

bhama dhammia vīsattho so suṇao ajja mārio deṇa | golāṇaīkacchakuḍaṅgavāsiṇā dariasīheṇa || Wander freely now, pious sir: that dog was killed today by the fierce lion that lives in the thickets on the bank of the Godā.

On its face the sentence is an invitation: the dog that troubled the pious man while he gathered flowers is dead, so he may walk about without fear. But a woman who uses the riverside thicket as a meeting-place with her lover says it, and what she suggests is a prohibition: if a dog frightened you, a lion will do worse — keep away. Nothing in the words expresses the prohibition; it is conveyed by the speaker, the situation and the implications of “lion”. For Ānandavardhana the example shows that a suggested meaning can differ in kind from the expressed one and cannot be reduced to denotation or indication.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Rasa Analysed: An Illustration
docs.text: The theorists analysed scenes in terms of the components of rasa. In the departure scene of the Abhijñānaśākuntala (Chapter 3), for example, the stable emotion is the affection and grief of parting. Śakuntalā and her impending absence are the “support” (ālambana); the forest, the trees and the fawn that she has tended are “exciting” determinants (uddīpana); Kaṇva’s choked voice and tear-dimmed eyes are consequents (anubhāva) and involuntary states (sāttvika); and anxiety, recollection and dejection are transitory states (vyabhicārin). The spectator, according to Abhinavagupta, does not grieve for a particular old man in a particular forest but tastes the generalised experience of parting from a beloved child — and finds in that tasting a kind of delight. This kind of analysis, applied verse by verse, was the staple of commentaries and of teaching.

docs.title: 6.5.4 Kinds of Suggested Meaning
docs.text:
What is suggested may be a fact or idea (vastu), a figure of speech (alaṅkāra), or an emotion (rasa, together with related states). Since an emotion can never be conveyed by naming it — to say “she was in love” does not evoke love — rasa can only be suggested, and rasa-dhvani is the highest form of poetry. Ānandavardhana graded poetry in three classes: poetry in which suggestion predominates (dhvani); poetry in which a suggested meaning is present but subordinate to the expressed (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya); and “picture poetry” (citra), which relies on verbal or ornamental effects with little suggestion.

The theory was not accepted without resistance (see below), but Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Dhvanyāloka, the Locana, and Mammaṭa’s Kāvyaprakāśa established the dhvani theory as orthodoxy. The Dhvanyāloka with the Locana is available in a fine annotated translation by Ingalls, Masson and Patwardhan (Ingalls et al. 1990).

docs.title: 6.5.5 The Critics of Dhvani
docs.text: The opponents whom Ānandavardhana anticipates in his opening verse were real, and the debate continued for two centuries. Some held that what he called suggestion was simply a form of indication (lakṣaṇā); others, following the Mīmāṃsā philosophers, that the “purport” of a sentence (tātparya) could extend as far as needed to cover any implied meaning; Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka argued that rasa is not suggested but “enjoyed” through special powers of poetic language; and Mahimabhaṭṭa, in the Vyaktiviveka (eleventh century), set out to show that every case of suggestion is an inference from the expressed meaning, and appended a long analysis of faults in Kālidāsa and other poets. Abhinavagupta and Mammaṭa answered these objections in detail, and the controversy sharpened the analysis of meaning on all sides. It is one of the best examples of the way Indian intellectual traditions advanced through sustained argument with opponents.

docs.title: 6.6 Vakrokti: Kuntaka
docs.text:
Kuntaka (c. 1000), in his Vakroktijīvita (“Oblique Expression, the Life of Poetry”), developed Bhāmaha’s notion of obliquity into a comprehensive theory. He defined poetry as follows:

Kuntaka, Vakroktijīvita 1.7

śabdārthau sahitau vakrakavivyāpāraśālini | bandhe vyavasthitau kāvyaṃ tadvidāhlādakāriṇi || Word and meaning together, set in a composition marked by the poet’s oblique craft and delighting those who know it, constitute poetry.

Kuntaka identified six levels at which obliquity can operate: the arrangement of sounds (varṇavinyāsa), the word-base (padapūrvārdha), the suffix (padaparārdha or pratyaya), the sentence (vākya), the episode (prakaraṇa) and the whole composition (prabandha). His analyses of how a dramatist alters a source story to create new effects invite comparison with modern narrative criticism. K. Krishnamoorthy’s edition and translation made the work widely known (Krishnamoorthy 1977).

Kuntaka’s discussion of “obliquity in the episode” and “obliquity in the whole composition” is especially original. He argues that a poet who takes a story from the epics shows his creative power by changing it: introducing an episode the source lacks, altering a motive, or shifting the emphasis so that the whole work acquires a new meaning. Kālidāsa’s introduction of the curse of Durvāsas into the story of Śakuntalā, which turns a tale of a king’s cynical denial into a drama of memory and recognition (Chapter 3), is the kind of transformation Kuntaka has in mind. Modern readers interested in adaptation and rewriting will find in him a sophisticated precursor, though his concern was with the poet’s craft rather than with intertextuality as such.

docs.title: 6.7 Aucitya: Kṣemendra
docs.text: The Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra (eleventh century), a pupil of Abhinavagupta, wrote in his Aucityavicāracarcā that propriety is “the enduring life of poetry perfected by rasa” (aucityaṃ rasasiddhasya sthiraṃ kāvyasya jīvitam). Every element of a poem — a word, a grammatical form, a figure, a quality, a sentiment, a detail of time and place — must be fitting to its context; a beautiful ornament becomes a fault if it is out of place. The principle was not new (Ānandavardhana had already called impropriety the main cause of the breaking of rasa), but Kṣemendra made it the organising idea of a whole treatise, illustrating it with good and bad examples from many poets.

docs.title: 6.8 Abhinavagupta, Mammaṭa and the Later Tradition
docs.text:
Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016), philosopher of Kashmiri Śaivism as well as critic, gave the tradition its most influential synthesis in his two commentaries, the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Locana on the Dhvanyāloka. His account of rasa as suggested, generalised and tasted by the responsive reader joined Bharata’s theatre theory to Ānandavardhana’s theory of poetry. His life dates are an estimate: the firm evidence is his own dating of some of his works, which fall between about 990 and 1015. Although Abhinavagupta drew on his philosophical commitments, his aesthetic theory does not require them, and it was accepted by writers of quite different religious views. Lawrence McCrea has argued that the Kashmiri theorists from Ānandavardhana to Mammaṭa turned poetics into a discipline of interpretation, which judged every element of a work by its contribution to the whole, above all to its rasa (McCrea 2008).

Mammaṭa’s Kāvyaprakāśa (c. 1100) arranged the whole subject — definition and purposes of poetry, the powers of words, dhvani, rasa, qualities, faults and figures — into a compact textbook that attracted more than seventy commentaries and dominated teaching for centuries. Later theorists include Ruyyaka, whose Alaṅkārasarvasva systematised figures; Bhoja (discussed below); Viśvanātha, whose Sāhityadarpaṇa became a popular textbook in northern and eastern India; and Appayya Dīkṣita.

The last major theorist was Jagannātha, who wrote at the Mughal court of Shāh Jahān in the seventeenth century and was also a fine lyric poet (Section 2.15). His unfinished Rasagaṅgādhara criticises his predecessors freely, defines poetry by the delightful meaning it conveys rather than by rasa alone (Section 1.2), and is illustrated almost entirely with verses of his own, since he declared that he would not borrow from others. It shows that the tradition remained capable of independent argument until the eve of the colonial period.

The theory also crossed into other domains: it was recast as a theology of devotion by Rūpa Gosvāmin (below), and the rasa and heroine classifications became the basis of Hindi rīti poetry, of the rāgamālā painting tradition and of classical dance.

docs.title: 6.9 The Science of Metre
docs.text:
Alongside poetics proper stood prosody (chandas), one of the six ancillary sciences of the Veda. The Chandaḥsūtra attributed to Piṅgala (perhaps the last centuries BCE) classifies both Vedic and classical metres; it describes each syllabic metre by means of groups of three syllables (gaṇa), each a combination of heavy and light, named by letters, so that a whole line can be encoded in a short formula. Piṅgala’s methods for enumerating all possible combinations of heavy and light syllables in a line of given length involve procedures that later commentators developed into what we would call binary representation and combinatorics, a subject treated in Volume 11, Gaṇita; prosody as a linguistic science is discussed in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā. Later handbooks such as Kedāra Bhaṭṭa’s Vṛttaratnākara and the Śrutabodha attributed to Kālidāsa, often composed so that each definition is itself written in the metre it defines, became standard school texts.

Prakrit poetry used moraic metres, in which a line is measured by the number of morae (a light syllable counting one, a heavy two) rather than by a fixed sequence of syllables; the āryā or gāthā is the most important. The Apabhraṃśa and modern Indo-Aryan literatures developed further moraic metres, with end-rhyme, such as the dohā and caupāī, while the Dravidian literatures had their own systems: the Tamil veṇpā and akaval, the Kannada ṣaṭpadi and ragaḷe, and the Telugu sīsa and dvipada. Metre was an essential part of how Indian audiences experienced poetry, and much is lost when it is read only in prose translation.

docs.title: 6.10 Two Later Departures: Bhoja and Rūpa Gosvāmin
6.10.1 Bhoja’s Śṛṅgāraprakāśa
docs.text: King Bhoja of Dhārā (eleventh century), patron and polymath, wrote two large works on poetics, the Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa and the Śṛṅgāraprakāśa (“Light on the Erotic”). The latter, one of the longest works in the tradition, argues that there is really only one rasa. Bhoja calls it śṛṅgāra, but he does not mean simply erotic love: śṛṅgāra for him is a kind of self-awareness or ego-sense (abhimāna, ahaṅkāra) in the cultivated person, which is the source of all emotional experience and which, when stimulated by literature, develops into the particular emotions that earlier theorists had called separate rasas. The theory had little following, but the Śṛṅgāraprakāśa preserves thousands of quotations from works otherwise lost and is a treasury for the history of Sanskrit and Prakrit literature. V. Raghavan’s classic study remains the guide to it (Raghavan 1963).

docs.title: 6.10.2 Rūpa Gosvāmin and Bhakti Rasa
docs.text: The most radical transformation of rasa theory came from the followers of Caitanya in sixteenth-century Vṛndāvana. Rūpa Gosvāmin’s Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu (“Ocean of the Nectar of the Rasa of Devotion”, 1541) and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi argued that devotion to Kṛṣṇa is the true and supreme rasa. Its stable emotion is love for Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇarati), which takes five principal forms according to the devotee’s relationship to God: tranquil contemplation, servitude, friendship, parental affection and erotic love, the last — modelled on the love of Rādhā and the cowherd women — being the highest. In this theory the devotee is not merely a spectator who tastes rasa but a participant who cultivates an emotional identity within Kṛṣṇa’s eternal play; the categories of the theatre become a discipline of religious practice. The Gauḍīya theology shaped Bengali and Braj devotional poetry, painting and music, and illustrates how the vocabulary of poetics could be put to entirely new uses.

docs.title: 6.11 Poetics beyond Sanskrit
docs.text: Sanskrit poetics provided a model for the theory of literature in many other languages. The Kannada Kavirājamārga (c. 850) adapted Daṇḍin to Kannada; Hindi rīti poets of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries composed handbooks (lakṣaṇa-grantha) in which each figure, heroine or rasa is defined and illustrated by the author’s own verses (Chapter 11); and Telugu, Malayalam and Bengali writers produced similar works. Persian poetics, with its own categories of figures (ṣanāʾiʿ) and its debates over “fresh speech” (tāza-gūʾī), developed in parallel at the Mughal courts, and Urdu criticism drew on both (Chapter 12). These traditions were not mere copies: they adapted the theory to new languages, metres and audiences, and sometimes challenged it.

docs.title: 6.12 Tamil Poetics
docs.text: Tamil developed its own poetics independently of Sanskrit. The third book of the Tolkāppiyam, with its division of poetry into akam and puṟam, its landscape (tiṇai) conventions and its techniques of implicit comparison and suggestion, is described in Chapter 7. It also lists eight emotions (meyppāṭu): laughter, weeping, humiliation, wonder, fear, pride, anger and joy. These overlap with Bharata’s stable emotions but do not match them. Later Tamil grammars such as the Taṇṭiyalaṅkāram adapted Daṇḍin’s work, and the two traditions influenced one another (Hart 1975).

docs.title: 6.13 Comparative Perspectives
docs.text:
Modern scholars from A. K. Coomaraswamy and V. Raghavan to Edwin Gerow and Sheldon Pollock have compared Sanskrit poetics with Western theory. Some parallels are suggestive: dhvani with the study of implicature and connotation; sādhāraṇīkaraṇa with “aesthetic distance”; vakrokti with the Russian Formalists’ “defamiliarisation”; aucitya with classical decorum. Others are misleading. Sanskrit theory was centred on the court poem and the play; it had little to say about the epic as a genre, the authority of the author’s intention or the historical context of a work, and it took for granted a highly trained audience. Its emphasis on the reader’s response is genuine, but the “reader” in question was the cultivated connoisseur, not any reader whatever. Table 6.6 sets some of these concepts beside their nearest Western analogues.

Table 6.6. Some Sanskrit critical concepts and approximate Western analogues Sanskrit concept Approximate analogue Important difference Rasa Aesthetic emotion; catharsis Concerns the spectator’s “tasting” of a generalised emotion, not purgation Dhvani Connotation; implicature Treated as a distinct power of language, ranked above expressed meaning Vakrokti Defamiliarisation Rooted in the poet’s craft at all levels, from sound to plot Aucitya Decorum Extends to every element of a work, judged by its contribution to rasa Sahṛdaya Ideal or implied reader A trained connoisseur, not an abstraction of the text

Comparisons are most fruitful when they illuminate particular texts and problems. Claims that one tradition is simply “more advanced” than the other are of little value. What is distinctive in the Sanskrit tradition is its sustained, cumulative debate over many centuries, conducted through commentary and counter-argument, on how literary language produces its effects.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Ingalls et al. (1990): Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta in annotated translation.

  • Pollock (2016): translations of the key texts of the rasa debate.

  • Gerow (1971): the standard reference on figures of speech.

  • Raghavan (1940) and Masson and Patwardhan (1969): the number of rasas and the tranquil rasa.

  • Krishnamoorthy (1977): Kuntaka’s Vakroktijīvita.

  • McCrea (2008) and Raghavan (1963): the Kashmiri theorists, and Bhoja.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Classical Tamil Literature: The Caṅkam Poems and After
docs.text: yātum ūrē yāvarum kēḷir tītum naṉṟum piṟartara vārā Every town is our town, everyone our kin. Evil and good do not come from others. — Kaṇiyaṉ Pūṅkuṉṟaṉār, Puṟanāṉūṟu 192

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Tamil is the only modern Indian language with a substantial literature that is as old as the classical literatures of Sanskrit and Prakrit and independent of them. Its earliest layer is a body of some 2,400 poems, by some 470 named poets, collected in eight anthologies and ten long poems. These are commonly called “Caṅkam” (Sangam) poems, after a tradition, first recorded in a commentary of about the eighth century on the Iṟaiyaṉār Akapporuḷ, that three successive “academies” (caṅkam) of poets met under the patronage of the Pāṇṭiya kings over many thousands of years, the first two in cities later swallowed by the sea. The legend is not history, but the name has stuck.

Most scholars date the bulk of the anthology poems to roughly the first three centuries CE, with some poems perhaps earlier, and place the later layers — the Kalittokai, the Paripāṭal and the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai — in the fifth to seventh centuries. The poems were collected and arranged, with colophons naming poets and situations, several centuries after their composition (Zvelebil 1973, 1974).

This dating has been seriously challenged. In Kāvya in South India (2001) Herman Tieken argued that the poems are not the remains of an ancient bardic culture at all, but a learned literature composed at the Pāṇḍya court around the ninth century, close in time to the commentary that first tells the story of the academies (Tieken 2001). He pointed out that no external evidence for the poems is earlier than that period; that their conventions closely resemble those of Sanskrit and Prakrit court poetry, above all Hāla’s anthology of village love (Section 5.4); and that the world of poor bards and generous chiefs they describe may be a literary fiction of the kind kāvya delighted in, rather than a record of a real society. Most Tamil specialists, George Hart among them, have rejected the redating. They point to the language of the poems, which is older than that of the devotional hymns of the sixth to ninth centuries; to the internal differences between the earlier anthologies and the later layers; and to the agreement between the poems and the evidence of Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions, hero-stones and the archaeology of Indo-Roman trade (Section 7.8). The debate has nonetheless sharpened a point that both sides accept: the anthologies as we have them, with their arrangement, colophons and commentaries, are the product of a later scholarly act of compilation, and the poems reach us only through it. This book follows the majority dating, with this caution. They were almost forgotten in the medieval period and were recovered in the late nineteenth century from palm-leaf manuscripts by C. W. Tāmōtaram Piḷḷai and U. Vē. Cāminātaiyar, whose editions transformed the understanding of Tamil literary history.

The poems are mainly secular: they speak of love and war, of kings and bards, of the landscapes and seasons of the Tamil country. Their idiom owes little to Sanskrit, though Sanskrit words and North Indian deities and ideas appear, increasingly in the later layers. David Shulman’s Tamil: A Biography is an engaging introduction to the whole tradition (Shulman 2016).

docs.title: 7.2 The Tolkāppiyam
docs.text:
The Tolkāppiyam, ascribed to Tolkāppiyar, is the oldest surviving Tamil grammar. It has three books: Eḻuttatikāram on sounds and letters, Collatikāram on words and syntax, and Poruḷatikāram on “subject matter”, that is, poetics. Its date is disputed. Some Tamil scholars, such as S. Ilakkuvanar, have argued for a date several centuries before the Common Era (Ilakkuvanar 1963). Most historians see the work as layered: the first two books may belong to the last centuries BCE or the early centuries CE, while the Poruḷatikāram, which systematises the conventions of the anthology poems, is generally considered later, perhaps as late as the fifth century (Zvelebil 1974). Its grammar is discussed further in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā.

The Poruḷatikāram divides poetry into akam, the “interior” world of love between man and woman, and puṟam, the “exterior” world of war, kingship, generosity, death and fame. Each is subdivided into situations (tiṇai). It also describes the conventions governing who may speak in a poem, the elements that make up a poem’s setting, and the eight emotions (meyppāṭu) discussed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 7.3 The Tiṇai: Landscape and Love
docs.text:
The most distinctive feature of classical Tamil poetics is the association of each phase of love with a landscape. Each landscape has its “first elements” (mutal: place and time), its “native elements” (karu: gods, people, animals, plants, occupations, music) and its human situation (uri). A poem need only mention a flower, a bird or a kind of terrain for an informed listener to recognise the emotional situation. A. K. Ramanujan’s translations and essays introduced this system to a wide readership (Ramanujan 1967, 1985). Table 7.1 summarises the five landscapes.

Table 7.1. The five akam landscapes (simplified, after the Tolkāppiyam) Tiṇai (flower) Landscape Situation (uri) Season and time Deity Kuṟiñci Mountains Lovers’ union, secret meetings Cool season; midnight Murukaṉ Mullai (jasmine) Forest and pasture Patient waiting of the wife Rainy season; evening Māyōṉ (Viṣṇu) Marutam Cultivated riverine land The wife’s sulking at the husband’s infidelity All seasons; dawn Vēntaṉ (Indra) Neytal (water-lily) Seashore Anxious pining All seasons; sunset Varuṇaṉ Pālai Parched wasteland Separation; the lover’s journey; elopement Summer; midday (later Koṟṟavai)

Pālai is not a separate region but any land parched by heat, and the Tolkāppiyam adds two further “situations” outside the five: one-sided love (kaikkiḷai) and mismatched love (peruntiṇai). Figure 7.1 shows the five landscapes schematically.

Figure 7.1. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of classical Tamil love poetry, with their situations and presiding deities.

docs.title: 7.4 Akam: The Poetry of Love
docs.text:
Akam poems are dramatic monologues. They are spoken by the heroine, the hero, the heroine’s friend (tōḻi), her foster-mother, the hero’s companion, or occasionally passers-by; the commentarial tradition supplies for each poem a “situation” (tuṟai) that explains who speaks to whom and when. By convention the lovers are never named: they are types, not individuals, and the poem’s meaning depends on the reader’s recognition of the conventions. Love is divided into premarital “secret” love (kaḷavu) and married love (kaṟpu).

The most famous akam poem, from the Kuṟuntokai, is known by the name of its poet only through its central image: Cempulappeyanīrār, “the poet of the rain on red earth”.

Kuṟuntokai 40

yāyum ñāyum yārā kiyarō entaiyum nuntaiyum emmuṟaik kēḷir yāṉum nīyum evvaḻi yaṟitum cempulap peyanīr pōla aṉpuṭai neñcam tāṅkalan taṉavē What was my mother to yours? How was my father kin to yours? How did you and I ever meet? Like rain falling on red earth, our loving hearts have mingled.

The poem is spoken by the hero, according to the commentary, to reassure the heroine after their first union. Its effect depends on the closing simile: as rain and red soil mix and cannot be separated, so their hearts, unrelated by kinship, have become one.

docs.title: 7.5 Puṟam: The Poetry of the Public World
docs.text: Puṟam poetry celebrates and laments the public world: the valour and generosity of kings, the hunger of bards seeking patrons, battles, cattle raids, hero-stones raised for fallen warriors, and the transience of fortune. The Puṟanāṉūṟu (“Four Hundred Poems of the Exterior”), translated by George Hart and Hank Heifetz, is the great collection (Hart and Heifetz 1999). Its poems range from praise of patrons to meditations on death. In poem 278 an old mother, told that her son fled from battle, swears to cut off the breasts that fed him if it is true; she searches the battlefield, sword in hand, turning over the bodies, and when she finds him lying cut to pieces her joy is greater than on the day she bore him. The poem embodies the harsh martial ethic of the society. Others, like poem 192 quoted at the head of this chapter, express a broad and humane wisdom.

docs.title: 7.5.1 The Situations of Puṟam
docs.text:
Just as akam poetry has its landscapes, the Tolkāppiyam divides puṟam poetry into situations (tiṇai), each named after a flower worn by warriors and each paired with one of the akam landscapes. The principal ones are listed in Table 7.2.

Table 7.2. The puṟam situations of the Tolkāppiyam Tiṇai Situation Veṭci Cattle raid, the opening act of hostilities Vañci Invasion of enemy territory Uḻiñai Siege of a fort Tumpai Pitched battle Vākai Victory, and excellence in one’s calling Kāñci The transience of life and fortune Pāṭāṇ Praise of a king or patron, and the bard’s request for gifts

The kāñci theme, meditation on impermanence, gives some of the most memorable puṟam poems, and the Maturaikkāñci takes its name from it: its long description of the splendour of Madurai is framed as a warning to the king that all this will pass.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Hero-Stones
docs.text: Several puṟam poems refer to the custom of erecting a memorial stone (naṭukal) for a warrior who fell in battle, especially in defending cattle against raiders. The stone was inscribed with his name and deeds, decorated with peacock feathers and worshipped with offerings. The Tolkāppiyam lists the stages of the rite, from finding a suitable stone to its consecration. Hundreds of hero-stones, some inscribed in Tamil-Brāhmī and early Vaṭṭeḻuttu script, have been found in Tamil Nadu and neighbouring regions, confirming the poems’ picture of a society in which cattle raids and the cult of the heroic dead were important, and showing how closely the poetic conventions were tied to actual practice.

docs.title: 7.5.3 Suggestion in Akam Poetry
docs.text: The commentators describe two techniques by which akam poems convey meaning indirectly. In uḷḷuṟai uvamam, “implicit comparison”, a description of nature parallels the human situation without any word of comparison: a poem spoken by a wife whose husband is unfaithful may describe a buffalo trampling a pond full of lilies, leaving the listener to see the husband in the careless animal. In iṟaicci, “suggestion”, a detail of the landscape implies something about the speaker’s feelings that she cannot say directly. Such techniques make the Tamil poems remarkably dense, and they invite comparison with the Sanskrit theory of dhvani (Chapter 6), although the two developed independently (Ramanujan 1985). Modern readers have also compared the juxtaposition of scene and feeling with Imagism or with the “objective correlative”; such comparisons can help a newcomer, but the poems belong to their own system of landscapes and situations, as Ramanujan and Hart have shown.

docs.title: 7.5.4 Bards and Patrons: Kapilar and Pāri
docs.text: The Puṟanāṉūṟu preserves something like the story of a friendship. Pāri, chief of the hill country of Paṟampu, was celebrated as one of the most generous patrons of the age; legend says he once gave his chariot to a jasmine creeper that had no support to climb on. The three crowned kings besieged his hill and, unable to take it, killed him by treachery. The poet Kapilar, his friend, wrote poems on the siege, mocking the kings with the boast that they could never take Paṟampu by force, though they could have it for the asking if they came as bards; and after Pāri’s death he mourned his friend. A short poem ascribed to Pāri’s daughters themselves (Puṟanāṉūṟu 112) recalls the moonlit night of a month ago, when they had their father and their hill, and contrasts it with the present, when enemies hold both. Kapilar then took the orphaned daughters in search of husbands among the chiefs. Whatever the historical basis of the story, these poems give the bardic relationship between poet and patron a moving human face.

docs.title: 7.6 The Corpus: Eight Anthologies and Ten Long Poems
7.6.1 The Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai)
docs.text:
The eight anthologies, their size and their character are summarised in Table 7.3.

Table 7.3. The Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) Anthology Poems Type Remarks Naṟṟiṇai 400 akam Poems of 9–12 lines Kuṟuntokai 401 akam Short poems of 4–8 lines Aiṅkuṟunūṟu 500 akam 100 very short poems for each landscape, each set by a different poet Akanāṉūṟu 400 akam Longer poems of 13–31 lines, ordered by landscape Kalittokai 150 akam Later; dramatic poems in kali metre, including unconventional loves Puṟanāṉūṟu 400 puṟam War, kingship, patronage, death (a few poems lost) Patiṟṟuppattu 100 puṟam Ten decads on Cēra kings; the first and last decads are lost Paripāṭal 70 mixed Later; hymns to Murukaṉ and Tirumāl, and poems on the river Vaiyai; about 24 survive

docs.title: 7.6.2 The Ten Long Poems (Pattuppāṭṭu)
docs.text:
The ten long poems, with the poets named in the colophons, are listed in Table 7.4.

Table 7.4. The Ten Long Poems (Pattuppāṭṭu) Poem Poet Subject Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai Nakkīrar A later devotional “guide” poem to the shrines of Murukaṉ Porunarāṟṟuppaṭai Muṭattāmakkaṇṇiyār A war-bard guides another to the Cōḻa Karikāl Ciṟupāṇāṟṟuppaṭai Nattattaṉār A bard guides another to a generous chief Perumpāṇāṟṟuppaṭai Kaṭiyalūr Uruttiraṅkaṇṇaṉār Guide to the chief Toṇṭaimāṉ Iḷantiraiyaṉ of Kāñci Mullaippāṭṭu Nappūtaṉār A queen awaits her husband’s return from war in the rains Maturaikkāñci Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉār 782 lines on the Pāṇṭiya capital Madurai and the transience of power Neṭunalvāṭai Nakkīrar The long cold north wind; a queen’s loneliness while the king is at war Kuṟiñcippāṭṭu Kapilar A love poem of the mountain landscape Paṭṭiṉappālai Uruttiraṅkaṇṇaṉār The port city of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam, in a frame of separation Malaipaṭukaṭām Peruṅkuṉṟūr Peruṅkaucikaṉār A guide poem for musicians to the chief Naṉṉaṉ

The āṟṟuppaṭai (“guide”) poems are a distinctive genre: a bard returning laden with gifts meets a poor bard and directs him to the generous patron, describing the route and the landscapes along it.

docs.title: 7.6.3 The Later Layer: Toward Devotion
docs.text: The later poems of the corpus show a changing religious world. The Paripāṭal contains hymns to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu) and Murukaṉ in which Purāṇic myths — Viṣṇu’s incarnations, the birth of Murukaṉ from Śiva’s seed — are told in Tamil, alongside lively descriptions of festivals on the river Vaiyai at Madurai, where townspeople bathe and make love. The Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai adapts the secular “guide” genre to religion: instead of directing a bard to a generous patron, the poet directs a devotee to the six shrines of Murukaṉ, describing the god’s forms and the worship at each. These works stand at the threshold of the devotional poetry of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs (Chapter 9), and show how classical Tamil forms could be turned to new purposes.

docs.title: 7.7 The Poets
docs.text: The colophons name some 470 poets. They include brahmins, kings, merchants, artisans and bards, and about thirty women. Among the most celebrated are Kapilar, the most prolific poet of the corpus and a master of the kuṟiñci landscape; Paraṇar, known for his historical allusions; Nakkīrar; Māmūlaṉār; and Avvaiyār, a woman poet of both akam and puṟam who appears in the poems as a confidante of the chief Atiyamāṉ. The name Avvaiyār was also borne, or given by tradition, to later poets, including the medieval author of the didactic verses Ātticcūṭi and Koṉṟaivēntaṉ that are still taught to Tamil children.

docs.title: 7.7.1 Women Poets of the Anthologies
docs.text: The women poets of the anthologies write in both akam and puṟam modes. Veḷḷivītiyār is remembered for poems of a woman’s longing and of her defiance of convention in following her lover; Okkūr Mācāttiyār and Kākkaipāṭiṉiyār Nacceḷḷaiyār, to whom the Puṟanāṉūṟu poem on the heroic mother (no. 278) is ascribed, wrote of women’s pride and grief in a warrior society; and Avvaiyār’s poems range from tender love lyrics to sharp exchanges with chiefs. George Hart has argued that the presence of women poets and the prominence of women’s voices reflect a society in which women’s sexuality and power were viewed with both reverence and fear (Hart 1975). Whatever the explanation, the Tamil anthologies and the Pali Therīgāthā together preserve the largest body of early Indian poetry ascribed to named women.

docs.title: 7.8 The Poems as Historical Evidence
docs.text: The poems refer to the three crowned dynasties, the Cēra, Cōḻa and Pāṇṭiya, and to many lesser chiefs; to trade with the Yavanas (Greeks and Romans) who brought wine and gold for pepper; to ports such as Muciṟi and Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam; and to a society of farmers, herders, fishers, hunters, bards and warriors. Much of this is consistent with external evidence: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (first century CE) and Pliny describe the pepper trade of the Malabar coast; Roman coins and amphorae have been found in South India; excavations at Arikamedu near Puducherry and at Pattanam in Kerala have revealed Indo-Roman trading sites; and Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions from the second century BCE onwards document the early written language. Recent excavations at Kīḻaṭi near Madurai have uncovered an urban settlement of the early historic period whose dating and interpretation continue to be discussed. The poems are, however, poetry, written within strict conventions; they should be used as historical evidence with care.

docs.title: 7.9 After the Anthologies: The Eighteen Minor Works and the Tirukkuṟaḷ
docs.text: The period after the anthologies, roughly the fourth to sixth centuries, produced a collection known as the “Eighteen Minor Works” (Patiṉeṇkīḻkkaṇakku), mostly short didactic texts in the veṇpā metre, together with a few works on love and war. Several show Jain influence. The most famous is the Tirukkuṟaḷ, and among the others the Nālaṭiyār, a Jain anthology of 400 quatrains on ethics, is the best known. Neither belongs to the Caṅkam anthologies proper, although popular accounts often treat them so.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Tirukkuṟaḷ
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ is ascribed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar, about whom nothing reliable is known; the traditional biographies are late legends. Most scholars date the work to about the fifth century CE, though earlier and later dates have been proposed. It consists of 1,330 couplets (kuṟaḷ veṇpā) in 133 chapters of ten, arranged in three books that correspond to three of the classical aims of life: virtue (aṟam, 38 chapters), wealth and polity (poruḷ, 70 chapters) and love (iṉpam or kāmam, 25 chapters). It speaks of God in general terms, and has been claimed by Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Jains and Buddhists; its ethic of non-violence and vegetarianism has led many scholars to see Jain influence, though this remains debated. The first couplet opens the work:

Tirukkuṟaḷ 1

akara mutala eḻuttellām āti pakavaṉ mutaṟṟē ulaku As all letters have the letter a as their first, so the world has the Primal Lord as its first.

The chapter on learning (kalvi) begins:

Tirukkuṟaḷ 391

kaṟka kacaṭaṟak kaṟpavai kaṟṟapiṉ niṟka ataṟkut taka Learn thoroughly, without fault, what should be learned; and having learned it, live in accordance with it.

The first book, on virtue, begins with praise of God, rain, ascetics and virtue itself, and then treats the life of the householder — the good wife, children, love, hospitality, gratitude, impartiality, self-control, patience, non-violence — and the life of renunciation. The book on polity contains a realistic treatment of kingship, ministers, alliances and war; one of its couplets states that all living beings are alike by birth and that distinctions arise only from the differing quality of their actions (972), a statement often cited against caste. The book on love, in the voices of the lovers, draws on the conventions of the akam poems. The Tirukkuṟaḷ has been translated into English many times, and into many other languages, since the nineteenth century. A statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar 133 feet (about 40 metres) high, one foot for each chapter, was erected in 2000 on a rock off Kanyakumari (Figure 7.2).

Figure 7.2. The statue of Tiruvaḷḷuvar off Kanyakumari (completed 2000), with the Vivekananda Rock Memorial on the left. Photo: N. Vivekananthamoorthy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 7.10 The Tamil Epics
docs.text:
Tradition speaks of “five great epics” (aimperuṅkāppiyam): the Cilappatikāram, the Maṇimēkalai, the Cīvakacintāmaṇi, and two works that survive only in fragments, the Vaḷaiyāpati and the Kuṇṭalakēci.

The Cilappatikāram (“The Tale of the Anklet”), ascribed to Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ, a prince-turned-ascetic of the Cēra line, is usually dated to the fifth or sixth century. Its three books are set in the three Tamil kingdoms. The merchant Kōvalaṉ leaves his wife Kaṇṇaki for the courtesan-dancer Mātavi, loses his wealth, and returns to Kaṇṇaki; they go to Madurai to rebuild their fortune by selling one of her anklets, but Kōvalaṉ is falsely accused of stealing the queen’s anklet and executed on the king’s order. Kaṇṇaki proves his innocence before the king, who dies of remorse, and in her fury tears off her breast and burns the city. She becomes a goddess, Pattiṉi, whose cult the poem’s last book describes. The work is a rich source for music, dance and urban life, and blends Jain, Hindu and local religious elements.

The Cilappatikāram is unusual among Indian epics in its heroes: not kings or gods but a merchant couple and a courtesan. Its second canto-group, set in Madurai, includes the songs of cowherd women dancing in a circle to Kṛṣṇa (the āycciyar kuravai) and of hunters worshipping the goddess Koṟṟavai, and its account of Mātavi’s dance performance and training is a primary source for the history of South Indian music and dance. Its framing — a prince-poet who renounces the throne, and a prologue that states the work’s three morals (that dharma destroys an erring king, that the world honours a chaste wife, and that karma bears its fruit) — gives it a moral structure that later Tamil readers took to heart; Kaṇṇaki became a symbol of Tamil womanhood, a figure revered and, in modern feminist criticism, questioned.

Its sequel, the Maṇimēkalai of Cīttalaic Cāttaṉār, follows Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi’s daughter Maṇimēkalai, who renounces the world and becomes a Buddhist nun; it includes expositions of Buddhist and other philosophies. The Cīvakacintāmaṇi of Tiruttakkatēvar (ninth–tenth century), a Jain epic in the manner of the Sanskrit mahākāvya, tells of a prince who wins eight wives and a kingdom before renouncing all. The devotional poetry that arose between the sixth and ninth centuries is the subject of Chapter 9.

docs.title: 7.11.1 Kampaṉ and the Cōḻa Age
docs.text:
Under the Cōḻa kings (ninth to thirteenth centuries) Tamil literature combined the devotional heritage of the Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs with the conventions of the Sanskrit court epic. Kampaṉ’s Irāmāvatāram, usually dated to the twelfth century, retells the story of Rāma in some ten thousand stanzas in six books, ending with Rāma’s coronation. It is not a translation of Vālmīki: Kampaṉ reshapes episodes, gives Rāvaṇa a tragic grandeur, and fills the poem with Tamil landscapes and a devotional vision of Rāma as the supreme God. Its passages on the death of Vāli and on Rāvaṇa’s last battle are among the summits of Tamil poetry.

Other works of the period include Jayaṅkoṇṭār’s Kaliṅkattupparaṇi (early twelfth century), a war poem of the paraṇi genre on the Kaliṅga campaign of Kulōttuṅka I, which describes the battlefield as a feast for ghouls; the court poems of Oṭṭakkūttar; and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam, the lives of the sixty-three Śaiva saints, written for Kulōttuṅka II and later added to the Śaiva canon. Villiputtūrār’s Tamil Mahābhārata (fourteenth century) and Aruṇakirinātar’s Tiruppukaḻ (fifteenth century), rhythmically intricate hymns to Murukaṉ, continued the narrative and devotional traditions.

docs.title: 7.11.2 Islamic and Christian Tamil Literature
docs.text: Tamil literature was never confined to one religion. Jains and Buddhists wrote some of its classics, as we have seen; later, Muslims and Christians adopted its forms. Umaṟuppulavar’s Cīṟāppurāṇam (c. 1700), a life of the Prophet Muḥammad in the form of a Tamil epic, with descriptions of Arabian landscapes rendered in the conventions of the tiṇai, is the classic of Tamil Muslim literature.
