The Italian Jesuit Costanzo Beschi, known in Tamil as Vīramāmunivar, wrote the Tēmpāvaṇi (1726), an epic on the life of Saint Joseph, as well as Tamil grammars and a dictionary; and H. A. Kiruṣṇapiḷḷai’s Iraṭcaṇiya Yāttirikam (1894) adapted Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress as a Tamil epic.

docs.title: 7.11.3 Towards the Modern
docs.text:
Modern Tamil literature begins in the late nineteenth century with Vētanāyakam Piḷḷai’s Piratāpa Mutaliyār Carittiram (1879), generally regarded as the first Tamil novel, and with the rediscovery of the classical anthologies. Subramania Bharati (1882–1921) created a modern Tamil poetry. A journalist and nationalist in Madras and later an exile in French Pondicherry, he wrote patriotic songs, devotional poems to Kṛṣṇa, Kāḷī and Murukaṉ, a long poem retelling the humiliation of Draupadī as an allegory of India in bondage (Pāñcāli Capatam, 1912), prose poems influenced by Whitman, and essays calling for the education and freedom of women and the abolition of caste; his language, close to everyday speech yet rich in classical echoes, became the starting point of modern Tamil verse. The short stories of Putumaippittaṉ in the 1930s and 1940s inaugurated Tamil modernism. The little magazine Maṇikkoṭi (from 1933) gathered the first generation of modern short-story writers, among them Putumaippittaṉ, Ku. Pa. Rājagōpālaṉ and the elliptical Mauṉi, and later magazines such as Eḻuttu (from 1959) fostered a Tamil putukkavitai (“new poetry”) in free verse.

The rediscovered Caṅkam poetry became central to Tamil cultural identity and to the politics of the Dravidian movement. Bhāratidāsaṉ (1891–1964), a disciple of Bharati, became the poet of the Self-Respect movement, celebrating the Tamil language and attacking caste and religious orthodoxy, and the Dravidian leaders C. N. Aṇṇāturai and M. Karuṇānidhi wrote plays and film scripts — Karuṇānidhi’s dialogue for the film Parāśakti (1952) is the best-known example — that carried the movement’s ideas to mass audiences. Novelists such as Akilaṉ and Jeyakāntaṉ, both recipients of the Jnanpith Award, wrote of urban and working-class life; Sundara Rāmacāmi, Ambai and others developed a modernist and feminist fiction; and from the 1990s Dalit writers such as Bama and Imaiyam (Chapter 13) gave a voice to communities the older literature had excluded. In 2004 Tamil became the first language to be officially declared a “classical language” by the Government of India.

docs.title: 7.12 Tamil and Sanskrit
docs.text: The relation between Tamil and Sanskrit has been debated, often passionately, since the nineteenth century. The classical anthologies show a literature with its own conventions, owing little to Sanskrit; yet Sanskrit loanwords, North Indian gods and Brahmanical institutions appear in them, increasingly in the later layers, and the Tamil grammarians knew Sanskrit grammar. In the following centuries the two languages lived side by side in the Tamil country: the Pallava and Cōḻa courts patronised Sanskrit as well as Tamil, the devotional poets drew on Purāṇic myth while asserting the equality of Tamil hymns with the Veda, and the maṇipravāḷam commentaries of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas mixed the two languages freely. In the twentieth century the Dravidian movement emphasised Tamil’s independence from Sanskrit and its antiquity, while others stressed the long interaction between them. Modern scholarship, represented by George Hart and David Shulman, tends to see both continuity and independence: Tamil developed a distinct classical literature of its own, which entered into a long and creative dialogue with Sanskrit (Hart 1975; Shulman 2016).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Ramanujan (1967) and Ramanujan (1985): translations of akam and puṟam poetry with essays on the conventions.

  • Hart and Heifetz (1999): the complete Puṟanāṉūṟu.

  • Hart (1975): the cultural world of the poems and their relation to Sanskrit.

  • Zvelebil (1973) and Zvelebil (1974): histories of Tamil literature.

  • Tieken (2001): the case for a late date of the anthologies, to be read with the replies it provoked.

  • Shulman (2016): an introduction to the whole Tamil tradition.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Nīti Literature: Fable, Maxim and Anthology
8.1 Introduction: Worldly Wisdom
docs.text:
Nīti (from the root nī, “to lead”) means “guidance”: prudent conduct, policy, the art of getting on in the world and, for a king, statecraft. A large literature in Sanskrit and the regional languages is devoted to it. It takes three main forms: the fable collection, in which stories, often of animals, illustrate maxims of policy; the gnomic verse (subhāṣita, “well said”), a single stanza expressing a general truth; and the didactic sections of the epics.

Nīti literature is closely related to the science of political economy (arthaśāstra), whose classic text, the Arthaśāstra ascribed by tradition to Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya), is a composite work dated by its most recent translator to c. 50 BCE–300 CE (Olivelle 2013); the text and its political theory are treated in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra (perhaps sixth to eighth century) restates its doctrines in verse. The fables and maxims, however, address a wider audience than kings, and their outlook is practical rather than moralising: they teach how to secure friends, defeat enemies, avoid being deceived and survive misfortune.

docs.title: 8.1.1 The Arthaśāstra and the Literature of Policy
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra itself is a technical treatise, not a work of literature, but its influence on literature was profound. It analyses the state into seven “limbs” — the king, ministers, territory, fort, treasury, army and ally — and treats foreign relations through the “circle of kings” (maṇḍala), in which a king’s neighbour is his natural enemy and his neighbour’s neighbour his natural friend. It discusses the training of princes, the employment of spies, the testing of ministers’ loyalty and the means of dealing with enemies: conciliation, gifts, dissension and force. These categories reappear in the Pañcatantra, in Viśākhadatta’s Mudrārākṣasa (Chapter 3), in the debates of the Kirātārjunīya (Chapter 2), and in the court episodes of countless poems. Kāmandaka’s Nītisāra put this political science into easy verse, and it was studied as far afield as Java and Bali.

docs.title: 8.2 The Pañcatantra
docs.text: The Pañcatantra (“Five Books”) is the most widely travelled work of Indian literature. Its original text is lost; it survives in many recensions, of which the Kashmiri Tantrākhyāyika is considered the oldest, and the work as a whole is usually dated to around the third to fifth century CE. Arthur Ryder’s lively translation of a later recension and Patrick Olivelle’s translation of a reconstructed text are both widely read (Ryder 1925; Olivelle 1997).

docs.title: 8.2.1 Frame Story and Structure
docs.text:
A king, Amaraśakti of Mahilāropya, despairs of his three dull-witted sons. The aged brahmin Viṣṇuśarman undertakes to make them expert in policy within six months, and composes the five books for the purpose. Each book has a frame story into which further stories are inserted, often several levels deep, and the prose narrative is punctuated by verse maxims that characters quote to one another as arguments (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. The five books of the Pañcatantra Book Title Frame story and theme I Mitrabheda (“Breaking of Friends”) The jackal Damanaka, against the advice of his brother Karaṭaka, sets the lion-king Piṅgalaka against his friend the bull Sañjīvaka, who is killed. How enmity is sown between allies II Mitrasamprāpti (“Winning of Friends”) A crow, a mouse, a tortoise and a deer become friends and rescue one another from hunters. The value of alliance among the weak III Kākolūkīya (“Crows and Owls”) A crow minister pretends to defect to the owls, learns their weaknesses and destroys them. War, peace and stratagem IV Labdhapraṇāśa (“Loss of What Was Gained”) A crocodile, urged by his wife, tries to get the heart of his friend the monkey, who escapes by his wits. How gains are lost through folly V Aparīkṣitakāraka (“Ill-Considered Action”) Stories of rash acts, including the brahmin’s wife who kills the faithful mongoose that has saved her child from a snake

Well-known stories include the lion and the hare (who tricks the lion into leaping at his reflection in a well), the talkative tortoise carried through the air by two geese, and the blue jackal who passes himself off as king of the beasts until he betrays himself by howling — all from the first book.

The third book applies the six measures of foreign policy (ṣāḍguṇya) of the arthaśāstra tradition: peace (sandhi), war (vigraha), marching (yāna), waiting (āsana), alliance (saṃśraya) and the double policy of peace with one and war with another (dvaidhībhāva).

docs.title: 8.2.2 The Travels of the Pañcatantra
docs.text:
The westward journey of the Pañcatantra can be traced through a chain of translations (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Some stages in the transmission of the Pañcatantra Date Language Version 6th c. Middle Persian (Pahlavi) Translation by the physician Burzōy for the Sasanian king Khusraw I (r. 531–579); lost c. 570 Syriac Kalīlag wa-Damnag, from the Pahlavi c. 750 Arabic Kalīla wa-Dimna of Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, a classic of Arabic prose and the source of most later versions c. 1080 Greek Stephanitēs kai Ichnēlatēs of Symeon Seth 12th c. Hebrew Version attributed to Rabbi Joel 1251 Castilian Calila e Dimna c. 1270 Latin Directorium vitae humanae of John of Capua, from the Hebrew c. 1480 German Das Buch der Beispiele der alten Weisen, one of the early printed German books 1570 English Sir Thomas North’s The Morall Philosophie of Doni, from an Italian adaptation

Persian versions such as the Anvār-i Suhaylī (fifteenth century) carried the stories into Turkish and back into India, and the French fabulist La Fontaine acknowledged a debt to “Pilpay”, a name derived from the Arabic versions, in his later fables. The stories also travelled east, into Southeast Asian, Tibetan and Mongolian literatures.

docs.title: 8.2.3 The Ethics of the Pañcatantra
docs.text: Readers since the nineteenth century have been struck by how little the Pañcatantra moralises. Its heroes are often the clever rather than the good: the jackal Damanaka wins by slander, the crow minister of the third book wins by treachery, and the hare kills the lion by deceit. Its verses frequently advise distrust — of kings, of enemies who seem friendly, of women, of servants. This is because the book belongs to the tradition of nīti and arthaśāstra, whose subject is how to succeed and survive in a world of competing interests, not how to attain moral perfection. As Patrick Olivelle’s introduction emphasises, the work is a textbook of nīti: its aim is practical intelligence — the ability to read situations, weigh advice and act at the right moment — and its characters use stories and maxims as arguments rather than as simple moral lessons (Olivelle 1997). Its teachings are not without ethical limits: the second book praises steadfast friendship, and many verses condemn greed, cruelty and ingratitude. But its ethics are those of a courtly and commercial world in which survival depends on prudence.

docs.title: 8.3 The Hitopadeśa
docs.text:
The Hitopadeśa (“Beneficial Instruction”), by Nārāyaṇa, a poet patronised by a king Dhavalacandra, probably of eastern India, reworks Pañcatantra material into four books: Mitralābha (“Winning of Friends”), Suhṛdbheda (“Separation of Friends”), Vigraha (“War”) and Sandhi (“Peace”). Its date is uncertain; the oldest manuscript is of 1373, and the work is usually placed between the ninth and fourteenth centuries. With its simple prose and abundant verse maxims it became a standard first reader for students of Sanskrit, in India and later in Europe. Among its introductory verses is a famous chain of causes:

Hitopadeśa, introductory verses

vidyā dadāti vinayaṃ vinayād yāti pātratām | pātratvād dhanam āpnoti dhanād dharmaṃ tataḥ sukham || Learning gives modesty; from modesty one becomes worthy; from worthiness one gains wealth; from wealth, righteousness; and from that, happiness.

docs.title: 8.4 Subhāṣita: The Single Stanza and the Anthologies
docs.text:
The single, self-contained stanza was a favourite form of Sanskrit poetry. Such verses, whether on love, nature, the seasons, kingship, poverty or the follies of mankind, were quoted in conversation and in learned discussion, and collected in anthologies arranged by topic. The anthologies preserve the work of hundreds of poets, many otherwise unknown, and include women poets such as Vijjakā (Vijjā) and Śīlābhaṭṭārikā. The major anthologies are listed in Table 8.3.

Table 8.3. Major Sanskrit anthologies Anthology Compiler Date Remarks Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa Vidyākara c. 1100 About 1,730 verses; compiled in a Buddhist monastery in Bengal Saduktikarṇāmṛta Śrīdharadāsa 1205 About 2,370 verses; Bengal, court of Lakṣmaṇasena Sūktimuktāvalī Jalhaṇa 1258 Yādava court of Devagiri Śārṅgadhara­paddhati Śārṅgadhara 1363 Over 4,000 verses on a wide range of subjects Subhāṣitāvali Vallabhadeva 15th c. (?) Over 3,500 verses; Kashmir Subhāṣita­ratna­bhāṇḍāgāra K. P. Parab (ed.) 1886 A modern printed compilation, often reprinted

Many subhāṣitas circulated anonymously and are still widely quoted. Two examples:

Anonymous; also in the Cāṇakyanīti (vulgate 14.1)

pṛthivyāṃ trīṇi ratnāni jalam annaṃ subhāṣitam | mūḍhaiḥ pāṣāṇakhaṇḍeṣu ratnasaṃjñā vidhīyate || There are three jewels on earth: water, food and a well-turned saying. Only fools give the name “jewel” to bits of stone.

Anonymous

paropakārāya phalanti vṛkṣāḥ paropakārāya vahanti nadyaḥ | paropakārāya duhanti gāvaḥ paropakārārtham idaṃ śarīram || Trees bear fruit for the good of others; rivers flow for others; cows give milk for others: this body too exists for the good of others.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Vidyākara’s Treasury
docs.text:
The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa (“Treasury of Well-Turned Verse”) shows what an anthology was and how one was made. Its compiler, Vidyākara, was a Buddhist scholar of the Jagaddala monastery in northern Bengal, a late Pāla foundation (see Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā), and he made it around 1100, apparently revising and enlarging it later. An earlier and shorter form was published in 1912 from a Nepalese manuscript under the title Kavīndravacanasamuccaya; the full work was edited by D. D. Kosambi and V. V. Gokhale from a palm-leaf manuscript preserved in Tibet (Kosambi and Gokhale 1957), and translated by Daniel Ingalls (Ingalls 1965).

Its some 1,730 stanzas are arranged in fifty sections (vrajyā). It opens, as a Buddhist compiler’s work would, with verses to the Buddha and the bodhisattvas, but passes at once to Śiva, Pārvatī and Viṣṇu, and then through the seasons, the many phases of love, the beauties of women, sunset and moonrise, the court, the village, the virtuous and the wicked, and the poets themselves. That a Buddhist monk should collect erotic and Śaiva verses in this way shows how far kāvya was a shared culture that crossed religious boundaries. The anthology preserves the work of more than two hundred poets, among them Kālidāsa, Bhavabhūti and Rājaśekhara, but many are known only from such collections. Ingalls drew particular attention to a group of poets of Pāla Bengal, such as Yogeśvara, who described the countryside with unusual realism: the village in the rains, the farmer’s fields, the poor man’s household with its leaking roof and hungry children, subjects that the court epic seldom admitted.

The anthologies were also a working tool. Compilers chose and arranged stanzas by topic so that a reader could find a verse for an occasion or a figure; they recorded authors’ names, though the same stanza is often ascribed to different poets in different collections; and theorists and commentators quoted from them. Many poets, including most of the women poets of Sanskrit (Section 2.11), survive only because an anthologist chose one or two of their verses.

docs.title: 8.5 Bhartṛhari’s Three Centuries
docs.text:
The best-known collection of single stanzas is the Śatakatraya (“Three Centuries”) attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly wisdom, the Śṛṅgāraśataka on love and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation. Tradition identifies the poet with a king who renounced his throne, and sometimes with the grammarian-philosopher Bhartṛhari (fifth century), author of the Vākyapadīya; neither identification can be confirmed. The collections exist in many recensions with widely varying contents. D. D. Kosambi’s critical edition (1948) showed that only a core of about two hundred verses is common to the manuscript traditions, and that the rest was added over time (Kosambi 1948). The verses move between ironic observation of human folly, celebration of women’s beauty and desire, and a weary longing for release, and the arrangement in three centuries invites readers to see these as stages of a life.

The Nītiśataka mocks the fool who cannot be taught, the arrogance of the rich, the servility of courtiers and the injustice of fate, and praises learning, courage, friendship and the steadfastness of the good, who do not abandon a task once begun however great the obstacles. The Śṛṅgāraśataka alternates celebration of women’s beauty with warnings against desire as a snare. The Vairāgyaśataka speaks of the humiliations of seeking patronage, the decay of the body, the passing of time that devours all, and the peace of the ascetic who lives in the forest with the earth for his bed and the sky for his garment. Many verses are among the most quoted in Sanskrit, and they were among the first Sanskrit poems translated into European languages, appearing in Dutch as early as 1651.

docs.title: 8.6 Satire: Kṣemendra and Others
docs.text: Worldly wisdom shades into satire, and Sanskrit has a lively satirical literature. The Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra (eleventh century), already met as a theorist of propriety (Chapter 6), wrote a series of satirical poems on the society of his time: the Narmamālā (“Garland of Jests”) on corrupt scribes and officials, the Deśopadeśa (“Advice to the Country”) on rogues, misers, quack doctors, false ascetics and procuresses, and the Kalāvilāsa (“Sport of the Arts”) on the many arts of deception practised by merchants, goldsmiths, astrologers and others. His Samayamātṛkā follows the career of a courtesan guided by a scheming old bawd. These works, with their unsparing portraits of the Kashmiri bureaucracy and of hypocrisy in every class, complement Kalhaṇa’s history and show that Sanskrit literature was not confined to idealised kings and lovers. Later satirists include Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita in the seventeenth century (Chapter 2), and the farces of the theatre (Chapter 3) belong to the same tradition.

docs.title: 8.7 The Cāṇakya Collections
docs.text:
Collections of maxims under the name of Cāṇakya, the minister of Candragupta Maurya to whom tradition ascribes the Arthaśāstra, circulated widely in many versions (Cāṇakyanīti, Vṛddhacāṇakya and others). They are medieval compilations, not works of the historical Cāṇakya, and their contents vary greatly. They deal with friendship, family, wealth, learning, women and the conduct of the wise, often in blunt and sometimes misogynistic terms. A typical verse:

Cāṇakyanīti 3.15 (vulgate)

ekena śuṣkavṛkṣeṇa dahyamānena vahninā | dahyate tad vanaṃ sarvaṃ kuputreṇa kulaṃ yathā || As a whole forest is burned by a single dry tree set on fire, so is a family by a single bad son.

docs.title: 8.8 Nīti in the Mahābhārata
docs.text:
The Mahābhārata contains two great bodies of nīti. The Viduranīti (Udyogaparvan, chapters 33–40) is the counsel given by the wise Vidura to the sleepless king Dhṛtarāṣṭra on the eve of the war: a series of maxims on the marks of the wise and the foolish, the duties of kings, and the dangers of greed and anger, framed by Vidura’s vain attempt to persuade the king to restrain his son.

Far longer are the teachings of the dying Bhīṣma to Yudhiṣṭhira in the Śāntiparvan and Anuśāsanaparvan: on the duties of kings (rājadharma), conduct in times of distress (āpaddharma) and liberation (mokṣadharma), and, in the Anuśāsanaparvan, on gifts, the duties of women and much else. These books are an encyclopaedia of the political and ethical thought of their time, including some of its harshest teachings on caste and gender, and the commentarial and scholarly literature on them is large.

docs.title: 8.9 Wisdom Literature in the Regional Languages
docs.text:
Every Indian literature has its own wisdom verse, often among its most popular and most quoted works (Table 8.4).

Table 8.4. Some wisdom literature in the regional languages Language Works and poets Remarks Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ; Nālaṭiyār; Avvaiyār’s Ātticcūṭi See Chapter 7 Telugu Sumati Śatakamu; Vēmana (c. 17th c.?) Śataka verse (Section 10.3) Kannada Sarvajña (16th–17th c.?) Pithy three-line tripadi verses on everyday life Hindi Kabīr’s sākhīs; Rahīm’s dohās; Vṛnd’s Satsaī Couplets quoted as proverbs Marathi Rāmdās’s Manāce Ślok Verses of instruction “to the mind” Persian and Urdu Saʿdī’s Gulistān (widely read in India); Urdu ghazal couplets Couplets as proverbs (Chapter 12)

docs.title: 8.10 Oral Wisdom: Proverbs, Riddles and Sayings
docs.text: Beside the written collections there has always been a vast oral literature of proverbs, riddles and sayings in every Indian language, much of it never recorded until modern times. Sanskrit theorists recognised the riddle (prahelikā) as a minor poetic form, and riddling verses appear in the epics and the anthologies. In Bengal, sayings ascribed to Khanā, a legendary woman astrologer, give practical advice on agriculture, weather and household life (“Khanār bacan”); in the Hindi region similar agricultural and weather sayings are attributed to Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī. Proverbs about castes, women and neighbouring peoples record social attitudes, sometimes harsh, that rarely appear so openly in written literature. Folklorists since the nineteenth century, Indian and European, have collected such material, and it forms an important link between written literature and the oral traditions discussed in Volume 23 of this series.

docs.title: 8.11 Women, Caste and the Limits of Proverbial Wisdom
docs.text:
Wisdom literature records the assumptions of the people who composed and transmitted it, and these were overwhelmingly men of the upper castes. Many nīti verses in Sanskrit and in the regional languages describe women as fickle, deceitful and in need of constant guardianship, echoing the prescriptions of the Dharmaśāstras; others treat low-caste people as naturally base, or wealth and birth as the measure of worth. Modern editions and popular anthologies often omit such verses, so that the tradition appears more humane than its manuscripts show. The same collections that teach shrewd advice on friendship and enmity also teach contempt for women and the low-born, often in the same metre and with the same wit.

The tradition also contained its own counter-voices. Bhartṛhari’s Vairāgyaśataka mocks the pride of wealth and birth; the Telugu verses of Vēmana and the Hindi couplets of Kabīr ridicule caste distinctions and ritual purity; and the Tirukkuṟaḷ declares that all living beings are alike by birth and differ only in their deeds. Proverbial wisdom, in India as elsewhere, was never a single consistent body of teaching but a store of contradictory sayings, each available to be quoted when it suited.

docs.title: 8.12 Shared Stories: Jātaka and Pañcatantra
docs.text: Many stories occur in both the Buddhist Jātaka and the Pañcatantra family, as well as in Jain collections and in the epics, which shows that all of them drew on a common stock of Indian folk narrative. The tale of the talkative tortoise carried by geese, for example, appears in the Pañcatantra as a warning against ignoring the advice of friends and in the Jātaka as a lesson told to a king who talked too much; the tale of the ass in the lion’s skin, betrayed by its braying, appears in the Jātaka and has close parallels in the Aesopic collections. Each tradition framed the shared stories for its own ends: the Buddhist collection made them illustrations of the virtues of the future Buddha, the Pañcatantra made them arguments in a debate on policy, and the Jain collections made them demonstrations of the workings of karma. The same story could thus carry very different morals in different hands — a fact that warns against reading any one moral as the “meaning” of an Indian tale.

docs.title: 8.13 Indian and Aesopic Fable
docs.text: The Indian fable is often compared with the Greek fables ascribed to Aesop. The two traditions share some stories, and scholars have long debated the direction of borrowing; in most cases it cannot be determined. The most obvious difference is structural: Aesop’s fables are short, self-contained stories with an appended moral, whereas the Pañcatantra embeds its stories in frames and has characters argue with stories and verses, so that each story serves as a move in a debate. Its “morals” are also more pragmatic: cleverness is rewarded even when it is ruthless, and the clever jackal Damanaka is, for much of the first book, its hero. On the Jātaka versions of the shared stories see the previous section and Chapter 5.

  • Ingalls (1965): Vidyākara’s anthology of Sanskrit court poetry.

  • Edgerton (1924): the classic reconstruction of the original Pañcatantra, with a translation.

  • Kosambi (1948): the critical edition of Bhartṛhari’s verses.

  • Kosambi and Gokhale (1957): the edition of Vidyākara’s anthology, with an introduction on its making.

  • Sternbach (1974): a survey of gnomic and didactic literature in Sanskrit.

  • Olivelle (2013): the Arthaśāstra, the political science behind much nīti.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Bhakti and Sufi Poetry
docs.text: pothī paḍhi paḍhi jaga muā, paṃḍita bhayā na koi | ḍhāī ākhara prema kā, paḍhai so paṃḍita hoi || The world has died reading books, and no one has become learned. Whoever reads the two and a half letters of “love” becomes learned. — A sākhī widely attributed to Kabīr (wording varies between collections)

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Bhakti, from the root bhaj, “to share, to partake”, means participation in and loving devotion to a deity. The idea is old: it appears in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad and is central to the Bhagavadgītā. What is new from about the sixth century CE is a great body of poetry, composed first in Tamil and later in almost every language of the subcontinent, in which devotees address God directly, in their own languages, with an intensity of personal feeling unknown to earlier Sanskrit literature.

Textbooks often speak of a single “bhakti movement” that began in the Tamil south and spread northward over a thousand years. John Stratton Hawley has shown that this narrative is largely a twentieth-century construction, shaped by nationalist and Hindi literary historians, and that the various devotional traditions had their own histories and connections (Hawley 2015). This chapter keeps the regional traditions distinct while noting their links. Good anthologies of translations are Hawley and Juergensmeyer (1988), Ramanujan (1973), Ramanujan (1981) and Peterson (1989).

It is also often said that bhakti “democratised” religion and literature. There is truth in this: bhakti poets composed in spoken languages, many of them were women or came from low-ranked castes, and much of their poetry criticises ritualism, caste pride and religious hypocrisy. But the relation of bhakti to social hierarchy was complex, and is discussed at the end of the chapter.

docs.title: 9.1.1 Sanskrit Sources and Bridges
docs.text: Two Sanskrit texts were especially important to the devotional literatures of the second millennium. The Bhagavadgītā provided the classical statement of devotion as a path to liberation and was commented on and retold in the regional languages, most famously in Jñāneśvar’s Marathi Jñāneśvarī. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa, composed probably in the Tamil country around the ninth or tenth century and deeply influenced by the Āḻvārs, told the life of Kṛṣṇa — his childhood in Braj and his love for the cowherd women — with an intensity of emotion that made it the scripture of Kṛṣṇa devotion across India. Its tenth book was retold in almost every Indian language, from Pōtana’s Telugu and Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia to Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese. Through such texts, and through pilgrimage and the movement of teachers, the regional traditions were linked to one another.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār
docs.text:
The earliest Tamil devotional poet whose works survive as a distinct corpus is a woman, Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār, “the Mother of Kāraikkāl”, probably of the sixth century. According to the hagiography in Cēkkiḻār’s twelfth-century Periya Purāṇam, she was Punitavati, the devout wife of a merchant of the port of Kāraikkāl. When a mango she served to her husband was miraculously replaced by Śiva, her frightened husband abandoned her and married again. She then asked Śiva to take away her beauty and give her the body of a pēy, a ghoulish spirit, and in that form she went to Tiruvālaṅkāṭu to sing of Śiva dancing in the cremation ground.

Her works — the Arputat Tiruvantāti (“Wondrous Linked Verses”, 101 stanzas), the Tiruvirattai Maṇimālai and two hymns on Tiruvālaṅkāṭu — are preserved in the eleventh book of the Śaiva canon. They are among the first poems to use forms that became standard in Tamil devotion, such as the antāti, in which the last word of each verse begins the next. Their imagery is unforgettable: Śiva dances among burning corpses, jackals and ghouls, and the poet, emaciated and fearless, delights in the scene. Her iconography as a skeletal woman with drooping breasts and wild hair, seated at the foot of the dancing Śiva, appears in Cōḻa bronzes and temple sculpture. Elaine Craddock’s study and translation examine her poetry and the ways in which her renunciation of conventional femininity has been read (Craddock 2010). She is honoured among the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs, one of only three women in that list.

docs.title: 9.2.2 The Nāyaṉmārs and the Tēvāram
docs.text:
The sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs (“leaders”) are the saints of Tamil Śaivism, listed by Cuntarar in his Tiruttoṇṭattokai and celebrated in the Periya Purāṇam. They include kings, brahmins, merchants, a hunter, a washerman, a potter and the untouchable Nantaṉār. Three poets of the seventh and eighth centuries — Tirunāvukkaracar (Appar), a former Jain monk; Tiruñāṉacampantar (Campantar), a brahmin child prodigy; and Cuntarar, whose relationship with Śiva is that of an intimate friend — composed the hymns collected as the Tēvāram. These hymns (about 800 patikams, generally of ten or eleven stanzas) form the first seven books of the twelve-book Śaiva canon, the Tirumuṟai, which was arranged by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi around the tenth to eleventh century, with the Periya Purāṇam later added as the twelfth.

The Tēvāram hymns are tied to places: they sing of Śiva at particular shrines, and the 270-odd temples so celebrated (pāṭal peṟṟa talam) form a sacred geography of the Tamil country that pilgrims still follow. They also contain polemic against Jains and Buddhists, reflecting the religious competition of the period. Indira Peterson’s Poems to Śiva translates a wide selection with a study of their performance as temple song (Peterson 1989).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Māṇikkavācakar
docs.text: Māṇikkavācakar (“he whose words are rubies”; probably ninth century) composed the Tiruvācakam (“Sacred Utterance”) and the Tirukkōvaiyār, which together form the eighth book of the canon. The Tiruvācakam expresses with great intensity the poet’s sense of unworthiness, his melting love and his gratitude for Śiva’s grace. A Tamil saying holds that “one who does not melt at the Tiruvācakam will not melt at any words” (tiruvācakattukku urukātār oru vācakattukkum urukār).

docs.title: 9.3 Tamil Vaiṣṇava Poetry: The Āḻvārs
docs.text:
The twelve Āḻvārs (“those immersed” in God), who lived between about the sixth and ninth centuries, are the poet-saints of Tamil Vaiṣṇavism. Their hymns were collected around the tenth century by Nāthamuni as the Nālāyira Divyaprabandham (“Four Thousand Divine Compositions”), which the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition of Yāmuna and Rāmānuja treats as a Tamil Veda equal to the Sanskrit (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. The twelve Āḻvārs (approximate, c. 6th–9th centuries) Āḻvār Remarks Poykai, Pūtam, Pēy The three “first” Āḻvārs, authors of the first three Tiruvantātis Tirumaḻicai Author of polemical and devotional hymns Nammāḻvār Author of the Tiruvāymoḻi (1,102 verses), regarded as the greatest of the Āḻvārs Maturakavi Disciple of Nammāḻvār; a single hymn in praise of his teacher Kulacēkarar A Cēra king; devotional verses on Rāma and Kṛṣṇa Periyāḻvār Poems on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ Āṇṭāḷ The only woman Āḻvār; Tiruppāvai and Nācciyār Tirumoḻi Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Devotee of Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam Tiruppāṇ From the Pāṇar caste of bards, regarded as low; a single hymn of ten verses Tirumaṅkai A chieftain; the most prolific Āḻvār (Periya Tirumoḻi and other works)

docs.title: 9.3.1 Nammāḻvār
docs.text: Nammāḻvār’s Tiruvāymoḻi is the theological and poetic centre of the canon. It moves between ecstatic union and the anguish of separation, often in the voice of a girl in love with Viṣṇu, and draws on the conventions of classical akam poetry — the lovesick heroine, her friend, her worried mother — while transforming them into devotion. A. K. Ramanujan’s Hymns for the Drowning is a fine selection in English (Ramanujan 1981).

docs.title: 9.3.2 Āṇṭāḷ
docs.text: Āṇṭāḷ (Kōtai), of the eighth or ninth century, was according to tradition a foundling raised by Periyāḻvār at Śrīvilliputtūr, who refused all human suitors and was united with Viṣṇu at Śrīraṅgam. Her Tiruppāvai (thirty verses) is sung in the voice of a girl waking her friends at dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi for a vow (pāvai) to Kṛṣṇa; it is recited in South Indian homes and temples during that month to this day. Her Nācciyār Tirumoḻi (143 verses) speaks with startling frankness of her bodily longing for the god, including a famous dream of her wedding to him.

docs.title: 9.4 Siddhas, Nāths and Yogic Poetry
docs.text:
Alongside devotional poetry there developed a poetry of yogic and Tantric adepts, often iconoclastic and enigmatic. The Buddhist siddhas of eastern India composed Apabhraṃśa couplets and the Old Bengali songs of the Caryāpada (Chapters 5 and 11) in a deliberately obscure “twilight language” (sandhyābhāṣā) whose images had both everyday and esoteric meanings. The Nāth yogīs, followers of the legendary Gorakhnāth, left Hindi verses (bānī) on the disciplines of the body and breath that strongly influenced Kabīr and the Sants.

In Tamil, the Tirumantiram of Tirumūlar (perhaps sixth to eighth century), the tenth book of the Śaiva canon, combines yoga, Tantric ritual and devotion in some three thousand verses. Later poets known as cittar (siddhas), such as Civavākkiyar and Pāmpāṭṭi Cittar, whose dates are uncertain, mocked idol-worship, caste and the authority of the Vedas in plain and forceful verse, and were associated with alchemy and medicine. Their poetry, popular among ordinary people, was long ignored by literary scholars and has been revalued in modern times.

docs.title: 9.5 The Vīraśaiva Vacanas of Karnataka
docs.text:
In twelfth-century Karnataka, a community of devotees of Śiva gathered around Basavaṇṇa, a brahmin who became chief minister to the Kalacuri king Bijjala at Kalyāṇa. Its members composed short, rhythmic prose-poems called vacanas (“sayings”) in colloquial Kannada, each ending with the poet’s chosen name for Śiva. The vacanas reject temple worship, sacrifice, caste and the authority of the Vedas in favour of the inner experience of the devotee, who wears Śiva’s emblem (the iṣṭaliṅga) on the body. In one of Basavaṇṇa’s best-known vacanas the poet contrasts the rich, who build temples for Śiva, with himself, who has nothing — and declares that his own body will be the temple, its legs the pillars and its head the golden dome — for what is built and stands will perish, while what moves endures (Ramanujan 1973).

Besides Basavaṇṇa (twelfth century) the best-known vacana poets are Allama Prabhu, a mystic of paradox; Dāsimayya; and Akka Mahādēvi, a young woman who abandoned marriage and, according to tradition, clothing, to wander as a devotee of her divine lover “Cennamallikārjuna, lord white as jasmine”. Tradition also preserves vacanas by washermen, ferrymen, cobblers and women of many backgrounds. According to the hagiographies the community at Kalyāṇa was broken up by violence after an inter-caste marriage between the son of a former untouchable and the daughter of a brahmin. A. K. Ramanujan’s Speaking of Śiva introduced the vacanas to readers of English.

docs.title: 9.6 Lal Ded of Kashmir
docs.text:
Lal Ded (“Granny Lal”), also known as Lallā or Lalleśvarī, a Kashmiri woman mystic of the fourteenth century, is the first known poet of the Kashmiri language. Almost nothing certain is known of her life. Tradition says that she was married young, suffered at the hands of her mother-in-law, left home to become a wandering ascetic in the tradition of Kashmiri Śaivism, and went about naked, singing her verses. She is revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal Ārifa, and is linked in legend with the Sufi Sayyid ʿAlī Hamadānī and with Nund Ṛṣi (Shaikh Nūr ud-Dīn), the founder of the Kashmiri Ṛṣi order of Sufis, who is said to have been nursed by her.

Her verses, called vākh (“speech”), are short four-line poems on the search for the self, the futility of ritual, the body as the site of spiritual discipline and the unity of the divine. They draw on the vocabulary of Kashmiri Śaiva yoga — breath, the inner channels, the experience of Śiva as consciousness — but address ordinary listeners in plain, vivid language. They were transmitted orally for centuries before they were written down, so that their wording and even their authorship are uncertain; the first scholarly edition was published by George Grierson and Lionel Barnett in 1920 (Grierson and Barnett 1920). Ranjit Hoskote’s translation and introduction discuss both the poetry and the contested ways in which Lal Ded has been claimed by Hindu, Muslim and Kashmiri nationalist narratives (Hoskote 2011). Her vākhs remain part of everyday Kashmiri speech.

docs.title: 9.7 The Vārkarī Poets of Maharashtra
docs.text:
The Vārkarī tradition centres on the god Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Paṇḍharpūr and on the pilgrimage (vārī) that devotees make there twice a year, singing the songs of the saints. Its first great poet, Jñāneśvar (Jñānadev, traditionally 1275–1296), composed the Jñāneśvarī (1290), a Marathi verse commentary on the Bhagavadgītā in the ovī metre that is regarded as the first great classic of Marathi literature, and the independent poem Amṛtānubhava. His contemporary Nāmdev (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor, composed abhaṅgas in Marathi and songs in Hindi, some of which entered the Sikh scripture. Around Nāmdev gathered poets whom the brahmin literary world would never have admitted. Janābāī, a servant woman in his household, wrote abhaṅgas that speak with intimacy and humour of a Viṭṭhala who helps her with her grinding and sweeping. Cokhāmeḷā (fourteenth century), a Mahar, of a caste treated as untouchable, wrote of the pain of being kept outside the temple and of the “impurity” imposed on his body; his wife Soyarābāī, his sister Nirmalā and his son Karmameḷā were poets too.

Two centuries later the brahmin Eknāth (1533–1599) of Paithan wrote the Eknāthī Bhāgavata, a commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, and comic devotional songs (bhāruḍ) in the voices of village characters. The best loved of all the Vārkarī poets, Tukārām (traditionally 1608–1649/50), was a Śūdra grain dealer from Dehu whose thousands of abhaṅgas turn on his failures, doubts and quarrels with God as much as on devotion. According to tradition the brahmins of his village forced him to sink his manuscripts in the river Indrāyaṇī, and they were restored after he fasted on its bank. His disciple Bahiṇābāī, a brahmin woman, wrote an autobiography in verse that speaks candidly of her husband’s anger at her devotion.

docs.title: 9.8 The Sants and Devotional Poets of North India
docs.text: From the fifteenth century the Hindi-speaking regions produced devotional poetry of two broad kinds. The “Sants” addressed a God beyond form and attributes (nirguṇa), while the poets of Kṛṣṇa and Rāma sang of God with form and attributes (saguṇa). The distinction is useful but not absolute.

docs.title: 9.8.1 Kabīr
docs.text:
Kabīr, a weaver of the Julāhā caste, a Muslim community, of Banaras, is the most famous of the Sants. His dates are uncertain: tradition gives 1398–1518, a span of 120 years that is hard to credit. Modern scholars most often place him c. 1440–1518, though an earlier death, around 1448, has also been argued, notably by Charlotte Vaudeville, whose study sets out the evidence (Vaudeville 1993). His poems — couplets (sākhī), songs (pad) and longer ramainīs — survive in three main collections: the Sikh Ādi Granth, the Rajasthani Dādūpanthī manuscripts and the Bījak of the Kabīrpanth. They differ considerably, and much that is popularly attributed to Kabīr cannot be traced to early sources. The Kabīr of the poems mocks both Hindu and Muslim religious authorities, rejects caste, idol-worship and pilgrimage, and points to the God within, reached through the guru, the Name and love.

Kabīr’s poetry is famous for its “upside-down” language (ulaṭbāṃsī): riddling verses in which the cow sucks the calf, the boat sails on dry land or the fish climbs a tree, images inherited from the Nāth yogīs that unsettle the listener’s assumptions and point to a reality beyond ordinary reason. Equally characteristic are his blunt challenges to religious authority — asking the brahmin why, if he is so pure, he was born by the same path as everyone else, or the mullah why he must shout from the minaret as if God were deaf. His images are drawn from the weaver’s loom, the market and the cremation ground, and his couplets entered the proverbial speech of North India.

docs.title: 9.8.2 Ravidās and Other Sants
docs.text: Ravidās (Raidās; fifteenth–sixteenth century), a leather-worker (Camār) of Banaras, sang of a city without sorrow, “Begampura”, where there is no tax, no fear and no ranking of people, and is today revered by a large community of Dalit followers. Other Sants include Dādū Dayāl (sixteenth century), a cotton-carder of Rajasthan, and Guru Nānak (1469–1539), founder of the Sikh tradition, whose hymns in a mixed Punjabi and Hindi idiom form the core of the Sikh scripture.

docs.title: 9.8.3 Sūrdās
docs.text: Sūrdās, traditionally said to have been blind and to have lived c. 1478–1583, is the great poet of Kṛṣṇa in Braj Bhāṣā. The Sūrsāgar (“Ocean of Sūr”) attributed to him grew over the centuries to thousands of poems; the earliest manuscript, of 1582, contains only a few hundred. The poems describe Kṛṣṇa’s childhood in Braj, the love of the cowherd women (gopīs), and their longing after he leaves for Mathurā (Hawley and Juergensmeyer 1988).

docs.title: 9.8.4 Tulsīdās
docs.text:
Tulsīdās (c. 1532–1623) composed the Rāmcaritmānas (begun 1574), the story of Rāma in Avadhi, in seven books, in stanzas of four-line caupāīs punctuated by dohās. It presents Rāma as the supreme God who became man, and the recitation and staging of the Mānas (as in the Rāmlīlā of Banaras) became central to North Indian religious life. A well-known caupāī from the first book addresses Rāma as a child:

Rāmcaritmānas, Bālakāṇḍa, before dohā 112

maṃgala bhavana amaṃgala hārī | dravau so dasaratha ajira bihārī || May he who is the abode of blessing and the remover of ill, who played in Daśaratha’s courtyard, be gracious.

Tulsīdās’s other works include the Vinaya Patrikā, a collection of devotional petitions, and the Kavitāvalī. His work upholds the order of caste and the duties of women as prescribed in Brahmanical texts, even while it makes devotion to Rāma the supreme value; it has been both venerated and sharply criticised for this.

docs.title: 9.8.5 Mīrābāī
docs.text:
Mīrābāī, a Rajput princess of Merta, traditionally dated c. 1498–1546, is said to have refused to treat her marriage into the royal family of Mewar as binding, regarding Kṛṣṇa as her true husband, and to have defied her in-laws’ attempts to poison her. Her songs survive in oral tradition and in late manuscripts in Rajasthani, Braj and Gujarati; few can be securely attributed to her. One of the most famous begins:

A song attributed to Mīrābāī

mere to giradhara gopāla dūsaro na koī | jāke sira mora mukuṭa mero pati soī || Mine is Giridhar Gopāl, and no one else; he who wears the peacock-feather crown, he is my husband.

The life of Mīrā illustrates the difficulty of separating poet from legend. Almost all that is told of her — the poisoned cup that turned to nectar, the snake in a basket that became a garland, her meeting with Tulsīdās or with the Bengali theologian Jīva Gosvāmī, her final merging into the image of Kṛṣṇa at Dvārakā — comes from hagiographies written long after her death, and her songs were sung and composed by many singers, especially women, in her name. For many of these singers Mīrā was the model of a woman who defied family and husband for the sake of devotion, and her songs have served as a vehicle for women’s protest as well as for piety.

docs.title: 9.9 Bengal, Odisha and Assam
docs.text:
In Bengal the lyric tradition of Jayadeva was continued by Vidyāpati, who wrote in Maithili in the early fifteenth century, and by the poets known as Caṇḍīdās, whose songs on Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa became the basis of the Vaiṣṇava padāvalī. The ecstatic devotion of Caitanya (1486–1534), who popularised the congregational singing of Kṛṣṇa’s names (nāmasaṅkīrtana) and who left only eight Sanskrit verses (the Śikṣāṣṭaka), inspired Bengali biographies such as Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Caitanyacaritāmṛta and the theology of his followers, the Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. In Odisha the “five companions” (pañcasakhā), among them Jagannātha Dāsa, author of the Odia Bhāgavata, composed devotional works in the sixteenth century.

In Assam, Śaṅkaradeva (traditionally 1449–1568) founded a Vaiṣṇava community devoted to the chanting of the Name (ekaśaraṇa nāma dharma), with prayer halls (nāmghar) and monasteries (sattra) that are still central to Assamese life. He and his disciple Mādhavadeva both composed devotional songs (borgīt) and one-act plays (aṅkīyā nāṭ) mixing Assamese and Brajabuli. Each also left a book of devotional verse that is still read in the prayer halls: Śaṅkaradeva the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, on the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, and Mādhavadeva the Nām-ghoṣā, on the chanting of the Name.

The Vaiṣṇava lyric of Bengal, the padāvalī, reached its height in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries with poets such as Jñānadās and Govindadās, who wrote in Bengali and in Brajabuli, a literary language modelled on Vidyāpati’s Maithili. Their songs follow the phases of the love of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa — first attraction, meeting, quarrel, separation and reunion — classified according to the theology of the Gosvāmins, and are still sung in the kīrtan of Bengal, Odisha and Manipur. In Manipur, Vaiṣṇavism adopted in the eighteenth century inspired the rāslīlā dance-dramas, one of the most refined forms of devotional theatre in India.

docs.title: 9.10 The Haridāsas of Karnataka
docs.text: The Haridāsas (“servants of Hari”) were Kannada devotional singers associated with the Dvaita Vedānta of Madhva and the worship of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi and of Viṭṭhala. After Śrīpādarāya and Vyāsatīrtha (fifteenth–sixteenth century) came Purandaradāsa (1484–1564), a wealthy merchant turned mendicant, whose songs in colloquial Kannada, signed “Purandara Viṭṭhala”, are the foundation of the Carnatic musical repertoire; tradition credits him with an impossible 475,000 songs, of which perhaps a thousand survive. His contemporary Kanakadāsa, from the Kuruba shepherd community, wrote songs and narrative poems, including the Rāmadhānyacaritre, an allegory in which the millet eaten by the poor triumphs over the rice of the rich, and the Nalacaritre. A famous legend tells how, refused entry to the Uḍupi temple because of his caste, he sang at the rear wall until the image of Kṛṣṇa turned to face him through a crack.

docs.title: 9.11 The Sikh Scripture
docs.text:
The Ādi Granth (later the Guru Granth Sahib), compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604, contains the hymns of the first five Sikh Gurus and, from the time of Guru Gobind Singh, those of the ninth, arranged by rāga. It also includes compositions of fifteen “Bhagats” of diverse backgrounds, among them Kabīr, Nāmdev, Ravidās, the Sufi Shaikh Farīd and Trilocan. It is thus an anthology of North Indian devotional poetry as well as a scripture (Table 9.2).

Table 9.2. Some contributors to the Ādi Granth (approximate numbers of compositions) Poet Background Compositions Guru Nānak Founder of the Sikh tradition About 970 hymns and verses Guru Arjan Fifth Guru and compiler The largest number of any contributor Kabīr Weaver of Banaras About 540 hymns and couplets Shaikh Farīd Chishti Sufi of the Punjab (12th–13th c.) 4 hymns and about 112 couplets (śaloks) Nāmdev Tailor of Maharashtra About 60 hymns Ravidās Leather-worker of Banaras About 40 hymns

The core of the scripture is the poetry of Guru Nānak (1469–1539), a Khatrī accountant from the Punjab who, after a mystical experience, travelled widely and founded a community of disciples at Kartārpur. His Japjī, recited each morning by Sikhs, opens with a statement of the oneness of God (ik oaṅkār) and meditates on the divine Name, the order of creation (hukam) and the stages of spiritual ascent. Nānak rejected the authority of both brahmins and mullahs, the observance of caste purity and the value of ritual and pilgrimage without inner devotion, and his successors institutionalised these teachings in the communal kitchen (laṅgar), where all sit and eat together. Later Sikh literature includes the vārs of Bhāī Gurdās (c. 1551–1636), which have been called the key to the scripture, and the Dasam Granth associated with Guru Gobind Singh, which contains devotional, martial and narrative poetry in Braj and Punjabi.

docs.title: 9.12 Sufi Poetry in the Indian Languages
docs.text:
The Sufi orders established in India from the twelfth century onwards, notably the Chishtīs, used music (samāʿ) and poetry as means of devotion. Sufi poets wrote in Persian (Chapter 12), but also in the spoken languages of India, and they used the language of human love — often with the soul as a woman longing for the divine beloved — in ways that parallel Vaiṣṇava devotion. The first known poet of Punjabi is a Sufi, Shaikh Farīd (Bābā Farīd, twelfth–thirteenth century), whose verses were preserved in the Sikh scripture. Amīr Khusrau, the greatest Persian poet of the Delhi Sultanate and a disciple of Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ, is credited with a large popular corpus of Hindavi verses and riddles, most of it of uncertain authenticity (Section 12.4). In Avadhi, Sufi poets from Mullā Dāʾūd to Jāyasī wrote long romances that can be read both as love stories and as allegories of the soul’s quest (Section 11.3). In the Punjab, Shāh Ḥusain, Sulṭān Bāhū and Bulleh Shāh (1680–1757) wrote kāfīs of great power, and Wāris Shāh’s Hīr (1766) became the classic Punjabi romance; in Sindh, Shāh ʿAbd al-Laṭīf Bhiṭāʾī (1689–1752) composed the Shāh jo Risālo, the greatest work of Sindhi literature (Section 11.9).

Scholarly Note: Bhakti and Sufism

Bhakti and Sufi poetry share an emphasis on love as the way to God, a critique of external ritual, devotion to the spiritual guide (guru or pīr), and the use of song. Poets and audiences crossed between the traditions, and figures such as Kabīr, Lal Ded and Nund Ṛṣi are claimed by both. Scholars caution, however, against treating these parallels as a simple “synthesis”: each tradition had its own theology, institutions and literary models, and their interaction took many different forms in different regions (Hawley 2015).

docs.title: 9.13 Bhakti, Caste and Gender
docs.text:
Many bhakti poets attacked caste pride and the exclusiveness of brahmin ritual, and the presence among them of women and of people from low-ranked and untouchable castes — Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār and Āṇṭāḷ, Tiruppāṇ and Nantaṉār, Cokhāmeḷā and Janābāī, Ravidās and Kabīr — is one of the most remarkable features of Indian literary history. Their songs gave a voice to people who had no place in Sanskrit learning.

The record is nevertheless mixed. The hagiographies that preserved these poets often domesticated their challenge. In the Periya Purāṇam, the untouchable Nantaṉār is admitted into the presence of Śiva at Chidambaram only after passing through fire and emerging as a brahmin sage; in the legends of Tiruppāṇ the Āḻvār is carried into the temple on a brahmin’s shoulders. Cokhāmeḷā’s abhaṅgas themselves voice the pain of being kept outside the temple door, and the caste rules that excluded him were not overturned by the devotional communities that revered him. Women poets frequently paid for their devotion with social exclusion, and their songs often speak of conflict with husbands and in-laws. Bhakti communities themselves sometimes developed into new castes.

In the twentieth century B. R. Ambedkar argued that the saints, while proclaiming the equality of all before God, had not campaigned against caste as a social system (Ambedkar 1936). Dalit writers and scholars have since reclaimed figures such as Cokhāmeḷā and Ravidās as forerunners of their own literature, while criticising the ways in which upper-caste traditions appropriated them (Limbale 2004). Cokhāmeḷā’s songs were sung for six centuries at Paṇḍharpūr, while he himself, by tradition, lies buried at the foot of the temple steps he was not allowed to climb.

docs.title: 9.14 The Character of Bhakti Poetry
docs.text: Bhakti poetry differs from classical kāvya in language, form and setting: it is composed in the vernacular, usually in short song forms with a refrain and a signature line naming the poet, and it is meant to be sung, often in groups. But the contrast should not be exaggerated. Many bhakti poets were learned, drew on classical conventions — the akam love situations in Tamil, the heroines and seasons of Sanskrit poetry in Braj — and were themselves drawn into courtly culture. The Gītagovinda stands at the meeting point of the two worlds.

docs.title: 9.14.1 Song and Performance
docs.text:
Devotional poetry was composed to be sung, and its forms reflect this. Most songs have a refrain, a short sequence of stanzas and a closing “signature” (mudrā, chāp or bhaṇitā) in which the poet names himself or herself, often in the third person (“Kabīr says”, “Tukā says”, “Mīrā’s lord is Giridhar”). Signature lines made it easy for later singers to compose in a famous poet’s name, which is one reason why the corpora of Kabīr, Sūrdās and Mīrā grew so large. The Tamil hymns were assigned to musical modes (paṇ) and sung in temples by hereditary singers (ōtuvār); the Vārkarī abhaṅgas are sung by pilgrims in procession and in all-night bhajan and kīrtan sessions; the Sikh hymns are arranged by rāga and sung as kīrtan; the Haridāsa songs became the core of Carnatic music; and in Assam the songs and plays of Śaṅkaradeva are performed in the monasteries as part of the Sattriya tradition. Sufi poetry lives in the qavvālī of the shrines. To read these poems only on the page is to miss much of their life. Table 9.3 summarises the major poets discussed in this chapter.

Table 9.3. Major devotional poets: summary Poet(s) Language Date Tradition Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār Tamil c. 6th c. Śaiva Nāyaṉmārs (Appar, Campantar, Cuntarar) Tamil 7th–8th c. Śaiva Āḻvārs (Nammāḻvār, Āṇṭāḷ) Tamil c. 6th–9th c. Vaiṣṇava Basavaṇṇa, Allama, Akka Mahādēvi Kannada 12th c. Vīraśaiva Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Cokhāmeḷā, Janābāī Marathi 13th–14th c. Vārkarī Lal Ded Kashmiri 14th c. Śaiva; revered also by Muslims Kabīr, Ravidās Hindi 15th–16th c. Nirguṇa Sant Guru Nānak Punjabi/Hindi 1469–1539 Sikh Sūrdās, Mīrābāī Braj, Rajasthani 16th c. Kṛṣṇa Tulsīdās Avadhi 16th–17th c. Rāma Caitanya; Śaṅkaradeva Bengali; Assamese 15th–16th c. Kṛṣṇa Purandaradāsa, Kanakadāsa Kannada 16th c. Haridāsa Tukārām Marathi 17th c. Vārkarī

  • Hawley (2015): a critical history of the idea of a “bhakti movement”.

  • Peterson (1989), Ramanujan (1981) and Craddock (2010): Tamil Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava poetry.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Literatures of South India: Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam
10.1 Introduction
docs.text: Tamil, discussed in Chapters 7 and 9, has the oldest literature among the Dravidian languages. Kannada and Telugu became literary languages in the late first millennium, and Malayalam emerged as a distinct literary language in the early second millennium. In each case the first literary works were produced by poets who knew Sanskrit well and who consciously fashioned a “Sanskrit-like” literary idiom for their own language, adopting Sanskrit genres such as the campū and mahākāvya while developing native metres and forms. Sheldon Pollock has made this process of “vernacularisation” central to his account of Indian literary history; the chapters on Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam in Pollock (2003), by D. R. Nagaraj, Velcheru Narayana Rao and Rich Freeman, are a good introduction (Nagaraj 2003; Narayana Rao 2003; Freeman 2003). The three literatures followed broadly similar paths: an early courtly phase in which Jain or brahmin poets adapted Sanskrit genres; a devotional phase in which saint-poets turned to native metres and spoken idioms, often in conscious opposition to the courts; epic retellings that became the most widely read works of each language; close ties with theatre and recitation; and, from the nineteenth century, a modern literature shaped by print, social reform and the movements against caste.

docs.title: 10.2.1 Beginnings
docs.text: The earliest Kannada inscription, at Halmiḍi, is usually dated to about the fifth century, and literary Kannada verse appears in inscriptions from the seventh century. The earliest surviving literary work is the Kavirājamārga (“The Royal Road of Poets”, c. 850), a treatise on poetics produced at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa Nṛpatuṅga (r. 814–878) — probably by the court poet Śrīvijaya rather than the king himself. Adapting Daṇḍin’s Kāvyādarśa, it celebrates the land “between the Kāvēri and the Godāvari” and its people, skilled in poetry, and shows that a literary culture in Kannada already existed. The prose Vaḍḍārādhane (tenth century), a collection of Jain stories, is the earliest surviving Kannada prose work.

docs.title: 10.2.2 The “Three Jewels”: Pampa, Ponna and Ranna
docs.text: The classical age of Kannada literature was dominated by Jain poets writing in the campū form. The first and greatest, Pampa (born 902), called the ādikavi (“first poet”) of Kannada, served Arikesari II, a Cāḷukya chief of Vemulavāḍa and feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas. In 941 he completed both the Ādipurāṇa, on the life of the first Jain tīrthaṅkara Ṛṣabha, and the Vikramārjunavijaya (or Pampabhārata), a retelling of the Mahābhārata centred on Arjuna, whom Pampa identifies with his patron. Ponna, at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, wrote the Śāntipurāṇa on the sixteenth tīrthaṅkara; and Ranna, patronised by the Cāḷukyas of Kalyāṇa, wrote the Ajitapurāṇa (993) and the Sāhasabhīmavijaya or Gadāyuddha (c. 982). The last concentrates on the final day of the Mahābhārata war and the mace-fight between Bhīma and Duryodhana, and like Pampa it gives the defeated Duryodhana a tragic dignity.

docs.title: 10.2.3 Pampa’s Mahābhārata
docs.text: Pampa’s Vikramārjunavijaya illustrates how a regional poet could transform an epic. Its story follows the Mahābhārata, compressed into fourteen cantos of mixed prose and verse, but its hero is Arjuna, who is identified throughout with the poet’s patron Arikesari; the wedding of Arjuna and Subhadrā, the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest and the war are told so as to celebrate a tenth-century Deccan chief. At the same time Pampa gives unusual depth to the defeated. His Karṇa, who learns the secret of his birth on the eve of the war and still refuses to abandon Duryodhana, is a figure of tragic loyalty, and his Duryodhana dies with dignity. The work thus combines panegyric of a living king with a moral seriousness that has made it the foundation of Kannada literature. Pampa’s other work, the Ādipurāṇa, written as a religious duty, shows the Jain world-view within which he wrote: the same poet could compose a Hindu epic for his patron and a Jain sacred biography for his own salvation.

docs.title: 10.2.4 Romance, Grammar and the “Pure” Kannada
docs.text: The Jain court tradition continued for three centuries after Pampa, and it became more varied. Durgasiṃha’s Kannada Pañcatantra (c. 1031) carried the fables into the language in campū form. Nāgacandra (c. 1100), called “the new Pampa”, wrote a Jain Rāmāyaṇa, the Rāmacandracaritapurāṇa, in which Rāvaṇa is a tragic figure and Rāma ends as a Jain ascetic. Nemicandra’s Līlāvati (c. 1170) is a romance of a prince and princess who fall in love through dreams, a Kannada kathā in the manner of Subandhu and Bāṇa (Chapter 4), and Janna’s Yaśodharacarite (1209) retold the Jain tale of the king who sacrificed a cock of flour (Section 4.6) with a sharpness of feeling that made it a school classic. The Kannada language itself became a subject. Āṇḍayya’s Kabbigara Kāva (“The Poets’ Defender”, thirteenth century) was written in a deliberately “pure” Kannada without words borrowed unchanged from Sanskrit, a first sign of the linguistic self-assertion that later histories made much of, and Keśirāja’s Śabdamaṇidarpaṇa (1260), a grammar written in Kannada verse, remained the authority on the classical language into the nineteenth century.

docs.title: 10.2.5 The Vacanas and After
docs.text: The Vīraśaiva vacanas of the twelfth century (Chapter 9) broke decisively with courtly campū. Vīraśaiva poets of the following centuries adapted courtly forms to Śaiva devotion and developed native ones. Harihara (c. 1200) wrote the Girijākalyāṇa, on the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, as a campū in the classical manner, but told the lives of the Śaiva saints in a sequence of poems in the native ragaḷe metre; his nephew Rāghavāṅka’s Hariścandrakāvya (thirteenth century) established the six-line ṣaṭpadi as the great narrative form of Kannada. In the fifteenth century Cāmarasa’s Prabhuliṅgalīle retold the life of Allama Prabhu at the Vijayanagara court. The Jain tradition, too, adopted the new metres: Ratnākaravarṇi’s Bharateśavaibhava (sixteenth century), on the life of the emperor Bharata, son of the first tīrthaṅkara, is a long poem in the song-like sāṅgatya metre. The Haridāsas (Chapter 9), the tripadi verses of Sarvajña, Lakṣmīśa’s Jaimini Bhārata and the Yakṣagāna dance-drama texts (Section 10.6) complete the pre-modern picture (Table 10.1); at the Mysore court of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries poets and scholars wrote both in the old campū manner and in prose.

docs.title: 10.2.6 Kumāravyāsa and the Village Audience
docs.text:
The most widely recited Kannada poem is the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjari (popularly the Gadugina Bhārata) of Kumāravyāsa (Nāraṇappa of Gadag, fifteenth century), a Mahābhārata covering the first ten books of the epic in the six-line bhāminī ṣaṭpadi, a metre that lends itself to musical recitation. Kumāravyāsa presents Kṛṣṇa as the true hero and the epic as a work of devotion, while retaining the full drama of the war, and his vivid metaphors and rapid narrative made the poem a favourite of the gamaka reciters who perform Kannada epics before village and temple audiences, one singing the verses and another explaining them. The gamaka tradition, still alive in Karnataka, shows how the “classics” of the regional literatures reached most of their audience: less through private reading than through public performance.

Basavaṇṇa, Allama, Akka Mahādēvi Vīraśaiva vacanas 13th–16th c. Harihara, Rāghavāṅka, Kumāravyāsa, Cāmarasa, Ratnākaravarṇi Native metres (ragaḷe, ṣaṭpadi, sāṅgatya); epic retellings 15th–17th c. Ananthamurthy, Girish Karnad, Devanoor Mahadeva Navodaya romanticism; Navya modernism; Dalit–Bandaya literature

docs.title: 10.3.1 The Telugu Mahābhārata
docs.text:
Telugu appears in inscriptions from the sixth century, but its literary history begins with the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu. Nannaya, court poet of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarājanarendra (r. 1019–1061) at Rājamahendravaram, began the work; Tikkana (thirteenth century) translated fifteen books, from the Virāṭaparvan to the end; and Errana (fourteenth century) completed the unfinished Āraṇyaparvan. The three are honoured as the “poet-trinity” (kavitrayam). Their Mahābhārata is not a literal translation but a recreation in the campū manner, and it fixed the literary language for centuries (Table 10.2).

Table 10.2. The kavitrayam of the Telugu Mahābhārata Poet Date Contribution Nannaya 11th c. The Ādi and Sabhā books and part of the Āraṇya; honoured as ādikavi Tikkana 13th c. The fifteen books from Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa; celebrated for dramatic dialogue Errana 14th c. The remainder of the Āraṇya book

docs.title: 10.3.2 Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava Poetry
docs.text:
Pālkuriki Somanātha (thirteenth century) wrote the Basavapurāṇamu on the Vīraśaiva saints in the native dvipada metre, a deliberate choice of a “people’s” form over the courtly campū. Bammera Pōtana (fifteenth century) wrote a Telugu Bhāgavatamu much loved for its devotional sweetness, and Annamācārya (1408–1503) of Tirupati composed thousands of songs to Veṅkaṭeśvara, preserved on copper plates. Later, Tyāgarāja (1767–1847) made the Telugu kṛti the centre of Carnatic music.

Pōtana, a farmer-poet who according to legend refused to dedicate his work to a king, made the tenth book of the Bhāgavata, with its stories of the child Kṛṣṇa, and the stories of Prahlāda and of the elephant Gajendra rescued by Viṣṇu, into the most widely memorised Telugu verse. Annamācārya’s songs, addressed to the god of the Tirumala hills in the voices of devotee, lover and philosopher, range from the erotic to the austere, and include songs that declare that the god makes no distinction between the brahmin and the outcaste. Their recovery from copper plates in the twentieth century made them a central part of the Carnatic concert repertoire.

The same temple and court world produced the Telugu padam, a short song for dance. Its master, Kṣetrayya (seventeenth century), who signed his songs with the name of the god Muvvagōpāla, wrote them in the voice of a courtesan addressing the god as her lover and customer: by turns jealous, mocking, tender and businesslike, they make the conventions of the Sanskrit heroine (Section 6.2) speak in colloquial Telugu. They became the core of the repertoire of the temple and court dancers and, later, of Bharatanāṭyam; A. K. Ramanujan, Velcheru Narayana Rao and David Shulman have translated them with an essay on their double world of devotion and the market (Ramanujan et al. 1994).

docs.title: 10.3.3 Śrīnātha and the Vijayanagara Court
docs.text:
Śrīnātha (c. 1365–1441), the most admired poet between the epic and the prabandha periods, wrote the Śṛṅgāranaiṣadhamu (from Śrīharṣa’s Naiṣadhīyacarita), the Kāśīkhaṇḍamu (from the Skanda Purāṇa) and the Palnāṭi Vīracaritramu, a heroic narrative of a local war.

Under the Vijayanagara king Kṛṣṇadevarāya (r. 1509–1529), who himself wrote the Āmuktamālyada — the story of the Tamil saint-poet Āṇṭāḷ, interwoven with a section on statecraft — the Telugu prabandha reached its classic form. The prabandha is a long narrative poem, usually on a Purāṇic theme, rich in description and wordplay. Tradition speaks of “eight elephants” (aṣṭadiggajas) at Kṛṣṇadevarāya’s court, though several of the poets usually named lived later in the sixteenth century (Table 10.3).

Table 10.3. Poets traditionally counted among the aṣṭadiggajas Poet Notable work Allasāni Peddana Manucaritramu (Svārociṣamanusambhavamu) Nandi Timmana Pārijātāpaharaṇamu Dhūrjaṭi Śrīkāḷahastīśvara Śatakamu and Māhātmyamu Mādayagāri Mallana Rājaśekharacaritramu Ayyalarāju Rāmabhadruḍu Rāmābhyudayamu Piṅgaḷi Sūranna Rāghavapāṇḍavīyamu, Kaḷāpūrṇodayamu Rāmarājabhūṣaṇuḍu Vasucaritramu Tenāli Rāmakṛṣṇa Pāṇḍuraṅgamāhātmyamu; hero of later comic legends

Peddana’s Manucaritramu, from a story in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, tells of the pious brahmin Pravara, who rejects the love of the celestial woman Varūthinī, and of the birth of Svarociṣ, father of the Manu Svārociṣa, from her later union with a Gandharva disguised as Pravara. Piṅgaḷi Sūranna’s Rāghavapāṇḍavīyamu tells the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata simultaneously through sustained double meaning, while his Kaḷāpūrṇodayamu, with its intricate plot of mistaken identities, has been called the first Telugu novel in verse. Velcheru Narayana Rao and David Shulman’s anthology gives a vivid picture of this literature (Narayana Rao and Shulman 2002); Yigal Bronner’s study discusses the double-narrative poems (Bronner 2010).

docs.title: 10.3.4 Śataka, Nāyaka Courts and the Modern Period
docs.text:
The śatakamu, a century of verses with a common refrain, was a popular form. The anonymous Sumati Śatakamu and the verses of Vēmana (perhaps seventeenth century), which attack caste, idol-worship and religious hypocrisy in plain language, are still widely quoted (compare Section 8.11).

After the fall of Vijayanagara the centre of Telugu court poetry moved south, to the Nāyaka kings of Tanjavur and Madurai in the Tamil country. At Tanjavur under Raghunātha Nāyaka (r. c. 1600–1634) and his son Vijayarāghava, the king and his poets wrote in Telugu and Sanskrit, and the court developed a new, more playful prabandha, of which Cēmakūra Veṅkaṭakavi’s Vijayavilāsamu, on Arjuna’s three marriages during his pilgrimage, is the classic, as well as Telugu dance-dramas (yakṣagāna) for court performance. Velcheru Narayana Rao, David Shulman and Sanjay Subrahmanyam have reconstructed this court culture, in which the king appeared as a connoisseur and lover rather than a conqueror (Narayana Rao et al. 1992). Women had an unusual place in it. Rāmabhadrāmbā wrote the Sanskrit Raghunāthābhyudaya on her patron, and Raṅgājamma wrote Telugu poetry at Vijayarāghava’s court. Under the Maratha kings who succeeded the Nāyakas at Tanjavur, the courtesan-poet Muddupaḷani wrote the Rādhikāsāntvanamu (eighteenth century), an erotic poem on Rādhā’s jealousy when Kṛṣṇa takes the young Iḷā as his bride, told from the women’s side. When the singer Bangalore Nagarathnamma republished it in 1910, the colonial government banned the edition as obscene, and the ban was lifted only after Independence.

Modern Telugu literature begins with the social reformer Kandukuri Veeresalingam and with Gurajada Apparao’s play Kanyāśulkam (1892), a satire on the sale of child brides; twentieth-century landmarks include Viswanatha Satyanarayana’s Rāmāyaṇa Kalpavṛkṣamu and Sri Sri’s revolutionary poetry.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Beginnings and Maṇipravāḷam
docs.text: The origin of Malayalam is debated. The commonest view is that it developed from the western dialects of Tamil after about the ninth century; others hold that Malayalam and Tamil descend together from a common ancestor and diverged gradually, so that early Malayalam is a sister rather than a daughter of literary Tamil. Whatever its origin, its early literature followed two streams. One, pāṭṭu (“song”), used a Tamil-like idiom and Dravidian metres; its earliest major work is the Rāmacaritam, attributed to Cīrāman and dated variously between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. The other, maṇipravāḷam (“rubies and coral”), mixed Malayalam and Sanskrit, using Sanskrit metres and inflected Sanskrit words. Its rules were set out in the Līlātilakam (late fourteenth century), a treatise in Sanskrit. Maṇipravāḷam literature includes campūs and messenger poems such as the Uṇṇunīlisandeśam (fourteenth century), and poems in praise of courtesans such as the Uṇṇiyacci Caritam.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Eḻuttacchaṉ and the Bhakti Poets
docs.text: Ceṟuśśēri’s Kṛṣṇagātha (fifteenth century), a life of Kṛṣṇa in a simple, musical idiom, prepared the way for Tuñcattu Eḻuttacchaṉ (sixteenth century), traditionally regarded as the father of modern Malayalam. His Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam and Mahābhāratam are composed in the kiḷippāṭṭu (“parrot song”) form, in which a parrot is invited to narrate the story. The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam is still read aloud in Kerala homes during the month of Karkkaṭakam. His contemporary Pūntānam Nampūtiri wrote the devotional Jñānappāna, and Mēlpattūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri composed the Sanskrit Nārāyaṇīyam (1586), a condensed Bhāgavata still recited at Guruvāyūr.

docs.title: 10.4.3 Āṭṭakkatha and Tuḷḷal
docs.text:
In the seventeenth century the dramatic poems known as āṭṭakkatha (“stories for enactment”) were composed for the new dance-drama Kathakaḷi. The prince of Koṭṭārakkara is credited with the Rāmanāṭṭam plays from which Kathakaḷi developed; the Kōṭṭayam Tampurān composed four plays on Mahābhārata themes; Uṇṇāyi Vāriyar’s Naḷacaritam (eighteenth century), in four parts, is regarded as the finest literary text of the genre; and Irayimman Tampi (1783–1856) wrote the popular Kīcakavadham. In the eighteenth century Kuñcan Nampyār created tuḷḷal, a solo performance of Purāṇic stories in rapid Malayalam verse, full of satire on brahmins, landlords and the foibles of Kerala society (Table 10.4).
